compiler the checker: a ninth variant is `error[E0004]: non-exhaustive
patterns` and the crate stops building. The length assertion sits after it for
the case the match is updated and the list is not.

**Rationale.** These are the two mechanisms available, and which one applies is
a property of what is being enumerated, not a preference. Enum variants can be
enumerated by the compiler, and where they can, that is strictly better than a
test: it fails at build time, in every configuration, without being run. A set
of `pub const` items cannot be, so the source is read instead — the same
technique D-157 used on `Ring.tla` and on `cli.rs`'s own match arms.

The general statement, which now covers three findings in one day: **a check is
only as good as the enumeration it sweeps, and an enumeration written by hand
beside its subject is a copy.** D-157 caught copies of a config and a parser;
this catches copies of a crate's own item list. The tell is identical in all
three — the check contains a copy of its subject.

**Consequences.**

- Two new tests in `libs/x86-apic`, four breaks, each red: a register defined
  and left out of `ALL`; a register dropped from `ALL`; a register with no MSR
  anchored to the manual; a `Divide` variant missing from `ALL`. The
  compile-time anchor was demonstrated separately — a ninth variant fails the
  build with `non-exhaustive patterns`, in the crate's production code as well
  as the test.
- The comment claiming `ALL` was complete is now a check that it is.
- `libs/timebase`'s `PLAUSIBLE_HZ` was examined and left. It is a list of real
  clock frequencies to test *against*, not an enumeration of anything the crate
  defines, so there is nothing for it to fall behind.

## D-162 The last unanchored scancode was a misread column — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** D-156 transcribed 68 of about 89 single-byte set 2 make codes and
stopped one short. Backslash read as `0x5C` in the source and the table had
`0x5D`; mainstream references sided with the table, a second primary source
could not be reached that day, and the entry was left out with the reason
written down — *"one code unanchored and said so beats sixty-nine with one
invented."*

**Decision.** It is settled and anchored. There was no conflict.

Brouwer's correspondence table gives the backslash key three codes, one per
set: **`0x2B` in set 1, `0x5D` in set 2, `0x5C` in set 3.** Vetra's
translation table says the same independently — set 2 `5D/F0 5D`, set 3
`5C/F0 5C or 53/F0 53`. The `0x5C` that looked like a contradiction is the
**set 3** value, read out of the wrong column of a table that carries all
three.

This kernel puts the keyboard in set 2 and never in set 3, so `0x5D` is the
code it will see. The table's value was right the whole time; what was missing
was the reason to believe it.

**Rationale.** Worth an entry of its own for what the shape of the mistake
teaches. The source was correct, the table was correct, and the reading was
wrong — which is not a case that "check your sources" catches, because the
source *was* checked. What caught it was going back with a specific question:
not "what is backslash" but "what is backslash **in set 2**, and what is at
`0x5C` if not this". A table with three columns answers a question that names
its column and misleads one that does not.

D-156's refusal to guess was right and is what made this cheap. An asserted
`0x5C` would have been a green test enshrining the set-3 value, and the failure
would have shown up as one key on real hardware — which is exactly the class
D-156 existed to remove.

**Consequences.**

- `libs/ps2-keys`' set 2 table is anchored at **69 codes**, up from 68, and
  nothing in it is now unanchored on purpose. Broken once: the table given the
  set-3 code goes red naming the code and the key.
- Two independent sources are cited in the test's doc comment rather than one,
  and the set the value belongs to is named — which is the detail whose absence
  caused this.
- D-156's "left owed" item is closed.

## D-163 The handle table works through a shared reference, and a promise is a value — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** Phase 6 slice 1 owes D-151: a completion must be able to carry a
handle. Two things stood in the way, and the second was not obvious until the
first was fixed.

**A program's table could not be written to after it was spawned.** `spawn`
built a `HandleTable`, inserted the bootstrap channel and wrapped it in an
`Arc`, and every mutating method took `&mut self` — so from that moment the
table was frozen. The ring is served from the syscall handler, where no
`&mut` to it exists and none can, because the table is reached through a
`BOOTSTRAPS` guard that must be dropped before anything else is taken (D-121).

**Wrapping it in a lock is the obvious answer and the wrong one.** `insert`
takes the handle arena's leaf guard. A table lock taken as a leaf and held
across that is leaf-under-leaf, which is what `lock_leaf` forbids and what the
machine check watches for; a token-bearing lock cannot be taken in trap context
at all, because `ThreadContext::claim` returns `None` inside a handler (D-55).
There is no lock that fits.

**Decision.** The count becomes an atomic and every method takes `&self`.

`id`, `mixer` and `quota` were already immutable after construction. The only
mutable state was `live: usize`, and it becomes one `AtomicU64` holding the two
counts `libs/handle-space`'s `Quota` packs — handles held, and slots promised.
No lock is added, no lock order changes, and `Arc<HandleTable>` becomes usable
exactly where it already was.

**A reservation is a value with a destructor, not a rule.** `reserve_slot`
returns a `SlotReservation` holding an `Arc` to the table. `install` consumes
it and keeps it; every other end — a refusal, a cancellation, a `?` on the way
through, the death of the program holding it — runs `Drop`, which gives the
promise back.

**Rationale.** D-151 asks that "the reservation is returned on every terminal
path", and names three paths. The trouble with a property stated as a list of
paths is that the list is a copy of the control flow, and it stops being a copy
the moment a path is added — which is D-157's rule one level down. Making it a
destructor obligation means the paths do not have to be enumerated in order to
be covered: there is no way to lose one, including down a path nobody has
written yet. Slice 3's dead-program path is the third in D-151's list and needs
no new code here to be correct.

The atomic is also what makes the two counts one word. Moving a promise to a
handle is a single compare-and-exchange, so no reader ever sees a table that
holds neither — which is what a quota check would otherwise be racing.

**Consequences.**

- `libs/handle-space` gains `Quota`: `reserve`, `commit`, `release`, `take`,
  `close`, all total, all host-tested, five deliberate breaks. The overflow
  test found a real edge on the first run — `reserve` could carry a full
  promise half into the held half — and the transitions are now guarded on the
  half being incremented as well as on the limit.
- `insert` splits: `fill` does the arena work and touches no count, so the two
  callers that charge differently share the part that does not.
- **One existing mutation had to be disambiguated.** `install`'s attenuation is
  the same line as `accept`'s, so `xtask/src/mutate.rs`'s one-site rule started
  failing — correctly, and immediately. The pattern now carries its next line.
- `live()` counts held handles and not promises. A check asking what a program
  can *reach* must not count what it has been promised, and the two are
  separately readable for exactly that reason.

## D-164 A wait that is a wait — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25) (amended by D-181)

**Context.** `014` opens by saying this is "the phase that gives the kernel
something to wait for", and D-149 puts the ABI first precisely so the waiting
shape is fixed before a filesystem depends on it. Slice 1 owes the first
operation whose honest answer is *not yet*.

Everything this kernel served through the ring until now answered immediately.
`perform` was a pure function of the submission: echo returns its argument,
uptime reads the clock. There was no in-flight state, and `Queue`'s wait queue
had been built in Phase 5 and never used.

**The obstacle is that a ring-3 thread had no way to stop running.** The
syscall arrives through an interrupt gate (D-96) and is served in trap context,
where `sleep_ns` cannot be used: it takes a `ThreadContext`, and there is none
inside a handler (D-55). A "wait" that could not block would be a spin, and a
program spinning is a program holding a CPU it is not using.

**Options.** Return "nothing yet" and let the program spin; run the ring from a
kernel worker thread that can block; or give the trap path its own way to yield.

**Decision.** All three of the pieces, each in its own place.

**An operation can be deferred.** `Opcode::Timer` is admitted, recorded in a
small pending table, and *not* completed. Its completion slot was reserved at
admission and stays reserved, which is what makes the later completion certain
rather than hopeful — the reservation is the difference between deferring an
operation and dropping one.

**A thread can sleep from a trap.** `thread::sleep_from_trap` is
`retire_from_trap`'s shape without the retirement: mark the caller `Sleeping`
with its deadline, hand the CPU on, and switch **through the frame**, which is
the mechanism preemption already uses and the only place a switch is legal
(D-54). The thread resumes inside its own handler and returns to ring 3 from
there.

**`RingWait` is the call that uses both.** Nothing in flight returns zero at
once — blocking on nothing is a hang. Something already due completes without
sleeping. Otherwise the thread sleeps to the soonest deadline and completes
what it finds on waking.

Not the worker thread. `012` §8 is emphatic that io_uring's history is a march
*away* from its pool, that its bounded pool alone would be `4 × nr_cpus`, and
that this kernel has sixteen thread slots in total. A state machine driven from
the waiting thread needs zero — the direction Linux was travelling and could
not finish because it had to keep every existing filesystem working. This
kernel has none yet, which is the one moment the cheap answer is also the right
one.

**Rationale.** The completion is posted by the kernel *after* the deadline, on
the waiting thread's behalf, so a woken program finds the entry already in its
queue. That is what makes it a wait rather than a poll dressed up, and it is
the shape storage was intended to reuse without changing the ABI. D-169 and
D-181 record the delivered limit: Read has the ring entry but still polls NVMe
inline while `RingEnter` serves it.

`Queue`'s `WaitQueue` is still not what a ring-3 waiter uses, and this entry
says so rather than leaving it looking like an oversight: `WaitQueue::wait`
takes a `ThreadContext`, so it is the mechanism for a *kernel* thread waiting
on a ring. A ring-3 thread waits through the scheduler, because that is where a
trap-context switch is legal.

**Cancellation is an operation, not a substitute.** `Opcode::Cancel` has its
own reservation and its own completion. The operation it ends still gets
exactly one terminal completion, carrying `STATUS_CANCELLED` rather than a
result. `012` §8 names the double-completion class behind two io_uring CVEs,
and this is the shape that has no room for it. A cancellation naming nothing is
`STATUS_NOT_FOUND` and **not an error** — io_uring's `-EALREADY` — because an
operation that completed between the submission of the cancel and its service
is a race the program cannot avoid.

**Consequences.**

- Three opcodes: `Duplicate`, `Timer`, `Cancel`. Seven statuses where there
  were two.
- Six machine checks, seven deliberate breaks, four mutations.
- `sleep_from_trap` returns whether it actually yielded. A machine with no
  other thread to run, or a clock that never started, gets an honest zero
  rather than a hang — a wait nobody can end is worse than no wait.
- The pending table holds one entry per submission slot, which is not
  arbitrary: an in-flight operation occupies a submission's worth of admission
  until it completes, so a larger table could never be filled.
- `Pending` is a timer and nothing more. The original expectation was that a
  block-device operation would become its second kind; it did not. D-41 still
  forbids generalising the table before deferred device service actually
  supplies that caller.

## D-165 A check that could not fail, found by breaking it — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** Slice 1's most important property is D-151's: **a promised handle
slot is given back on every terminal path.** A leak there is not a crash. It is
a table that shrinks by one every time a program asks for something it cannot
have, and it surfaces hours later as a process that cannot open anything.

The check written for it set up a table with room for exactly one handle, put
the source handle in it, and submitted three operations that were refused. It
asserted afterwards that nothing was still promised, and it passed.

**It could not have failed.** With the table already full, all three refusals
happened *at the reservation* — `reserve_slot` returned `QuotaExhausted` and no
promise was ever made. `promised() == 0` was true because nothing had been
promised. Deleting the destructor whose entire job is returning promises left
the check green.

**How it was found.** By D-28, and only by D-28. The break was applied, the
boot went red — and it went red on a *different* check, which is what gave it
away. `a completion cannot widen what was offered` also asserts `promised() ==
0`, and its table has room, so its refusal happens after a promise is taken.
The check that was *about* the property could not see it; a check that
mentioned it in passing could.

**Decision.** The check is rebuilt so that every submission reserves and then
fails, at a different point each time: at the lookup (a value naming nothing of
this table's), at the right (a handle held without `DUPLICATE`), and at the
attenuation (asking for more than is held). The table is deliberately roomy,
which is the opposite of the instinct that produced the first version.

The full-table case is not deleted — it is a different claim and gets its own
check. *A full table refuses at submission* is about the moment the program is
told, which D-151 argues is the whole point of reserving at all. Merging the
two is how the first one came to be unfailable: it was trying to be about both.

**Rationale.** This is D-155's rule — choose inputs where the answers differ —
arriving from a direction that rule did not cover. There the inputs made two
*answers* indistinguishable. Here the input made the code path under test
**unreachable**: the check never ran the lines it was written about. That is
worse, because no amount of staring at the assertion reveals it. The assertion
is correct.

The general form, and it is the third thing this rule has cost:

> **A check must reach the code it is about.** Set-up chosen to make the failure
> easy to trigger can make it impossible to reach — a full table refuses early,
> a closed channel refuses early, an unmapped page faults early. If the refusal
> under test is the *second* thing that could go wrong, the input has to get
> past the first.

`005`'s testing section carries it.

**Consequences.**

- One check rebuilt, one check added, and the break that found it is now a
  mutation, so it cannot rot back.
- Two checks now assert `promised() == 0` from different set-ups, which is the
  redundancy that caught this and is worth keeping.
- Nothing in the kernel changed. The destructor was correct; the check could
  not show it.

## D-166 The time is a page, not a call — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25) (amended by D-181)

**Context.** D-152 settled the shape of a published clock and D-149 put it in
this phase, before a filesystem exists to want it, because a call that becomes
a load later is two doors to one operation for ever. `sys_clock_get` was OWED
over `libs/timebase` (D-114): the mechanism was complete and the door was
missing.

**Decision.** One page, mapped read-only into every program at a fixed address,
with two regions.

**The constants region has no sequence counter and needs none.** Version, page
size, counter rate — written once, before the page can be mapped anywhere, and
never again. Zircon's arrangement, and it removes the most error-prone reads
from the protocol entirely.

**The clock region carries Linux's seqlock**, both barriers written out even
though on x86 the store-store one is a compiler barrier and no instruction —
because an aarch64 port should not have to rediscover that it is not free
everywhere.

**D-181 corrects the claimed reason this clock has no periodic update.** Linux
rewrites a published clock for adjustable or idle-stopping sources and for NTP.
D-57 deliberately does *not* veto calibration when CPUID omits invariant TSC:
two believable, agreeing measurement windows are accepted and the missing bit
is warned about. The conversion and origin remain fixed for the supported
uptime, so the page and `time::now_ns` compute the same value, but on a machine
whose rate later changes both clocks are only as steady as that counter. The
mode permits revocation; suspend, NTP adjustment and an instability detector
remain absent.

**The base is split, and the obvious form is wrong.** `base_ns << shift`
overflows a `u64` after about eight seconds of uptime at a 1 GHz counter's
shift, so "store the nanoseconds pre-shifted" cannot be taken literally. What
is stored is whole nanoseconds beside a carried *fraction* of one, always below
`1 << shift`. Linux splits it the same way. The fraction is not decoration: a
clock updated at a kilohertz that dropped it would fall a microsecond behind
every second.

**The revocation gate is why the Uptime fallback stays.** `mode` is the reader's
permission to use the page at all, and D-152 requires the fallback to be always
reachable — so the ring's `Uptime` opcode is not decoration either, and the
check that revokes the clock asks the ring for the time on the way past.

**Rationale, and the three things that were wrong first.**

*The page exists even when the clock does not.* The ABI says there is a page at
`WIZ_TIME_ADDRESS`, and a program that reads it and takes a page fault has been
lied to. So the page is built at boot whatever the clock did, `mode` is
`MODE_NONE` on a machine that never calibrated, and a spawn that cannot show it
is refused rather than quietly given a space with a hole in it.

*The preemption precondition was measured in the wrong place.* D-152 asks that
"the writer is not preemptible" be established rather than assumed, and the
first counter recorded **calls** made with the interrupt flag set. The check
built on it failed immediately — correctly, because a kernel thread calling
`publish` with interrupts on is fine: the guard clears the flag before the
counter goes odd and restores it after it goes even. What matters is the
*window*, so that is what is counted now.

*The odd marker has no witness on one CPU.* Deleting the write that marks the
window open left every check on this page green. Nothing else runs between the
two increments — the guard clears the interrupt flag — so there is no observer.
This is the class D-154 handles by building the seam and checking what can be
checked: the writer now reads its own marker back and counts a failure, so a
writer that stops announcing itself is caught by the only observer that exists.
A second CPU would give a better one.

**Consequences.**

- `libs/timebase` gains `resume`, `advance`, `from_parts` and `Seq`, all
  host-tested, four deliberate breaks. The drift test needed two attempts: the
  first chose a step of 3,192,000 ticks at 3.192 GHz, which is exactly a
  millisecond, so the conversion had no fraction to lose and dropping the carry
  left it green — D-155's rule, hit again by the person who wrote it down.
- Six machine checks, six breaks, all red. The page-and-kernel-clock check is a
  **sandwich rather than a tolerance**: the page's reading is taken between two
  calls and must lie between them, so a multiplier or shift off by one fails
  immediately and no slack hides it.
- `sys_clock_get` moves from OWED to MAPS and is now a load. The sysdep tally
  is 5/10/1 where it was 4/11/1. This is the historical one-axis transition;
  D-181 records the checked monotonic reader and missing fallback/realtime
  semantics as PARTIAL/PARTIAL.
- `WIZ_CALL_CLOCK_GET` is **deleted** from the ABI, and `WIZ_CALL_RING_WAIT`
  takes 3. At this decision the speculative owed calls renumbered, which cost
  nothing because none was implemented. D-181 later deleted those unimplemented
  call numbers instead of preserving a fictitious future ABI.
- The C header gains the time page's address, version, modes, offsets and
  layout, and the cross-check compares **every one of them** against
  `timepage.rs`, including each field offset. A `mode` read from the wrong
  place is a clock that reads as revoked, or worse as usable when it is not.
- One more entry on D-46's KASLR ledger: `TIME` at `0x0000_1000_0000_0000`.
  It costs nothing while no two programs share a table (D-113), and it is what
  makes the address a `#define` rather than a lookup.

## D-167 A dead program's work is finished, not forgotten — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** D-153 said an operation in flight becomes one more thing the
zombie holds, and `012` §10 added the part the original entry did not say:
**exit must be a wait, not a signal.** io_uring cancelled out of line for six
years and the symptom was mount points staying busy after the process had
exited.

Until slice 1 there was nothing to say this about. Every operation this kernel
served completed inside the call that submitted it, so a retiring program had
no work in flight by construction. `Opcode::Timer` changed that, and D-153's
debt became reachable in the same commit that made it possible.

**The hazard is specific.** A retired program's ring pages go back to the
allocator in `reclaim`. An operation still in flight is one that will later
write a completion, and the page it would write into is about to be somebody
else's. That is not a leak; it is a write to freed memory, arriving at whatever
time the operation happens to finish.

**Decision.** The ring is quietened before anything it could touch is released.

`Queue::abandon` ends every operation in flight and **posts the completion it
was owed**, into pages the zombie still holds. When it returns, nothing is left
that could reach them, and `reclaim` drops the ring immediately after.

Not "marked abandoned and left". The completions go into a ring nobody will
read, and that is not waste: posting them is what *spends the reservations*.
A reservation never spent is a ring whose accounting says work is outstanding
for ever, which is invisible until something asks — and slice 5's device will
ask.

**No grace period and no refcount.** `012` §10 names the third consequence and
it is the easiest to violate by accident: a teardown that waits for a count to
reach zero "eventually" is exactly the out-of-line cancellation that took
io_uring six years to undo. Every operation this kernel has today ends
synchronously, so one sweep is the whole wait. An operation that could not — a
read the device has already been told to do — is slice 5's, and the shape it
must fit is this one: the sweep ends when `is_quiet` is true and not before.

**The handle promise needs no code at all**, which is the part worth recording.
D-151's third terminal path is "a retired program's", and D-163 made the
reservation a value holding an `Arc` to its table. So a program that dies
holding a promise leaves the table alive exactly as long as the promise does,
and the promise's destructor gives the slot back and lets the table go. The
teardown drops its reference and the table simply does not leave. "The zombie
holds every resource any in-flight operation can still touch" is true by
construction rather than by remembering, which is what D-163 predicted and this
slice is the confirmation of.

**Rationale.** Three checks, and each is a different claim.

*Work in flight is ended before the ring is released* asserts the completions
arrive, say `CANCELLED` rather than pretending to be results, and — the part
that matters — that `outstanding` returns to zero. It also sweeps twice, so
teardown is idempotent: `reclaim` is not the only path that can reach a zombie.

*A promise outlives the program that made it* observes the table through a
`Weak`, which is the only way to ask "is it still there" without being the
reason it is, and then **uses** it: the promise is spent against the orphaned
table, because surviving and working are different claims. Then the `Weak` must
stop upgrading, because a table nothing will ever free is the other failure.

**Consequences.**

- `Queue::abandon` and `Queue::is_quiet`; `Reclaimed` gains `abandoned`.
- Two machine checks, three breaks, all red. Breaking the promise's `Arc` —
  giving the reservation a table of its own — reddens four checks at once,
  which is the redundancy D-165 argued for doing its job.
- The ordering in `reclaim` is now load-bearing and says so: quieten, then drop
  the table, then drop the ring, then release the space.
- Slice 5 inherits the shape rather than the code. A polled NVMe read cannot be
  ended by writing a completion — the device has the command — so `abandon`
  will have to wait for the controller there. What it must not do is return
  before `is_quiet`.

## D-168 A driver claims a device, not a port range — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** D-77 closed half an authority debt and named the other half. A
port claim proves **exclusivity** — nobody else drives these ports — and says
nothing about **entitlement**, about whether the claimant is the driver for
whatever is behind them. The port registry cannot answer that, because a port
range is not a device: it has no identity, no vendor, and no way to be asked
what it is.

`014` lists it as the first of the phase's open decisions: *does a device claim
replace a port claim, or sit above it?*

**Decision.** It contains it. A driver claims a **function** — a bus, device
and function triple — and the claim carries every window that function decodes
with it. A bare port claim inside a claimed device's I/O window is then refused
by the port registry itself, because the device already holds those ports.

Not "authorises claiming", which is the alternative `014` names, because that
leaves two mechanisms and a gap between them: a driver could hold a device
capability and never claim the ports, or claim ports it has no device for, and
nothing would connect the two. One object holding both makes D-138's
permanence a property of the device rather than of every range separately.

**Claims are permanent**, exactly as port claims are. There is no release, so
there is no window in which a device is half-claimed, and a refusal strands
nothing: the holder is unaffected and the refused caller has taken nothing.

**Rationale, and five things the specification decides rather than taste.**

**CF8/CFC, not ECAM.** ECAM needs an MCFG table; QEMU's i440fx publishes none
and VMware emulates a 440BX. The 1992 mechanism is the only one guaranteed on
**both** targets D-18 makes this project answer to, and it reaches every byte a
read-only driver needs. An ECAM path later is purely additive (`012` §2).

**Enumeration must recurse, and the check machine had to be given something to
recurse into.** q35 as QEMU ships it has no PCI-to-PCI bridge, so a kernel that
scanned bus zero and stopped would have found all six functions, reported a
plausible number, and passed — while being unable to find a controller on a
real machine, because VMware places functions behind `pciBridge0`–`pciBridge7`.
The check machine now gets a `pci-bridge`, and the survey counts **buses**, not
only functions: the function count says nothing about descent and the bus count
says everything.

**A bridge has two base address registers, not six.** A type 1 header puts its
primary, secondary and subordinate bus numbers where a device's third register
would be. A claim that read six would decode those bus numbers as a window and
then *probe* it — writing all ones into the register that says which bus is
behind this bridge. The probe restores what it found, so nothing downstream
would necessarily notice; the check asserts the claim decodes two.

**The window size is complemented in the register's own width.** The first
version had one `window_size` taking "pass all ones for a narrow register",
and the I/O path then complemented a thirty-two-bit mask in sixty-four bits and
answered eighteen quintillion. Caught by a doctest on its first run. It is two
functions now — `memory_window_size` with an explicit `wide`, and
`io_window_size` returning a `u16` — because a width you must remember to pass
correctly is a width that will be passed wrongly.

**Bus master is set by the thing that holds the claim.** Without it a
controller cannot DMA, queues never advance, and *there is no error anywhere to
read* (`012` §2). It is the most expensive bit in this subsystem to forget, so
the claim owns it rather than a driver that might not.

**The lock check earned its keep on the first boot.** `pci::init` took this
module's guard and then called `port::claim_pair`, which takes the port
registry's — leaf under leaf, which is exactly what `lock_leaf` forbids and
what D-121's machine check watches for. It went red on the first run, naming
both sites. The claim happens outside the guard now.

**Consequences.**

- `libs/pci-config`: address encoding, header offsets, class codes, header
  types, BAR decoding, window sizing. Fifteen host tests and three doctests,
  five deliberate breaks, all red.
- `wost::arch::pci`: the two ports, claimed as a pair (D-138), and the probe
  that restores what it found. A register left holding `0xFFFF_FFFF` is a
  device claiming four gigabytes at the top of memory, and the next thing to
  enumerate believes it.
- `wost::arch::port::claim_span`: a run whose length the *machine* supplies.
  `claim_block` wants a constant, which is right for a PIT with three ports and
  a UART with eight; a device's I/O window is whatever the probe says.
- `kernel::pci`: an iterative walk over a bus worklist, each bus visited once —
  recursion would put a bridge topology on a thirty-two-kilobyte stack, and a
  bridge that names itself as its own secondary bus is a cycle.
- Three machine checks, five breaks, all red.
- **The `Device` is a kernel-side capability, not yet a handle.** It is
  obtainable only from the registry, exactly as `Port<T>` is, which is the same
  discipline one level up. Slice 8 makes it resolvable internally through devfs
  but does not create a handle. A user-visible Device handle is explicitly
  post-compiler-gate work in D-184's register, not pre-Wizzy foundation debt.

## D-169 An NVMe controller, polled, and a disk with something on it — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25) (amended by D-181)

**Context.** `012` §2 disqualified virtio-blk rather than deprioritising it:
VMware exposes no virtio device of any kind, so under D-18 it could never close
a phase, and none of the virtqueue work carries to a driver that could. AHCI
spans both hosts and is a worse first driver for the same prerequisites. NVMe
is the only overlap between the two boot targets with a freely published
specification.

**Decision.** One controller, one I/O queue pair, polled, read-only.

**Polled is what makes it affordable.** `Create I/O Completion Queue` with
`IEN = 0` disables interrupts for that queue, which removes "this kernel has no
interrupt sharing" from the critical path entirely. The cost is that a read
spins. Slice 9 gave Read a submission/completion shape but did not make device
service deferred: `Queue::read` still reaches the VFS and polls NVMe inline
while `RingEnter` serves the queue. Only Timer currently exercises in-flight
completion.

**`CAP` is read, never assumed.** The queue size, the doorbell stride, the
timeout and the page-size range all come from it, and every one changes what a
correct driver does. `012` §11 records that VMware's values are unmeasured, so
a driver that assumed QEMU's would be a driver that fails the phase's
definition of done.

**The ring parallel is a trap, and the arithmetic is shared without the
structure** (`012` §3). Four things differ from `kernel::queue` and each is a
bug if assumed away: there is no completion tail to read, so entries are found
by their **phase tag**; completions are matched by **command identifier**, not
by slot; **capacity is `size - 1`**, whose symptom is a hang; and the doorbell
is **write-only**, so the tail is shadowed. `libs/nvme` holds the arithmetic;
there is no shared `Ring<T>`.

**Rationale, and the two places a check could not have failed.**

**A disk of zeros proves nothing.** The first version of the read check read
block zero out of a zero-filled backing file and compared it to zero — which is
what a buffer nobody wrote also contains. So `xtask` writes a **different
signature into every block**, and the check reads four of them: a driver that
ignored the logical block address would answer block zero to every request and
pass against a uniform disk. D-155's rule applied to a corpus rather than to an
argument.

**Reading one block too many is invisible at the front.** Every count in this
specification is zero-based, so `CDW12` carries `blocks - 1`. A driver that
sent the count unadjusted reads *two* blocks, and the first block's bytes are
still exactly right — the check went green against that mutation. It now clears
the buffer, reads one block, and requires the bytes **after** it to still be
zero. The extent of a read is only observable past its end.

**The queue wrap needs more commands than the queue has entries.** The phase
tag flips on every wrap, and a driver that never flipped it works perfectly
until the first one and then sees either every entry or none. The check does
three times the queue's depth, because the seam is the only place the defect
exists.

**Consequences.**

- `libs/nvme`: register offsets, `CAP` decoding, the `size - 1` capacity rule,
  doorbell placement, command building, completion decoding, and PRP
  construction. Thirteen host tests and three doctests, six deliberate breaks,
  all red.
- `kernel::nvme`: the initialisation sequence, `Identify Namespace`, one I/O
  queue pair with `IEN = 0`, and a read. Four machine checks, five breaks, all
  red.
- **The register window is mapped uncacheable**, which `map_device` already
  chose, and there is now a check that says so. `012` §2 names write-back
  mapping as a silent, hard-to-debug bug; an emulator forgives it and hardware
  does not, which is exactly the class of thing that has to be caught here.
- The check machine gains an NVMe controller and a two-megabyte backing file.
  The file is the *machine's*, not the disk image's: nothing on it is booted
  and the kernel writes nothing to it.
- The signature is written by `xtask` and looked for by `selftest.rs`, which is
  two transcriptions of one table — so a host test compares them (D-158).
- **A read still spins in the serving thread.** `POLL_ATTEMPTS` bounds it,
  because a controller that does not answer is a controller to report, and on a
  machine without bus master enabled a hang is the only symptom there is.
  D-188, D-199, D-200 and D-245 later supplied teardown and deferred VFS
  ownership; only replacing polled service with a deferred or interrupt-driven
  throughput policy remains stopped behind PW-704's measured workload trigger.

## D-170 FAT32, an oracle, and a block layer that is one trait — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** `012` §1 chose the format on the **corpus**, not on the code, and
was blunt that the roadmap's premise was wrong: measured against GRUB's own two
readers — one project, one style, both read-only — FAT is 673 lines to ext2's
~772. Thirteen per cent. What decided it is that `xtask` already builds a FAT32
volume through `fatfs`, two volumes built seconds apart hash identically, every
pure-Rust ext2 image builder fails to run on this machine, and the reference
read-only ext2 crate generates its corpus by shelling out to `mkfs.ext2`, which
D-16 forbids.

`014` left two decisions open that this slice must take: **is the block layer a
trait or a concrete NVMe**, and **does a page cache exist in this phase**.

**Decision.**

**The block layer is a trait, and it belongs to the reader.** `libs/fat32`
defines `Sectors`, because that is the parameter the reader needs — not a
speculative kernel-side abstraction over a device this kernel has one of
(D-41). The host backs it with a byte slice and the kernel with the controller,
and the *same reader* runs over both. That is not a convenience: it is what
makes an oracle possible at all.

**The oracle is `fatfs` on the host.** Two independent implementations of one
format over one corpus, and the disagreement between them is the test. `012` §1
called this "a better arrangement than a dependency", and the reason is exact:
a dependency cannot disagree with itself.

**No page cache.** `014` carries it as a deliberate hole and the reasoning
holds: reading a directory means reading the same sectors repeatedly, whether
that is affordable is a *measurement*, and the measurement does not exist. A
cache is a decision for whoever has the numbers. The volume is also mounted per
call rather than kept, for the same reason — a boot sector is one sector and the
volume is not going anywhere.

**Rationale, and the corpus doing the work.**

`012` §1 warned that FAT's traps are differently shaped rather than fewer, and
three of them shaped the checks:

- **A cluster number is biased by two**, so the sector of a cluster is
  `first_data + (cluster - 2) * per_cluster`. Forget it and every file is read
  two clusters late, with no error anywhere.
- **A FAT32 entry is twenty-eight bits.** Compare all thirty-two against the
  end-of-chain marker and a chain that has ended is followed into whatever the
  reserved bits were — which is a cluster number, and reads as data.
- **A directory ends at a name beginning zero; `0xE5` is one deleted entry.**
  Confusing them either loses every file below or resurrects deleted ones.

**Four machine breaks passed at first, and the corpus is why.** The end-to-end
checks could not reach the twenty-eight-bit mask (the corpus's reserved bits are
zero), the file-size bound (the check's buffer was cut to the file's length),
the deleted marker (the corpus had no deletions) or the split first-cluster
field (every cluster fits sixteen bits). All four are caught by host tests over
synthetic entries, which is the right division — but two of them were reachable
on the machine for almost nothing, and a real disk is where a real disk lives:

- The corpus now creates a file and **deletes it**, leaving an `0xE5` slot
  *between* live entries. A reader that stopped there loses everything below,
  and the check counts the survivors.
- The read check now offers **a whole sector of buffer for a file that is not
  one**. A reader bounded by the cluster hands back its previous occupant's
  data, and a buffer cut to the file's length could never see it.

That is D-165 again — a check must reach the code it is about — arriving
through the *corpus* rather than through the set-up.

**Consequences.**

- `libs/fat32`: BPB parsing, the table, directory decoding, chain walking,
  per-call offsets, path resolution. No allocation and no panic on hostile
  input: every length checked against what remains, every cluster against the
  data area's bounds, and every walk bounded — a FAT is a linked list a hostile
  volume can make circular, and following one is a hang.
- Eight host tests in the crate, eight more in `xtask::image::corpus` including
  the oracle, four machine checks. Six breaks, all red; two of them made
  reachable on the machine by improving the corpus.
- **512-byte sectors only**, and a volume that says otherwise is refused rather
  than misread. That is what lets every buffer be a fixed array: supporting 4096
  would need a caller-supplied buffer everywhere or an allocator, and no volume
  this project builds or boots uses one.
- The volume sits at **sector 2048** of the namespace, where a partition table
  would put it, and the reader takes a base rather than assuming zero — a reader
  that could not be given an offset is one nothing can be put in front of.
- Three transcriptions meet: the corpus's names and contents, the kernel's copy
  of them, and the base sector stated in two files. A host test compares all of
  them (D-158).
- **The corpus still has one writer.** `014` budgets for it: until a
  foreign-produced FAT32 image is obtained, a shared misreading of the
  specification would pass both implementations. That is the honest limit of an
  oracle built from one tool.

## D-171 A VFS over directories, and a resolver with no way up — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** `012` §7 was explicit that Linux's shape is the wrong one to copy:
its five operation tables and the dcache exist to serve a global namespace with
a mount tree and a shared lookup cache, and this kernel has none of the three.
Importing the shape without the requirements is how a VFS becomes premature.

`012` §5 was equally explicit about the resolver, and the reason is a security
property rather than a design preference.

**Decision.**

**The abstraction is over directories.** The delivered surface resolves,
reads and enumerates. Mutation remains reserved for the future write path
rather than appearing as an inert method. This compact surface replaces five
Linux-style operation tables because path resolution is the code that must be
backend-agnostic.

**Enum dispatch while every backend is in-kernel.** Monomorphic,
allocation-free, and exhaustively checked by the compiler when a fourth
arrives. Promotion to dynamic dispatch waits for a backend that must be added
*without editing the enum*, which here means a filesystem living in userspace —
and at that point the abstraction is the protocol and the trait is irrelevant.

**The resolver cannot ascend, and that is a property of its input rather than a
check it performs.** `libs/path-walk` resolves `..` lexically and refuses
underflow, so what reaches the resolver is a list of names that only descends.
There is **no parent pointer anywhere in `vfs.rs`** — not a private one, not an
unused one. That is stronger than `RESOLVE_BENEATH`, which enforces a predicate
on a resolver still *capable* of ascending: here there is no capability for a
predicate to be about.

Fuchsia reached the same answer — *Dot Dot Considered Harmful* — and moved it
client-side. This kernel has no trusted client library, so it goes in the
resolver.

**Two refusals, and they are different things.** An absolute path is
`PathError::Absolute` because **there is no root** for it to be relative to; an
escaping `..` is `PathError::Escapes` because there is no parent. Neither is a
denial. Reporting either as a permission failure would suggest that some other
program could, which is false in a way that would send someone looking for the
program that can.

**Nothing is clamped.** An escape is refused rather than resolved to the
starting directory, a name too long is refused rather than truncated, and a
path deeper than the buffer is refused rather than cut short. Each of those
would silently answer a *different* question than the caller asked — and on a
walk that ends in an open, open a different file.

**Rationale, and the thing that hung the harness.**

The enumeration check's first version resolved each listed name from inside the
enumeration callback. Both operations reach the controller through
`nvme::with_controller`, which holds a leaf guard — so the inner call re-entered
the same lock and spun. The harness reported it as a sixty-second timeout,
which is `lock_leaf`'s rule arriving in the only form a same-lock re-entry can
take: the "no lock under a leaf guard" check watches for a *different* lock, and
a spin on the same one is not something a counter can see.

The check now collects the names and resolves them after the enumeration
returns, which is also the shape a caller must use — and the comment says so,
because the next person to write a VFS operation inside a callback will hit the
same wall.

**Consequences.**

- `libs/path-walk`: splitting, `.` and `..` resolution, name validation, depth
  bounds. Nine host tests and a doctest, six deliberate breaks, all red. One of
  the tests is exhaustive over every three-component path built from `a`, `.`,
  `..` and the empty component, because the property is about *every* input.
- `kernel::vfs`: `Directory`, `File`, `Node`, `resolve`, `read`, `enumerate`.
  Four machine checks, five breaks, all red.
- **The depth bound is on the deepest point reached, not on the answer.**
  `a/b/c/../../d` is two components and passes through three, so a buffer of
  two refuses it. Bounding the intermediate is what keeps the work bounded by
  the buffer rather than by the length of an argument ring 3 wrote.
- **Offsets are per operation**, which is `012` §6 and D-152 arriving at the
  file layer: no seek, no tell, no cursor on anything. A shared cursor is a
  lock on the hot path and the only reason two handles to one file would have
  observable coupling — which in a capability system is a covert channel.
- **One namespace per program and no way to compose two.** `014` carries it as
  a deliberate hole; Plan 9's `bind` and Fuchsia's namespace construction are
  out of scope. A program gets the directory handles it was given.
- Enumeration and traversal are **separate authorities**, and the check
  requires them to agree: an enumeration that returned a name traversal cannot
  find is a directory listing that lies. The rights that gate them arrive in
  slice 9.

## D-172 A second backend, and a device that is not a file — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** `014` is blunt about why this slice exists: *the VFS needs at least
two backends before its abstraction is anything but a guess.* A directory trait
with one implementation is a description of that implementation, and slice 7's
three operations had only FAT32 to be about.

`012` §7 is equally blunt about the second thing: **devfs does not go through a
byte interface.** A devfs entry has no bytes; it is a name that resolves to a
device object *of another type*. Forcing it to implement `read_at` is the
"everything is a file" conflation, and WASI's own README rejects it on exactly
these grounds.

**Decision.** Two more backends, chosen to be unlike the first in different
directions.

**tmpfs is unlike FAT32 in the ways that matter.** No clusters, no chains, no
device; its directories are a flat table with parent indices rather than a
linked structure on a disk. If `lookup`, `enumerate` and `read` fit both, they
are about directories rather than about FAT — which is the whole claim.

**devfs is unlike both in the way that matters most.** `Node` gains a third
variant, and `vfs::read` takes a `File`. **There is no way to pass a device to
it** — not a refusal at run time, an absence at compile time. That is the
difference between a design that says devices are not files and one that
enforces it.

**Fixed-size and read-only.** The tmpfs arena is a `static`, because the write
path is this phase's largest deliberate hole and a tmpfs that could grow would
be the write path arriving through the back door.

**Rationale, and the corpus catching the check again.**

Adding a `Node` variant was a compile error in every match that handles one,
which is exactly what the enum-dispatch decision (D-171) was for: a fourth
backend is a build failure rather than a number that means nothing. Promotion
to dynamic dispatch still waits for a backend that must be added *without*
editing the enum.

**A tmpfs lookup that ignored the parent passed.** Every name in the first tree
was unique — `MOTD`, `NOTES`, `ONE.TXT` — so a lookup that searched the whole
arena found the right entry anyway, and deleting the containment check left the
boot green. The tree now holds `MOTD` **twice**, once at the root and once
inside `NOTES` with different content, and the check reads both. That is D-155's
rule for the third time in this phase, and the third different place it has
arrived from: an input, a corpus, and now a directory tree.

**Consequences.**

- `kernel::tmpfs` and `kernel::devfs`; `vfs::Directory`, `File` and `Node` each
  gain the variants they need. Three machine checks, five breaks, all red.
- The no-ascent invariant is checked on **every backend**, not on FAT — it is a
  property of the resolver, and a check that only exercised one backend would
  be a property of that backend.
- **A directory handle names its own backend.** A tmpfs handle cannot resolve a
  name that exists only on the volume, and the check requires each name to
  resolve where it belongs *and* nowhere else — so the refusals are about the
  backend rather than about the name.
- devfs is **one directory, not a tree**: `storage/anything` is refused for the
  same reason a path through a file is. A devfs with subdirectories would be a
  namespace nobody asked for.
- `Device` is an enum rather than an index into a registry, so a fourth device
  is a compile error everywhere that matches on it. There is one driver and a
  registry with one entry is a description of that entry (D-41).
- What a program will eventually receive from devfs is slice 4's `Device`
  capability. Today the name resolves; the handle it becomes is Phase 7's, and
  saying so is better than building a table nothing puts anything in.

## D-173 The file handle, and a buffer with no pointer in it — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25) (amended by D-181)

**Context.** `014` left three decisions for this slice: what a `File` handle's
object is, whether `read` takes a length or a provided buffer, and — implicitly
— how a program comes to hold a file at all.

D-149 put the ABI slices first because a caller freezes the interface it uses.
Read is the first storage/data caller: it needs a handle, an offset, a buffer
and a length. The submission entry was sixteen bytes and is thirty-two now,
which is cheap today and an ABI break tomorrow. Timer, not Read, was the first
operation that genuinely waited. D-200 later moved Read service out of its
`RingEnter` trap and into one bounded worker.

**Decision.**

**A `File` handle's object is the thinner of the two.** `vfs::File` names a
backend and a node within it — not an inode-like structure the VFS owns. The
fatter one is what a write path and a page cache both want, and this phase has
neither; building it now would be building for a caller that does not exist
(D-41).

**`read` takes a provided buffer, and the buffer is part of the ring.** `012`
§8 warns that `-ENOBUFS` at completion is the same late-failure shape D-151
refused for handles, and the usual answer is to validate a caller's pointer at
submission. This kernel does something simpler and stronger: a third shared
page is the data area, so the buffer is always mapped, always the right size,
and its bounds are two comparisons. **There is no user pointer to validate, no
SMAP window to open and no fault to recover.**

The cost is a copy — device → kernel frame → data area, where a caller's own
buffer could have been the DMA target — and it is named rather than hidden.
Zero-copy needs the memory-object work of a later phase, and paying one copy
for a boundary with no pointer in it is the right trade until then.

**`OpenAt` is how a program comes to hold a file**, and its rights are
**derived, never asked for**. Opening a directory preserves the same-type
rights unchanged. Opening a file preserves only universal rights already held
and derives `READ` from `TRAVERSE`, because traversal authorized reaching the
named bytes. That cross-type derivation is not a subset relation between the
two raw bitsets; the non-escalation rule is that it never recreates a universal
right or admits a type-specific power with no authorizing operation. `WRITE`
is not granted because there is no write path, and a program wanting fewer
rights can `Duplicate` with fewer.

A device is refused. What a program will hold for one is slice 4's `Device`
capability, and putting it in a table is Phase 7's (D-172).

**Rationale, and three checks that could not fail.**

*A read without the right to read.* The refusal table was built entirely from
`OpenAt`, so nothing exercised `Read`'s rights check at all — deleting it left
the boot green. A file handle held without `READ` is in the table now.

*A zero-length buffer.* Refused by `data_bounds`, and the check covered it — but
only through `OpenAt`, where a zero-length path is also refused by the path
splitter. The two refusals are different and the check now distinguishes them.

*The buffer bound checked before the read rather than after.* This is the one
worth recording. Removing it changes **no output**: `Shared::write_at` bounds
the copy anyway, so the completion carries the same status either way. What it
changes is *when* — a bound checked after the read is `-ENOBUFS` with the work
already done, which is precisely the shape this design refuses.

Making it observable took a counter on the driver: the controller's command
identifier advances once per command, so "the device was not asked" is a
number. The check submits a readable handle with a buffer that runs off the end
of the data area and requires the count **unchanged**. Every refusal that
happens before the read is now visible as a device that was never told.

**Consequences.**

- At this decision four transcriptions of the entry layout existed: the kernel
  parser/serializer, C header, emitted ring-3 program and test helpers. The host
  check compared only total sizes and stride, not fields; D-181 found the gap.
  The repair uses one kernel offset map for parser, serializer and helpers,
  derives C offsets, widths and sizes, and checks the emitted ELF's actual
  operands plus entry base and count. A persistent mutation changing submission
  `argument` from offset 24 to 8 must make the program-ring check red.
- Three raw rights were added: `TRAVERSE`, `ENUMERATE`, `MODIFY`. The current
  masks admit `READ` for File and `TRAVERSE | ENUMERATE` for Directory. `WRITE`
  remains meaningful for Channel but no File admits it; no Directory admits
  `MODIFY`, and no type admits `EXECUTE` or `MAP`. Leaving those raw bits in
  place avoids renumbering later without pretending an unenforced power exists.
- **Two rights tests were restated lists and are now derived.** One named the
  eight rights that existed; the other named `1 << 12` as an undefined bit,
  which `TRAVERSE` then became. Both read the source now (D-161).
- A third test's premise was simply wrong once `ALL` grew: it asserted that
  every right this kernel defines is meaningful for a memory object, which was
  true only while `ALL` was the universal four plus the memory ones. A memory
  object has no names in it.
- `Submission::simple` and `Submission::about` exist so that eighteen call
  sites did not each grow four zeroes. A zero handle is a *value*, and writing
  it out invites a reader to think it matters.
- **A ring-3 program still cannot reach any of this**, and that is the slice's
  named limit rather than an omission: `spawn` gives a program exactly one
  handle — its bootstrap channel (D-111) — and receiving a directory handle
  over that channel needs `sys_channel_receive`, which was called OWED under
  D-114's former vocabulary. D-181 states the live fact directly: there is no
  ring-3 receive operation. Giving a program a second handle at spawn would
  break the invariant that makes pillar 1 checkable, so it waits for the
  channel.

## D-174 The Phase 6 audit: one defect in three places, and a claim nothing checked — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** D-77's pattern for a phase close: treat every green check as a
claim to attack. Phase 6 added four `libs/` crates, six kernel modules, two
opcodes that take a *pointer-shaped* argument from ring 3, and an ABI entry
that doubled in size. The sweep looked for the classes the phase had already
been bitten by — a check that restates its data, a check that cannot reach its
code, an input where the answers coincide — and for the class a storage phase
adds: a value ring 3 chooses being read as something else.

**What it found.**

**Three silent truncations, and they are one defect.** Every word a submission
carries is written by ring 3 into a page ring 3 owns, and three of them reached
the kernel through an `as` cast:

- A **rights word**: `Rights::from_bits(submission.argument as u32)`. The cast
  drops the high half, so `0xFFFF_FFFF_0000_0003` was read as `DUPLICATE |
  TRANSFER` rather than refused — which defeats the entire reason `from_bits`
  returns an `Option`. A program could set every undefined bit in the world and
  be told yes.
- A **file offset**: `submission.offset as u32`. An offset of four billion and
  one wrapped to one, so a program asking for a byte past every file this
  kernel can hold was handed a byte *inside* it.
- A **cancellation token**: `submission.argument as u32`. `0x1_0000_DEAD` would
  end the operation tagged `0xDEAD` — a program ending an operation it did not
  name.

None is a crash. All three are a program being answered about something other
than what it asked for, which is the worst shape a boundary can fail in: there
is no fault, no log line and no wrong-looking value, only a correct answer to a
different question.

All three are now `try_from`. The rights word and the token are **refused**;
the offset is clamped to `u32::MAX`, which is past every file this kernel can
hold and therefore reads nothing — which is what an offset past the end reads
everywhere else here.

**A doc comment claimed a test that did not exist.** `devfs::DEVICES` said it
was "checked against [the enum] by a test that counts (D-161)". There was no
such test. The compiler does check the match in `Device::name`, so a third
variant is a build failure *there* — and the array would go on listing two,
which would make the listing incomplete and every check that counts devices
agree with it. The test exists now, and it is the same exhaustive-match shape
D-161 used for `Divide`.

That is the more uncomfortable finding. A wrong claim in a doc comment is worse
than a missing test, because it is a reason not to write one.

**What it did not find.** No panicking call in any of the phase's production
code — `libs/fat32`, `libs/path-walk`, `libs/nvme`, `libs/pci-config` and the
six kernel modules have none outside tests and doctests. No reachable indexing
that is not behind a proven bound. No lock taken under a leaf guard that the
machine check did not already catch during the slice that introduced it.

**Consequences.**

- Three fixes, one machine check covering all three, three deliberate breaks —
  each of which reddens it.
- The check is written from the *claim*: it submits a valid low half with a
  garbage high half, so a cast produces a **plausible** answer rather than an
  absurd one. An input where the truncated and untruncated readings both look
  wrong would not have caught anything.
- `devfs` gains the test its documentation promised.
- The pattern for the next phase: **every field a submission carries is a value
  ring 3 chose.** `as` is not a conversion at that boundary; it is a silent
  reinterpretation, and the only casts that belong there are widening ones.

## D-175 A break that does not compile is not a break — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** The Phase 6 close ran the full sweep and one of sixty-four
mutations did not come back caught: *a device window is uncacheable*. The
summary line said **survived**, which means "a property nothing checks" — the
most alarming thing that task can say.

It was not that. The per-mutation line, five thousand lines earlier in the log,
said `inconclusive: kernel build failed`. The mutation's replacement was
`Flags::empty()`, and `Flags` has no such function: it has `NONE`. The mutation
had never run.

**Two failures, and the second is mine rather than the harness's.**

**The summary conflated two different things.** `run` already kept a build
failure apart from a survivor in its reasoning — the comment says so
explicitly, "a build failure is not a survivor" — and then pushed it onto the
same `survivors` list and reported it with the same word. A reader who sees
"survived" goes looking for a missing check. There is no missing check.

**The break that introduced it had the same defect and hid it.** Slice 5's
break script wrote `Flags::empty()`, booted, and reported red because the boot
produced no `verdict v1 PASS` line. A build failure produces no PASS line
either. So the break was recorded as red, the property was recorded as
verified, and it was not: until this sweep, nothing had ever shown that
`the controller's registers are uncacheable` can fail.

**Decision.** Three things.

`Flags::NONE` is the mutation, and it builds. Measured directly rather than
argued: the device window's entry is `0x8000_0000_0000_0073` normally and
`0x8000_0000_0000_0063` under the mutation — bit 4, `PCD`, is exactly what
disappears, and exactly what the check reads.

**The sweep reports a mutation that will not build as itself.** Separate list,
separate line, separate message: *"did not build … each is a defect in the
mutation, not a missing check"*. The two want different work, and naming them
alike sends the reader to the wrong one.

**The rule, which is what this entry is for:**

> **A break is only red if the thing that went red is a check.** Absence of a
> pass is not a failure — a build error, a harness crash, a timeout and a red
> check all produce no `PASS`, and only one of them is evidence. A break script
> that greps for the absence of success is measuring the wrong thing.

**Rationale.** D-28's whole argument is that a check which cannot fail is worth
less than no check, *because it is also a claim*. A break that cannot run is
the same defect one level out: it produces the appearance of having verified
something, and it is the appearance that does the damage — the property goes on
the record as checked and nobody looks again.

The reason this was caught at all is that the mutation sweep exists. Breaking a
check by hand happens once, when it is written; `cargo xtask mutate` is D-119's
answer to *that* being unrepeatable, and here it caught not a rotted check but a
rotted **break** — a claim made in a commit message six slices ago that was not
true when it was made.

**Consequences.**

- One mutation corrected. The property it tests is now genuinely verified,
  measured at the page-table entry rather than inferred from a boot's exit.
- `cargo xtask mutate` distinguishes survivors from mutations that would not
  build, in the summary as well as in the per-mutation line.
- Slice 5's break record is amended rather than left standing: *"a register
  file the cache may answer for"* was reported red and was not. `014`'s slice 5
  section says so.
- `005` carries the rule beside D-28's.
- Every other break in this phase used an edit that compiled — the sweep's
  sixty-three catches are what says so, since a mutation that does not build is
  now impossible to mistake for one that does.

## D-176 A boot target without the device is not a second boot target — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** Phase 6 closed green: 180 machine checks under QEMU, 64 mutations
each caught, the model clean. Then the first VMware boot of that kernel came
back `verdict v1 FAIL passed=117 failed=63`.

Sixty-three failures on a machine whose kernel passes 180 checks on another is
not a regression, it is a **measurement that had never been taken**. Two causes,
and each teaches something different.

**The VM had no NVMe controller.** `012` §2's entire argument for choosing NVMe
over AHCI was that it is the one storage controller with a published
specification that spans both of this project's boot targets — and the VMX
template written in Phase 2 declares a SATA disk to boot from and nothing else.
So Phase 6 was developed for ten slices against a machine that could satisfy it
and shipped to one that could not. The checks did exactly what they should:
`pci: 8 functions ... 0 nvme`, then ten dependent checks red.

**The clock refused to calibrate, and would not say why.** `measure` returns
`Option<Calibration>` and has six ways to produce `None` — a crystal that
stepped, a window that never closed, a counter that read backwards, an
overshoot, a rate outside belief, and no measurement at all. The warning printed
one sentence for all six: *no believable rate from any measurement*. That
sentence names the least likely of the six. Roughly forty checks depend on a
running clock, so one unexplained refusal is most of the remaining failures.

**Decision.** Three things.

**The VMware machine gets the controller Phase 6 drives.** `qemu::nvme_image`
becomes a function both runners call, so the namespace behind VMware's second
VMDK is byte-for-byte the file QEMU's `-drive` points at. One corpus, one
builder, two machines. The VMX test asserts the controller is present, so this
cannot silently revert.

**The clock says which guard tripped and what it measured.** `measure` becomes a
wrapper over a `Result<Calibration, Refusal>` with the six named, and the two
measured rates are recorded whether or not they are believed — because "which
number was wrong" is the rest of the diagnosis, and a refusal that keeps it to
itself costs another boot to learn.

**The rule, which is what this entry is for:**

> **A boot target that cannot present the device is not testing the driver, it
> is testing the absence.** D-18 makes a VMware boot every phase's definition of
> done because that machine reaches hardware QEMU's does not. A phase that adds
> a device must add it to *both* machines in the slice that adds it — otherwise
> the second target's silence is mistaken for agreement.

**Rationale.** The alternative was to let Phase 6's VMware boot be a partial
one, recorded with the ten storage checks excused. That is the shape of every
claim this project has spent six phases refusing: a green result whose
exclusions live in prose. D-18's value is entirely in the checks QEMU cannot
run, and a phase whose new device only exists on QEMU has none of that value.

On the diagnosis half: this is D-28's argument moved one step earlier. A check
that cannot fail is worth less than no check because it is also a claim; a
**refusal that cannot be attributed** is worth less than a crash, because it
looks like information and is not.

**Consequences.**

- `cargo xtask vmware` builds a second VMDK and copies the namespace into it.
  The VM is ~64 MiB larger and takes one file copy longer to generate.
- The VMX template gains three lines and a test that reads them.
- `kernel/src/time.rs` grows a `Refusal` enum and three statics. The warning is
  longer by a clause and a pair of numbers.
- **Seven refusals, not six.** `init` reaches `Implausible` a seventh way — five
  windows that were each believable and never agreed within `AGREEMENT_DIVISOR`
  — and on an emulated crystal that is the one it reaches first. It names
  itself too.
- A machine check sweeps every refusal and requires it to decode as the one that
  was recorded, because a diagnosis that names the wrong guard is worse than one
  that names none, and a discriminant drifting from its `match` arm is how that
  happens. 181 checks; the mutation that breaks it is number 65.
- Phase 6's VMware boot is **not** recorded as done until it is re-run against a
  machine with the controller. `014`'s close says so rather than claiming a
  boot it did not get.

## D-177 A check that names an address names a machine — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** With D-176's controller in place the VMware boot went from
`passed=117 failed=63` to `passed=172 failed=9`. Five of the nine were the
keystroke checks in a headless run with nobody to press `a`. The other four were
real, and they had one thing in common:

```
a boot mapping cannot claim ownership          FAILED
a user space cannot reach the kernel half      FAILED
a user mapping cannot widen a supervisor table FAILED
a differing remap is refused                   FAILED
```

Those four, and no others, call `BootRegion::describe(PAGE_SIZE, PAGE_SIZE)`.
`describe` answers `None` unless the boot memory map covers the range **with
memory**, and VMware's firmware does not describe physical `0x1000` that way.
QEMU's does.

**So none of the four failed.** Each fell out of its setup's `else` arm and
returned `false` — the same value the harness gets when the property is
genuinely violated. Four checks that never reached the code they are about,
reported identically to four security properties coming apart. It took
elimination across ten checks to tell which.

**Decision.** Two things.

**A caller that needs a described range asks for one.**
`MemoryMap::first_memory_run(len)` returns the first page-aligned run of that
many bytes the map covers with memory, never physical zero. The four probes cut
their pages from it. On QEMU the answer is the page they already named, so
nothing about the existing boots changes; on any other firmware the checks now
run instead of evaporating.

**A precondition that can fail gets its own line.** *the map offers a run to
probe* is checked before the four that depend on it, so a machine that cannot
supply one says so once rather than reddening four unrelated properties.

**The rule:**

> **A check that hardcodes an input hardcodes the machine that supplied it.**
> D-165 says a check must reach the code it is about; this is how it stops —
> not by being deleted, but by having its setup quietly answer `None` somewhere
> the author never booted. Where the setup can fail, the failure is a separate
> check, because "the property is false" and "the check did not run" are
> different findings and the harness renders them the same colour.

**Rationale.** This is D-155's rule (choose inputs where the answers differ)
arriving from the other side. `0x1000` was not chosen to make anything differ;
it was chosen because it was there, and being there is a fact about QEMU. The
four properties involved are among the most load-bearing in the kernel — they
are the ones standing between safe code and a second owner of a frame the
kernel is running on — and on the machine D-18 makes this project answer to,
none of them had ever been evaluated.

That is the reason D-18 exists, stated more sharply than the project has yet
had cause to state it: **a second machine does not re-run the checks, it
discovers which of them were about the first machine.**

**Consequences.**

- `wost::boot::MemoryMap` gains `first_memory_run`; `wost::mm` re-exports it
  through the map's lock. No unsafe, no new lock.
- 182 machine checks. The new one is broken by mutation 66.
- The four probes are unchanged on QEMU by construction, which is what makes
  this a fix rather than a rewrite: the gate's result before and after is the
  same because the run it finds is the page that was named.
- Phase 6's VMware boot is closer but still not clean: the keystroke checks
  need a human at the VM, and the clock's refusal is intermittent — it
  calibrated on the boot that found all this, having refused on the one before.
  D-176's diagnosis is what will name it when it recurs.

## D-178 Ask the device what it is, not what it is set to — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** With D-177's probes fixed, the VMware boot reached
`passed=177 failed=5`. Four of the five need a human at the machine to press a
key. The fifth does not:

```
[warn ] keyboard: reports scancode set Some(65), not 2
[error] selftest: the keyboard is speaking scancode set two FAILED
```

That warning is D-176's rule paying for itself two commits after it was
written: the check had known only that the answer was not two, and one boot's
worth of extra prose turned an unexplained red into a number to reason about.

**`0x41` is not obviously anything.** It is not `2`. The controller's
configuration byte says translation is *off* — the neighbouring check reads
that bit and passes. So either the controller reports its own configuration
falsely, or its answer to *this particular query* is rewritten, or it answers
the query with something else entirely.

The distinction is not academic. If bytes reaching the decoder are translated
into set 1 while the decoder reads set 2, the keyboard types the wrong
characters, and the only checks that would notice are the four that need a
human. A property this kernel depends on would be resting on a keypress.

**Decision.** Ask the keyboard who it is.

An MF2 keyboard answers `0xF2` with `0xAB 0x83`. The same keyboard behind a
translating controller answers `0xAB 0x41`, because translation rewrites that
reply exactly as it rewrites the scancodes — which is why Linux's `atkbd` reads
the pair rather than trusting the configuration bit. The pair is therefore a
question about **the path the bytes take**, answerable with no human, where the
set query and the configuration byte are both questions about what something
was *told* to be.

**The rule:**

> **A device's configuration says what it was asked for; its identity says what
> it is.** Where a check depends on the second, read the second. A controller
> that reports its own translation bit is reporting a value it was written,
> and the byte that arrives at the decoder is the only evidence of what it
> actually does.

**Rationale.** Three checks now stand between the decoder and a wrong-set
keyboard, and they fail in different places on purpose: the configuration byte
catches a controller that was never configured, the set query catches a
keyboard that was never switched, and the identity catches a controller that
answers both correctly and rewrites the bytes anyway. Only the third is immune
to being lied to, and only the third was missing.

`0x41` remains unexplained as a scancode-set reply, and this entry does not
pretend otherwise. What it does is make the *consequence* of that reply
observable without a human, so the next boot says whether the number matters or
is merely strange.

**Consequences.**

- `Controller::identity`, `input::identity`, and the check *the keyboard
  identifies as one the decoder reads raw*. 183 machine checks, mutation 67.
- The self-test now names both the set and the identity when either is not
  what it expects, so a machine that disagrees says how in one boot.
- Phase 6's VMware close still needs one boot with a human at it: four
  keystroke checks cannot run headless, and whether the fifth is a VMware
  quirk or a real mis-decode is a question the identity answers and the
  keystrokes confirm.

## D-179 The set the keyboard speaks is a fact about the controller — Status: Accepted (2026-08-25)

**Context.** D-178 established that VMware's controller translates set 2 into
set 1 while reporting its translation bit clear. `libs/ps2-keys` is a set 2
crate by construction — its first line says so — so on that machine every
keystroke reached a decoder reading the wrong numbering, and typing did
nothing. That was the symptom this whole sequence started from.

**Options.**

*Turn translation off.* Already attempted: the driver clears the bit at
bring-up and reads it back clear. The controller agrees and translates anyway.
There is nothing to fix on this side.

*Untranslate the bytes.* A filter in front of the existing decoder, mapping set
1 back to set 2 so the tested state machine handles everything. Attractive
until Pause: set 1 spells it in six bytes and set 2 in eight, so the filter
cannot be byte-local and would need its own state machine — the thing it exists
to avoid. It also needs a byte-to-byte table with nothing to check it against.

*Decode set 1.* A second table and a second state machine, sharing the key
identities, the shift state and the layout — which is all the two sets have in
common.

**Decision.** Decode set 1. `Decoder::translated()` beside `Decoder::new()`,
`set1::key_for` beside `table::key_for`, and the driver picks by asking the
keyboard who it is at bring-up rather than by reading the configuration byte.

**A second transcription is worth more than two transcriptions**, and that is
the argument for this shape rather than the filter's. Set 1 and set 2 are
different numbers for the same hundred-odd keys, so the two tables check each
other: `both_sets_name_the_same_keys` fails if either drops a key, duplicates
an arm so the one below is shadowed, or files a key in the base table that
belongs behind `E0`. There is no third table to ask, and this is the nearest
thing to one. D-156 had to resolve a single backslash against two sources by
hand; that entry is now an assertion, and the other hundred are covered by
construction.

**`0xAA` is a key, not a reply.** The one genuine collision: it is the
self-test result and it is `0x2A | 0x80`, the left shift's release. Swallowing
it would leave shift held down for ever after the first capital letter.
Decided in favour of the key, because the self-test result is read by the reset
path directly, before scanning is enabled, where no decoder can see it. Set 2
keeps swallowing it, where nothing else claims that byte.

**Rationale.** The alternative was to leave VMware's keyboard dead and note it.
D-18 makes that machine the definition of done for every phase, and a boot
where the machine accepts keystrokes and does nothing with them is not a
definition of done — it is the thing a person sees first and concludes the
kernel is broken from, which is exactly what happened.

**Consequences.**

- `libs/ps2-keys` decodes either set. Two new tables, one new state machine,
  eleven new host tests; the layout, the shift state and the event type are
  untouched, which is the measure of whether the split was drawn in the right
  place.
- The bring-up reads the identity before enabling scanning, and the boot line
  says which set it is reading rather than asserting set 2.
- A controller that will not answer `0xF2` is taken at the configuration
  byte's word, which is the old behaviour and the right fallback.
- The self-test checks the decoder against a *translating* QEMU, which is the
  only way to run the set 1 path where the expected key is known
  independently. The harness injects in two rounds, and the second round's
  marker is asserted to exist in the kernel's source beside the first — a
  round waiting on a line nothing prints would be red for the harness's reason
  rather than the kernel's.

**And the break found what reading would not.** The translated round first
pressed `a`, the same key the untranslated round presses. With set 1's code for
`a` deliberately wrong the check stayed **green**: an `a` still in the queue
from the first round satisfied the wait, and the set 1 tables were never
consulted. One character's difference — the round presses `b` now — turned the
same break red.

This is D-155's rule (*choose inputs where the answers differ*) and D-165's (*a
check must reach the code it is about*) arriving together, in the phase that
recorded both. The input was not chosen to make the two paths differ; it was
chosen because the first round already had one, which is the same reasoning that
put `0x1000` in four paging checks two decisions ago. **Reusing a fixture is
how a check stops reaching its subject**, and neither reading the check nor
