running it green would have said so.

## D-180 Wizzy gets the first native system-language/runtime proof — Status: Provisional (2026-08-26), amends D-05's sequencing

**Context.** D-05 names an own userland, shell, Python and document web as the
destination. D-06 makes the native ABI capability- and completion-oriented;
D-10 already confines POSIX to an adapter. Phase 5's mlibc pressure test then
did what D-74 asked without producing a runtime (D-114). The next caller can
therefore be a real compiled direct-native program rather than making the
POSIX translation layer the OS's first application model.

`wizards-ink` is a plausible fit: its implemented effects, normal-path resource
cleanup and VM-backed structured concurrency expose the questions this ABI
was built to answer; panic cleanup and parity on other backends remain open.
The local evidence snapshot is `limbwizard/wizards-ink` commit
`9035c2e8f78ee64fa1db2b24c3bfc2ff7a6c5e8e`. It was six commits ahead of that
repository's remote when recorded, so slice 1 must replace it with a reachable
pin before deciding the route. The fit is not proof. Its tracked design says
runtime capability values and a Wasm backend are future v0.3 work,
native code generation is v0.4+ work, there is no `wzi build`, and the VM is
not a `no_std` userland runtime. The OS also lacks ring-3/native operations or
contracts for channel send/receive, handle close, user-controlled mapping,
terminal I/O, directory enumeration, spawn-from-image and child status. Its
`wost`-only unsafe rule also has no place yet for a user runtime's platform
instructions and volatile ring access.
Choosing static AOT ELF as the next slice would make the highest-cost route a
premise instead of a result.

**Options.** (a) Grow the compiled Rust boundary probe into the native
`init`, shell and tools; (b) make the mlibc/POSIX layer the first real userland;
(c) wait for a Wizzy AOT backend before doing any userland work; (d) evaluate
Wizzy through a measured user-mode delivery route while preserving a
language-neutral platform contract; (e) put a Wizzy interpreter in the kernel.

**Decision.** (d), provisionally. D-116's emitted ring-3 program is already the
first direct native caller and drives its own ring. The compiled Rust program
in the early slices is the first delegation-capable boundary probe: it proves
a real build, the wire layout and Duplicate's completion-carried handle
delegation without choosing the language of `init`, the shell or the tools.
Terminal and directory I/O delegation arrive only in later slices. Wizzy is
the provisional choice for that first system-language/runtime proof.

"Native" means that a program uses handles, completion rings,
directory-relative names and bootstrap protocols directly. It does **not**
mean AOT. Phase 7 begins with a bounded comparison whose default hypothesis is
bytecode in a static user-mode Rust runner, because the VM is the execution
engine that exists. Core Wasm + `wasip1` remains D-72's first-class app format
and Phase 7 milestone; the Component Model remains only a watch item in this
repository. Wizzy's own Component Model decision conflicts with that target
and must be resolved before Wizzy can supply the D-72 module. WASI does not
substitute for the direct-native qualification. AOT is a later optimisation
unless measurement reverses that order.

The kernel stays Rust and language-neutral. The interpreter, allocator,
scheduler and language runtime stay in userland. POSIX remains the Phase 9
compatibility gateway, and the established identities of Phases 8–13 do not
move. RustPython moves from Phase 7 to the Phase 9 compatibility-runtime work;
the Python and CPython destination remains.

**Rationale.** A user-mode runner can test Wizzy against the native boundary
without waiting for an unrelated compiler backend. It also makes the
proposition falsifiable: runtime dependencies, image size, heap cost and
process density can be measured before kernel interfaces grow around them.
Preserving the language-neutral boundary means a failed Wizzy experiment still
leaves useful bootstrap, lifecycle and service protocols. Putting an
interpreter in the kernel would instead enlarge the trusted computing base and
bind privileged code to language policy.

The Rust-native alternative is the baseline, not a straw man. It reuses the
already pinned compiler, has the smallest bootstrap dependency set and remains
the fallback if the Wizzy gate fails. The boundary probe proves the platform
contract before Wizzy runs; it does not prove Wizzy's runtime, capability
representation or semantics. Choosing Rust permanently would avoid that
runtime experiment, but would also create `init`, the shell and the first tool
surface before testing the language this decision exists to test. That trade
is why the Wizzy choice is measured and provisional.

Effects are evidence for launch policy, not authority. Wizzy capability values
are not implemented yet, an image can be forged, and no manifest grants itself
a handle. The launcher chooses what to send; the kernel enforces possession and
rights. The first Wizzy-level security claim waits for a real unforgeable
runtime value rather than exposing an integer handle and calling the wrapper a
capability.

**Promotion gate.** Accepted only when a reproducibly built Wizzy `init` runs
in user mode with exactly one handle-table entry—the bootstrap channel—while
the fixed ring, time page and handleless operations are accounted separately.
It must receive a terminal handle through that channel, drive the native ring,
print, launch two Wizzy children—one successful and one deliberately failed—
observe and reclaim both, and exit with observable status. Capability values
and their private runtime constructors must exist; forged artifacts and effect
metadata must not manufacture one. The programs must agree with the host semantic
backend, and four simultaneous Wizzy processes must fit the measured memory
budget. Two clean builds from pinned source, compiler/runtime revisions and
locked dependencies must produce identical bytes, one of which matches the
artifact in the OS image. A checksum-pinned artifact is enough to keep the
normal OS gate self-contained, but proves only artifact identity, not
reproducible compilation; that gate may not depend on a mutable sibling
checkout.

**Consequences.** `015-wizzy-userland.md` records the dependency chain and
slice proposal. Phase 6's interactive VMware checks remain the entry gate.
Phase 7 adds no speculative kernel API: channel, memory, process and terminal
operations arrive with the concrete caller named by each slice. The
user-runtime unsafe boundary gets its own decision rather than being hidden in
`wost` or generated assembly. Persistent writes remain WizFS's Phase 13 work;
Phase 7 mutating tools use explicitly volatile tmpfs.
If the promotion gate fails, the language-neutral platform work stays and the
Wizzy selection is revisited without weakening W^X, ambient-authority rules or
the POSIX boundary.

**Amended by D-183.** The Rust boundary probe remains a wire-contract oracle
and integration scaffold, not a permanent native-userland fallback. D-183
makes Wizzy the settled default for feasible first-party target-side userland,
puts an earlier compiler-readiness gate in front of Phase 7 product work, and
turns the promotion gate above into a later integration qualification. A failed
qualification returns work to that gate; it does not reopen the language choice
without a new decision.

## D-181 The POSIX register separates source truth from platform work — Status: Accepted (2026-08-26), amends D-06, D-10, D-72, D-80, D-114, D-116, D-118, D-149, D-150, D-151, D-152, D-164, D-166, D-169 and D-173

**Context.** The D-180 audit followed Phase 5's mlibc pressure test back to its
evidence and found that the checked 5/10/1 tally was precise arithmetic over
false categories. `sys_libc_log` was counted as MAPS while its body was a
silent no-op. `sys_read` had a shipped explicit-offset ring operation, while
`sys_write` had no operation at all; calling both OWED hid the difference.
`sys_seek` needs POSIX open-file-description cursor state the native protocol
deliberately omits. `WaitQueue::wait_unless` closes an internal wakeup window,
but is not a futex keyed by a validated userspace atomic and its lifetime.
Phase 6 built native OpenAt, so calling the entire `sys_open` mechanism ABSENT
confused the rejection of an ambient root with the absence of relative lookup.

The implementation transcription disagreed with its labels too.
`sys_clock_get` ignored the requested clock ID and returned monotonic uptime
as realtime, sampled a bare `rdtsc` after the sequence snapshot, and performed
the fixed-point multiply in `u64`. At a 3 GHz counter that multiply can wrap
in a few seconds. `sys_close` invoked proposed call 4 even though the kernel
decodes only 0–3. The header numbered eight such unimplemented calls, assigned
`WIZ_OP_SIGNAL = 3` on top of Duplicate, and described signals as opcodes even
though a completion has no opcode field or unsolicited-event discriminator.

D-114 also recorded no mlibc source revision. Its C++ has never been compiled.
The local toolchain measurement changed by 2026-08-26—WinLibs GCC/G++ 16.1,
Ninja 1.13.2 and Python 3.14.3 through `py` appeared (`python` and `python3`
remain non-working Store aliases). Meson, pinned mlibc source, Wizard target
integration and a repository-owned toolchain are still absent. A
current-looking function signature is therefore not current upstream evidence,
and executables found on one workstation are not a D-16 build.

**Decision.** Preserve D-114's counts as a dated pressure-test result and
retire its one-dimensional taxonomy for present-tense claims. Every one of the
sixteen inspected functions now has two separate fields in
`userland/README.md`.

The **BODY** axis describes only active code in the uncompiled transcription:
WIRED invokes a call the kernel decodes; COMPOSED obtains its required
behavior from another entry; PARTIAL has a valid success path for a strict
subset; STUB has none. The **REMAINDER** axis describes platform work: WORKS
has no known missing platform semantic; COMPAT needs POSIX-only state or
policy over existing native operations; DOOR has a matching internal
operation but no user entry; PARTIAL has useful substrate or a semantic
subset; MISSING lacks the kernel operation itself.

The exact per-name register is canonical rather than another prose count.
Notable consequences of applying it are that Read and Seek share COMPAT
because both need the same cursor; Exit is WIRED/PARTIAL because the kernel
retires only the calling thread and discards its status; Panic is
COMPOSED/PARTIAL because composing that Exit cannot supply process-wide death
or observation; and the futex entries are STUB/MISSING rather than promises
that WaitQueue is nearly a futex. Open is STUB/PARTIAL: OpenAt exists, but the
first directory still has no ring-3 delivery path in addition to its adapter
policy.

**Repair the consumer, not only its labels.** The time reader now accepts only
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`, validates the constants version, page extent and counter
rate, reads a doubly fenced TSC inside the seqlock window, validates the
conversion, uses a 128-bit intermediate and saturates rather than wraps. Page
revocation, an incompatible layout and an unstable snapshot route to one
explicit ENOSYS fallback. That fallback remains incomplete until a shared
ring client can submit Uptime with a unique token and reap its matching
out-of-order completion without stealing another caller's; the register
therefore stays PARTIAL/PARTIAL. Realtime remains absent until the system has
an epoch.

The surrounding page contract also claimed calibration required CPUID's
invariant-TSC bit. D-57's live policy does the opposite deliberately: two
believable, agreeing windows admit the clock and a missing invariant promise
produces a warning. The page and kernel clock share that fixed conversion, so
they agree even when the hardware guarantee is absent; neither becomes more
stable than the underlying counter. D-225 later supplied automatic post-boot
revocation; suspend/resume and NTP adjustment remain later policy.

The C header now assigns numbers only to the four calls `Call::decode`
accepts. Proposed close, duplicate, channel, mapping and futex call numbers are
deleted; Duplicate already belongs to the ring, channels are planned as ring
traffic, mapping's execution contract is unresolved, and the futex substrate
does not exist. The colliding signal define is deleted. D-80's one-event-plane
constraint remains, but a signal representation waits for a versioned record
and its first caller. Unused errno defines are removed, the Duplicate comment
uses the actual separate handle and rights fields, and the header distinguishes
handle-authorized objects from its enumerated ambient ring/time facilities.
`WRITE`, `MODIFY`, `EXECUTE` and `MAP` remain transcribed raw rights, with the
explicit fact that no current File admits `WRITE`, no current Directory admits
`MODIFY`, and no current object type admits `EXECUTE` or `MAP`.

The same audit found two authority defects behind the prose. OpenAt gave every
file `UNIVERSAL | READ`, recreating universal rights even when the directory
was held with `TRAVERSE` alone; it now intersects the parent's universal rights
before deriving file `READ`, with a ring check beginning from no universal
rights. The File and Directory object masks also admitted `WRITE` and `MODIFY`
although neither operation exists. Those masks are now `READ` and
`TRAVERSE | ENUMERATE`, and the meaningless-right refusal check covers File
`WRITE`/`EXECUTE`/`MAP` plus Directory `MODIFY`. Persistent mutations restore
each defect.
OpenAt also copied the submitted path before reserving its result slot, while
Duplicate's slot-first comment hid rights validation ahead of its reservation.
Both contradicted D-151's common admission order. Reservation now comes first;
the full-table check pairs exhausted quota with a valid Duplicate, malformed
Duplicate rights and a malformed OpenAt path, so either validation moving ahead
of the promise changes the observable refusal. Two persistent mutations require
that check to go red.

This also narrows D-10 and D-72. A POSIX or WASI descriptor can carry authority
that aligns with a native handle without being that handle. Its userspace
adapter still owns descriptor numbering, preopens, cursor and inheritance
state, and root/cwd policy. Those are COMPAT semantics; their cost does not
justify putting a cursor or a descriptor table into the native ABI.

**Alternatives.** Broaden OWED to include “some related primitive exists” was
rejected because it would continue to equate Read with no Write and WaitQueue
with a futex. An implementation-only classification was rejected because a
correct stub can still expose valuable platform design work. A platform-only
classification was the original mistake: it let a no-op body inherit a claim
from prose. Keeping exact per-function prose without a machine check was
rejected by D-124's rule.

**Consequences.** The host check masks both C++ comment forms, permits only
include directives, discovers active definitions rather than listing their
names, refuses duplicate bodies, requires the historical domain of sixteen,
and compares one source marker per definition with the README register. It
checks BODY evidence with exact compact bodies for the WIRED calls, composed
panic path and one-path stubs. The clock checks pin named source shapes:
validation gates, snapshot order, output stores and return forms. They are not
a general C++ reachability or dataflow proof, and runtime evidence still waits
for the port to compile.

REMAINDER is platform judgment, not something a C++ body can prove; named
kernel witnesses guard the disputed distinctions between explicit-offset Read,
internal Close, missing Write/futexes, composed Panic and thread-only Exit.
D-182 adds the trap-time reclamation witness that narrows Close from DOOR to
PARTIAL, alongside VM unmap and anonymous free.

The ABI check removes comments from both the C header and the Rust sources,
compares the complete C call and opcode domains with the kernel decoders,
checks the errno values the C++ consumes, and derives C submission, completion
and time layouts — offsets, widths and total sizes — before comparing them with
the kernel's access maps. It also inspects the emitted ELF's actual operands for
opcode, token, argument, status and value, plus entry base and count. Another
speculative member, commented-out decoder arm, reordered field or stale program
operand cannot hide after the known members. Aggregate counts are derived facts
and are not restated as authority.

The first check was broken four ways and red each time (D-28): Exit actively
rang the wrong call; Read and Close exchanged remainder labels in both C++ and
README; the clock's 128-bit intermediate narrowed to `u64`; and proposed call
4 returned to the C enum. The two-file label swap had gone red only because
the test contained a third copy of the whole register, violating D-157. That
result was rejected rather than counted: the copied map was removed, named
platform witnesses were added, and the same swap then went red for the
Read/Close evidence it actually contradicted.

The repaired checks were broken thirteen further ways and red: a duplicate
active definition, a body hidden behind `#if 0`, the Exit call hidden in a
block comment, a stub with an extra success return, EINVAL renumbered, the C
clock's first two fields exchanged, a non-literal decoder arm, and the TSC
halves recombined backwards; then a spaced macro directive, a dead conditional
that called Exit, a block-commented errno definition, a block-commented kernel
decoder arm, and a 64-bit C `shift` over the kernel's 32-bit field. These are
host repository-claim checks, not QEMU verdicts, so they do not add a machine
mutation to `cargo xtask mutate`.

The authority and layout repair added seven more observed host reds: the
kernel submission `argument` offset moved from 24 to 8; an eighth opcode entered
the decoder; the OpenAt witness was hidden in a block comment; the clock's
seconds store was commented out; rights intersection became union; and Panic
and Open were each relabelled with the broader remainder their platform witness
contradicts. Six target breaks were then booted and red: OpenAt restored every
universal right, File admitted inert `WRITE`, Directory admitted inert
`MODIFY`, the kernel parsed `argument` at offset 8, and OpenAt read a malformed
path before reserving against a full table; finally Duplicate validated malformed
rights before making the same reservation. The six target defects have
persistent mutations; the then-current register held 188 machine checks and 75
mutations.

No kernel ABI was added and no libc was claimed compiled. Phase 7 slice 2 now
starts from an honest pressure-test transcription; Phase 9 still owns the
pinned mlibc port, POSIX state and signal representation.

## D-182 A trap-served handle is paid for before the trap — Status: Accepted (2026-08-26), amends D-78, D-128, D-141, D-151, D-171, D-180 and D-181

**Context.** D-181 made Duplicate and OpenAt reserve a table slot before
validating the rest of their submissions, but that promise covered only the
table's count. Installing the result still called `reserve_a_slot`, which grew
the global arena's `Vec` when its existing buffer was full. The heap correctly
refuses allocation in trap context: an interrupt can arrive while the heap is
refilling itself, so re-entering it would corrupt or deadlock the allocator.

That made a successful ring operation an unprivileged machine panic. The
shipped bootstrap channel carries `DUPLICATE`; enough valid Duplicate
submissions reached `HandleTable::fill` from the `int 0x80` handler and crossed
the arena's next capacity boundary. The self-tests missed it because their
queue submissions called `Queue::serve` from kernel-thread context, while the
one emitted ring-3 program submitted only Echo. OpenAt held a second instance
of the same class: wrapping D-171's copyable `File` and `Directory` values in a
fresh `Arc` allocated after the trap had begun.

**Decision.** A handle table is not made reachable until the global arena has
capacity for its entire quota. Construction is fallible and commits that quota
outside trap context. The arena records the sum of every live table's quota;
its `Vec` capacity is always at least that sum. A charged insertion therefore
finds either an existing free slot or unused capacity and never grows the
buffer. Dropping a table releases the commitment after removing its entries,
but retained capacity is harmless and avoids a shrink/allocation cycle.

The invariant is stronger than pre-growing by a convenient number:

> `arena capacity >= sum(live table quotas) >= live handles + promised slots`.

It covers every interleaving, not only the capacity seen by a caller before it
drops the arena lock. Construction may race another construction, so a buffer
is allocated with no lock held, the current required commitment is rechecked,
and a winning buffer is exchanged under the leaf lock. Both the replaced and
losing buffers are freed only after that guard is gone. A failed candidate
allocation also rechecks under the leaf before reporting exhaustion: a
concurrent constructor may already have installed enough backing.

`ObjectRef` now represents stateful Event and Channel objects with `Arc`, while
it carries VFS `File` and `Directory` identities inline. D-171 deliberately
made both filesystem identities copy values with no cursor or per-open mutable
state; allocating a refcount solely to copy one into a handle bought no
lifetime property. OpenAt can consequently resolve, wrap and install either
node kind without touching the heap.

The concrete ring-3 proof needs the authority it exercises. A program's entry
block therefore contains three words: version 1, its launch argument, and the
numeric identity of its sole bootstrap handle. Version comes first so a program
can refuse a shape it does not understand before interpreting either payload
word, paying D-180's versioning requirement with the first new caller. The
handle remains unforgeable authority only because the table validates it;
hiding its number did not strengthen that property and made the bootstrap
channel unusable. A new emitted-program behaviour validates the version, reads
the handle, submits Duplicate through its own ring, validates the completion
and exits. This is the first caller of the versioned entry block rather than a
speculative process-start structure.

D-182 also narrows three rows in D-181's POSIX register. An internal method is
not merely a missing door when invoking it can reclaim memory in trap context:
Close can release the last object reference, while VM unmap and anonymous free
carry flush and reclamation obligations. All three are STUB/PARTIAL until a
deferred or otherwise trap-safe user execution contract exists.

**Alternatives.** Growing on demand before taking `ARENA` was the old design.
It kept the lock order sound but could not make a trap allocator-safe. Returning
`ArenaFull` at the capacity boundary was rejected because admission had already
promised the result and free machine-wide handle capacity still existed.
Preallocating all 262,144 arena slots at boot would remove the trap edge by
charging every machine for the maximum; quota commitment pays only for the
tables that exist. Deferring Duplicate and OpenAt to a worker was rejected for
this slice: both operations are bounded and allocation-free once their result
storage is backed, so a scheduler handoff would add latency and state without
removing any remaining blocking work.

**Consequences.** Table construction can now report arena exhaustion or an
allocation failure, and `user::spawn` preserves that reason. `fill` contains no
reserve/grow loop. Table teardown releases objects one at a time outside the
arena guard rather than allocating a temporary vector in order to drop them.

The C transcription names the entry version, all three field offsets and its
24-byte extent. The host ABI check compares those values with the kernel's
writer and inspects the emitted program's actual entry loads, so moving a word
or accepting the wrong version cannot leave two agreeing private
transcriptions.

The former growth check is replaced by one that chooses a quota larger than
the arena's uncommitted spare capacity, observes the commitment and capacity
grow at construction, fills the table without either changing, and observes
the commitment return on drop. The emitted-program check reaches Duplicate in
an actual ring-3 trap and requires the process to retire with two handles and a
successful authority-bearing completion. OpenAt's attenuated-directory check
covers both the File and Directory result branches. Each new branch was broken
once before acceptance. The quota-undercharge mutation replaces D-128's
obsolete arena-growth mutation; two new mutations change the ring-3 request
away from Duplicate and restore universal rights on a directory result. The
ring-3 mutation targets the rebuilt kernel launch route rather than the
already-running image builder; the mutation driver now refuses any entry aimed
at its own `xtask/` source. The register holds 189 machine checks and 77
mutations.

D-163's promise-lifetime mutation also preserves the allocation-free trap arm
while giving a kernel-thread reservation the wrong table. Constructing the
wrong table unconditionally would now panic on the earlier ring-3 Duplicate
check and hide the named lifetime failure, so it would test D-182 twice and
D-163 not at all.

## D-183 The Wizzy compiler gate precedes native-userland product work — Status: Accepted (2026-08-26), amends D-01, D-05, D-20 and D-180

**Context.** D-01 settled Rust as the kernel language. D-04 put drivers,
filesystems and the network stack in that kernel, so D-08's WizFS is Rust too;
the shared name is not a language exception. D-05 chose an own userland but did
not choose its implementation language. D-180 then chose Wizzy for a measured
first native language/runtime proof while keeping a compiled Rust probe and a
permanent Rust fallback.

That left two different properties under the word "language-neutral." The ABI
must not privilege one source language: ports, runtimes and future compilers all
consume the same handles, rings and bootstrap protocols. The product still
needs a language identity. Leaving that identity revisitable after building
`init`, a shell or tools lets schedule pressure turn temporary scaffolding into
the userland by default, then charges a rewrite to the language it was meant to
test.

The other missing boundary is readiness. The D-180 snapshot had no reachable
pin, non-interactive build command or target-suitable separated runtime. A full
Wizzy `init` is too late to discover that no reproducible program can be built;
building the OS userland in Rust while waiting is too early to make Wizzy the
system language.

**Decision — privilege fixes the first language boundary.** The kernel and all
first-party code that executes in kernel context remain Rust. That includes the
architecture boundary, drivers, filesystems and network stack. Required
platform assembly remains contained by the existing Rust abstractions; no
Wizzy compiler, interpreter, allocator, scheduler or language runtime enters
the kernel.

**Decision — feasible first-party target userland is Wizzy.** Every
first-party program, service, library, tool or application authored to run on
this OS outside the kernel defaults to Wizzy. This includes `init`, service
management, the shell, native commands, administration and repair tools, the
compositor, native toolkit code and first-party applications. "Default" is an
admission rule, not a preference: a different implementation language needs
one of the narrow exceptions below, a recorded reason and an exit condition.

"Feasible" means the qualified toolchain and runtime can express and ship the
required target behavior without weakening safety, reproducibility or the
platform contract. Schedule pressure and missing convenience libraries do not
make a component infeasible; a missing language or runtime capability must be
named and evidenced.

The exceptions are:

- the smallest audited runtime, entry, ABI and instruction shims needed to run
  Wizzy safely on the target;
- host-only build, image, test and verification tooling;
- third-party libraries and ports, plus compatibility layers including mlibc's
  POSIX gateway;
- foreign runtimes whose purpose is to execute another format or language,
  including the WASI interpreter and Python runtimes.

These are bootstrap, interoperation or verification boundaries, not alternate
native userlands and not precedents for first-party product code. Project-owned
code inside an exception migrates to Wizzy when the language can express it
without weakening safety, reproducibility or the platform contract. Unmodified
third-party source remains foreign by definition; its first-party adapters
still carry that migration obligation. The exceptions do not independently
waive the closed-gate sequencing below.

**Decision — compiler readiness is an early gate.** The gate is **CLOSED**
until one evidence record establishes all four conditions together:

1. A reachable Wizzy repository revision and every dependency are pinned; an
   unpublished local commit is not a pin.
2. One documented non-interactive command consumes source and emits a
   versioned, standalone program artifact that the target runner can identify
   and reject when unsupported.
3. The target runtime is separated from the compiler and its AST behind a
   documented platform seam, and is suitable for the OS's `no_std + alloc`
   environment. The compiler does not ship merely to execute its output.
4. Two clean builds from the recorded revision, dependencies and toolchain
   produce byte-identical artifacts.

The artifact may be bytecode or native code. Requiring AOT would confuse an
optimisation with deliverability; carrying compiler or AST internals into the
target runtime would confuse a development environment with a system runtime.
Opening the gate is recorded by a decision with the pins, commands, hashes and
seam named, rather than inferred from a successful developer checkout.

**Decision — a closed gate stops product implementation.** While it is closed,
Phase 7 product implementation and every later first-party target-side userland
product slice stop. Work is in scope only when it is one of:

- kernel correctness work;
- a language-neutral platform prerequisite with a concrete, named Wizzy caller;
- integration specification or scaffolding needed to exercise the artifact,
  runtime seam or gate; or
- work in `wizards-ink` that advances the gate itself.

**Current amendment (D-184/PW-601).** In this repository, the third item means
specification and validation of the versioned handoff only. Consumer
scaffolding remains stopped until both a pinned draft artifact and its runtime
seam exist. The fourth item names externally owned work in the separate
`wizards-ink` repository; it never authorizes compiler implementation here.

Host tooling is allowed only in support of that work. The compiled Rust
boundary probe may remain as an oracle and may validate a language-neutral wire
contract, but it does not grow into `init`, a shell, a service or a product
tool. A proposed prerequisite with no concrete Wizzy caller waits; "needed by
userland eventually" is not a caller.

**D-180's promotion gate becomes integration qualification.** Once compiler
readiness is open, D-180's Wizzy `init`, bootstrap-only authority, terminal,
child lifecycle, capability-construction, semantic-parity and process-density
requirements remain the definition of a successful OS integration. They no
longer decide whether Wizzy is the native-userland language. The Rust baseline
remains a test oracle, not a permanent fallback. A failed qualification is fixed
in Wizzy, its runtime or the language-neutral platform seam; if it invalidates
compiler readiness, the early gate closes and work returns to the bounded list
above. Substituting a Rust native userland or revisiting the language requires a
new decision that explicitly supersedes this one.

**Rationale.** Rust has the mature freestanding and safety machinery needed in
ring 0; putting an experimental language runtime there would enlarge the trusted
computing base and bind privilege to language policy. Above that boundary,
Wizzy is the product choice, and making the compiler prove basic delivery before
product work is the only ordering that prevents both a speculative OS contract
and a completed alternate userland.

The ABI stays language-neutral because authority and wire layouts are platform
facts, not compiler features. The exceptions keep bootstrapping honest: mlibc,
CPython, a WASI interpreter and host `xtask` do not become Wizzy by declaration.
Narrowing them and requiring migration of first-party portions prevents
"temporary shim" from becoming a second native application model.

**Alternatives.** D-180's measured choice with a permanent Rust fallback was
rejected because the fallback can consume the product surface before the
measurement happens. Building a Rust userland and rewriting it later was
rejected as two implementations and an ABI shaped by the disposable one.
Waiting for AOT was rejected because a reproducible standalone bytecode artifact
is sufficient to begin integration. Freezing all OS work was rejected because
kernel correctness, concrete language-neutral prerequisites and compiler work
retire real risk without pre-empting the product language. Making the ABI
Wizzy-specific or putting its interpreter in the kernel was rejected because
either would turn a userland policy into platform lock-in.

**Consequences.** The compiler-readiness gate is closed at this decision. The
Phase 7 proposal may refine specifications and the runner seam, but its product
slices do not begin until a later decision opens the gate. No Rust `init`, shell
or native tool is accepted as schedule-preserving interim work.

D-10 and D-74's mlibc work remains a compatibility exception, not native
userland and not an independent reason to cross the closed gate. D-72's WASI
runtime remains a foreign-runtime exception. WizFS remains Rust because it is
in the kernel; its first-party target-side repair and administration tools
default to Wizzy once the gate opens. Where a roadmap or the D-180 slice
proposal admits broader work, this decision controls the sequencing.

An `xtask` host check reads `015`'s canonical language and gate rows, requires
the contributor instructions, current-facing README, vision, architecture and
platform charter to point at this decision, and rejects D-180's retired
provisional/fallback phrases in those files. It was broken once by changing the
gate row to **OPEN** and failed on that exact disagreement before the row was
restored. This is a repository-claim check, not a machine behavior mutation.

## D-184 The closed compiler gate has one finite, evidence-bound foundation register - Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), refines D-18, D-77, D-135, D-175 and D-183

**Context.** D-183 permits kernel correctness, concrete language-neutral
prerequisites and artifact-handoff specification while its compiler gate is
closed; gate work in `wizards-ink` is externally owned. Consumer scaffolding
waits for PW-601's pinned-draft-artifact and runtime-seam trigger. D-183
deliberately does not enumerate every legitimate kernel debt. Calling the
resulting space "polish" would make it unlimited; freezing the OS repository
completely would leave safe-abstraction, DMA, privilege and verification
defects in the foundation Wizzy must trust.

The Phase 6 slices had landed and QEMU reported 189 checks, but the current
189-check VMware round and current 77-mutation full sweep were not recorded.
A fresh source audit also found five P0 boundaries which a product-language
decision cannot waive: shared-mapping lifetime, mapping rollback ownership,
DMA lifetime after timeout, transactional PCI BAR/claim handling, and CR0.WP.

**Options.** Leave D-183 categorical; admit anything described as kernel
polish; freeze all OS work; or keep one checked register whose entries require
a concrete defect, invariant, proof gap, handoff consumer or explicit trigger.

**Decision.** The last option. `016-pre-wizzy-foundation.md` is the sole live
closed-gate OS backlog. It records state, priority, why each item is admissible,
the finite deliverable and the evidence that closes it. `REQUIRED`, `READY`,
`VERIFY` and `DECIDE` rows must become `DONE` or `SUPERSEDED` before the kernel
is called the polished Wizzy foundation. `TRIGGER` means stopped, not overdue.
Post-gate product APIs and later roadmap phases are classified explicitly and
do not enter the register by being renamed foundation work.

A new row needs falsifiable evidence: a live defect, violated invariant,
missing qualification proof, concrete artifact handoff consumer, or named
trigger. "State of the art", convenience and eventual usefulness are not
evidence. A decision-changing item gets its own ADR. Unknown future defects
may therefore be added without making the list an open-ended feature backlog.

The compiler gate still opens only when all four D-183 conditions hold together
at one reachable pinned `wizards-ink` revision. Ordinary OS CI remains
self-contained; a sibling checkout never becomes an implicit dependency.

**Rationale.** A finite register makes "ready" a testable claim while keeping
the language boundary intact. Risk is retired before Wizzy depends on it, but
an imagined runtime cannot freeze APIs for the real compiler. Separating
confirmed, verify-first, decision and trigger states also prevents a static
audit observation from being reported as an established exploit.

**Consequences.** Phase 6 is better described as planned-slices-complete and
not closed, rather than code-complete. Its close now includes the register's
P0/P1 work and the exact exceptional evidence on one commit. The old
`014-storage.md` mutation sentence is historical source-count evidence, not a
claim that the current 77-entry sweep ran. The missing Phase 3 VMware result and
old non-self-test VMware boots remain historical limits and are not recreated.

An `xtask` prose test checks that the register is finite in shape: unique IDs,
known states/priorities, substantive close evidence, the boundary markers and
current-plan references to D-184. Like the D-183 check, it is a host repository
claim and does not add a machine mutation.

## D-185 Shared mappings keep their frames, and mapping rollback owns only new entries — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-113 and D-115, closes PW-100 and PW-101

**Context.** The D-184 foundation audit found two safe paging doors whose
ownership claims were weaker than their signatures. `map_shared` borrowed a
`Shared`, wrote a reachable user mapping and retained nothing; dropping the
borrowed owner returned those frames while the page-table entries still named
them. Separately, `map_range` allowed an identical rewrite and, on a later
failure, cleared every earlier entry in the request. An identical entry that
predated the request was therefore erased by rollback even though the call did
not create it.

**Decision — shared mappings retain ownership.** `Shared` has one inaccessible
reference-counted allocation. It remains the sole safe data-access handle and
is deliberately not `Clone`; a private keepalive can extend the allocation's
lifetime but exposes no bytes. Every successful `map_shared` stores one such
keepalive in the `AddressSpace`. A successful `AddressSpace::reclaim` drops the
keepalives only after the existing `Released` proof says no task can install
the tables. Dropping an unbound, inactive space also releases them because no
safe root token can reach those mappings. Dropping a bound or active space
leaks the keepalives with the already-leaked tables: loss is preferable to
recycling a frame a CPU may still reach.

**Decision — a mapping transaction has one initial state.** `map_range`
preflights every target entry without allocating or writing. A range that is
entirely absent may be installed and its partial failure may clear everything
written so far. A range that is entirely identical succeeds without writing.
A mixed old/new range is refused before either part changes. This deliberately
narrows idempotence: callers may repeat a whole mapping, but may not use a
larger mapping to absorb an older prefix. No current caller needs the latter,
and refusing it is a checkable transaction boundary rather than a rollback log
whose size depends on the mapping length before the heap exists.

**Rationale.** A prose outlives obligation cannot make a safe function sound.
The keepalive makes frame lifetime a property of the mapping owner, and the
private non-accessing reference preserves `Shared`'s exclusive safe accessor.
For rollback, preflight keeps the boot-time path allocation-free and makes the
old `undo` argument true: every leaf it clears was absent when this transaction
began.

**Alternatives.** Making `map_shared` unsafe was rejected because the lifetime
is mechanically enforceable. Leaking every shared run forever was safe but
discarded deterministic cleanup. A public clonable `Shared` was rejected
because two clones would expose simultaneous mutable access. Recording every
created leaf in a `Vec` was rejected because the kernel builds its first tables
before the heap exists; a fixed rollback log would replace one defect with an
arbitrary mapping ceiling. Tagging transient entries with a software PTE bit
was rejected as a new architectural state for a property a read-only preflight
can establish.

**Consequences.** An address space grows one empty `Vec`; only shared mappings
allocate capacity, and `try_reserve` turns that allocation failure into
`MapError::OutOfMemory`. One machine check drops the original shared owner and
requires the allocator to withhold its frame until the now-unreachable space
is reclaimed. A second constructs an identical first entry and conflicting
second entry and requires both older entries to survive the refusal. Each
protection has a persistent mutation targeting its exact named check.

## D-186 Supervisor writes obey read-only mappings by this kernel's act — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-12 and closes PW-300

**Context.** Kernel text and read-only data have read-only leaves, but x86
allows supervisor writes through those leaves while `CR0.WP` is clear. The
kernel neither set nor read that bit, so the W^X claim depended on firmware or
the bootloader leaving it set. A readback added in isolation would preserve the
same dependence because contemporary firmware commonly does leave it set.

**Decision.** Write protection is an unconditional member of the CPU
protection contract: unlike the optional CPUID-advertised CR4 features,
`CR0.WP` exists on every supported x86-64 processor. `enable_protections` sets
it before the kernel builds and activates the W^X tables, and `Protections`
reads it back alongside NX, SMEP, SMAP and UMIP.

The machine witness is driven rather than observational. With interrupts
excluded, it clears WP, confirms the clear, and reaches the same private setter
boot uses. It then attempts one assembly write which stores a byte's existing
value back to a private `.rodata` symbol. The trap path recovers only when the
saved privilege is ring 0, the page-fault error is exactly present-page write,
and both the instruction and `CR2` match the probe's private labels. Any other
kernel fault remains terminal. If the driven setter fails, the diagnostic path
repairs WP independently before returning a red result.

**Rationale.** Setting the bit makes page-table write permission meaningful to
the supervisor; driving it through an off/on transition proves that this
kernel, rather than inherited state, owns the result. Writing back the byte
already present means the deliberate mutation which omits WP can return a red
verdict without corrupting the image. The exact recovery window does not turn
arbitrary kernel protection faults into resumable events.

**Alternatives.** Trusting the bootloader was the defect. Readback alone could
not distinguish inherited state from the kernel's action. Making all read-only
data executable or writable to avoid the probe would surrender the invariant
being checked. A general kernel fault-fixup API was rejected because redirecting
an arbitrary live trap frame is authority only the narrow assembly window can
justify.

**Consequences.** The boot log now includes `wp`. The machine check
`supervisor writes obey read-only pages` proves the driven write and the actual
fault consequence. Its persistent mutation removes the bit from the common
setter; the driven transition makes that mutation deterministic even when
firmware arrived with WP already enabled.

## D-187 PCI BAR discovery and function ownership are transactions — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-119 and D-168, implements PW-201 and closes PW-202

**Context.** D-168 made a PCI function the authority for its decoded windows,
but three implementation details contradicted the unchanged-on-refusal
contract. The claim key included a configuration-register offset, so two
addresses inside one header were two apparent devices. The device registry
committed before header reads, BAR probes and permanent port claims, and I/O
windows were claimed one by one, so a later refusal could strand both kinds of
ownership. A 64-bit BAR was also probed as two separate save/write/read/restore
operations while memory and I/O decode remained enabled. Hardware therefore
never saw both halves holding all ones, and could transiently decode the probe
value.

**Decision — configuration probing is one restored transaction.** The pure
algorithm lives in `pci-config`; `wost` holds the CF8/CFC pair once and performs
the cycles it requests. The algorithm first saves the command register and
every BAR allowed by the header layout. It rejects an announced wide BAR in
the final slot before writing anything, clears both decode-enable bits with a
sixteen-bit command value, writes both halves of a wide BAR before reading
either, and restores modified BARs in reverse order before restoring command
last. A write is treated as possibly effective even when its adapter reports
failure. Rollback therefore attempts every remaining restore, and a refused
restore is distinct from the initiating access error. Status bits are never
echoed into their write-one-to-clear halfword.

**Decision — a claim has one identity and one commit point.** `Address` exposes
its canonical bus/device/function identity with the register offset cleared.
A bounded `ClaimRegistry` canonicalizes again at its boundary, checks the
duplicate and capacity conditions, runs one fallible preparation closure, and
records only the value that closure successfully returns. The kernel holds the
registry's token-bearing lock across that operation. Preparation probes the
header and asks the port registry for every I/O window in one `reserve_all`
operation; after a successful permanent port reservation no fallible work
remains. There is still no release and no half-claimed interval.

**Decision — pure mutations name exact host tests.** D-119 assumed every
meaningful defect needed a QEMU boot. Transient configuration ordering is both
hardware-free logic and something QEMU can permissively hide. A mutation may
now name an exact host package and test. The runner accepts only that test's
own `FAILED` verdict; a compile failure or failure elsewhere remains
inconclusive. Machine mutations continue to boot and correlate the exact
machine-check name. Restoration of the source precedes either verdict.

**Rationale.** Disabling decode and restoring command last are the ordering
constraints the PCI protocol needs, while the pure event interface makes every
intermediate state observable without putting a fake device in the kernel.
Putting the registry commit after a closure mechanically enforces rollback for
every future preparation exit instead of relying on a carefully placed
assignment. `PortSpace::reserve_all` already owns the atomic bitmap operation;
the new `wost` wrapper preserves that all-or-none result as typed `PortSpan`s.

**Alternatives.** Serializing two old per-dword probes was rejected because a
lock cannot make their restored interval a simultaneous wide probe. Leaving
decode enabled was rejected because emulator tolerance is not a device
contract. Releasing an early device or port claim on error was rejected
because the registries intentionally have no release and adding one would
create the lifetime race D-138 avoided. Permanently poisoning a failed claim
was safe but contradicted the documented unchanged-on-error API and prevented
a later corrected driver from trying again.

**Consequences.** Host fake configuration tests assert the exact command/BAR
trace, inject a refusal at every access after mutation, continue after restore
failures, and cover malformed masks and final-slot wide BARs. A claim-registry
test injects failure at every preparation edge, and `PortSpace` places a
conflict at every requested-span index; neither may retain an earlier claim.
QEMU still discovers the NVMe controller's 64-bit BAR and boots storage. Its
machine checks prove two offsets cannot claim one bridge twice and a claimed
device's whole I/O window refuses bare access. Ten new persistent mutations
cover the pure ordering/rollback and transaction properties; the two changed
machine mutations were also driven red. PW-201 is `REQUIRED`: the
implementation is established, and the current VMware close must still observe
the controller BAR named by its register row.

## D-188 Uncertain NVMe commands stop the controller or retain every DMA frame — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-169 and closes PW-200

**Context.** D-169 bounded every polled command, but its timeout returned while
the command was still outstanding. The local Identify buffer then dropped;
partial I/O-queue construction dropped queue frames; a failed caller could
drop its read buffer; and a failed bring-up dropped the controller's Admin
queues while the enabled device still held every physical address. A wrong
completion identifier and a queue-memory or MMIO error after ringing the
doorbell had the same ambiguity. Rust ownership covered the host but said
nothing about an independent DMA agent.

NVM Express Base 2.2 sections 3.4.5 and 3.7.2.1 provide the boundary the driver
can prove. Clearing `CC.EN` initiates Controller Reset; observing `CSTS.RDY = 0`
means the outstanding command can no longer be processed. The reset also
deletes the I/O queues, resets the Admin queues and brings the controller idle.
Writing the bit without observing readiness is not that proof.

**Decision.** Pure `nvme::DmaState` records `Idle`, `InFlight`, `Quiesced` and
`Retained` ownership. The driver enters `InFlight` immediately before the
submission doorbell write may publish the command. Only its matching completion
returns to `Idle`; another identifier, a poll failure and timeout remain
outstanding. Every ambiguous exit clears `CC.EN` and waits for `CSTS.RDY = 0`.
Fatal status may end an enable wait, but it cannot substitute for the cleared
ready bit while disabling.

`wost::mm::DmaSegment` is the safe memory owner at that boundary. It exposes a
physical address and host reads/writes while ordinary ownership is certain. If
reset or its observation fails, `retain` removes all safe access and forgets
the underlying `Segment`, permanently withholding those frames from the
allocator. Cleanup retains both Admin queues, both optional I/O queues and the
current command buffer together. A later completion cannot reverse that state.
The I/O pair is moved into `Controller` before its first Create Queue command,
and `Controller::drop` applies the same stop-or-retain rule to partial bring-up
and configured queues.

**Rationale.** Reset plus the readiness observation is the controller's own
proof that DMA has ceased. Permanent retention is the only sound fallback when
that proof cannot be obtained: reusing even one frame would let the device
write into an unrelated future owner. A dedicated owner makes the fallback
unrepresentable as an ordinary `Segment` rather than depending on every error
site remembering not to drop one.

**Alternatives.** Returning directly was the defect. Waiting longer still
leaves a finite timeout with the same edge. Abort is an Admin command that
itself needs live queues and a completion, so it cannot close failures of those
objects. Reset without waiting for `RDY = 0` assumes the exact asynchronous
transition at issue. Leaking all NVMe memory on every error was safe but would
discard the specification's positive quiescence proof and make recoverable
completed-command errors unnecessarily permanent.

**Consequences.** A delayed fake device proves that a failed stop remains
unrecyclable even after a late completion, while a verified stop and a matching
completion permit recycling. QEMU withholds a deliberately retained frame and
runs the production timeout arm after every storage/VFS check; the latter
submits a real read, skips polling, resets the controller and observes
`RDY = 0` before the buffer can return. The three checks were each broken and
observed red, and three persistent mutations preserve those exact failures.
The image now carries 194 machine checks and the register 93 mutations.

## D-189 The running address space exposes operations, never its mutable owner — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-86 and closes PW-102

**Context.** D-86 retained the kernel's `AddressSpace` after activation so a
later stack or device mapping could be added safely. Its access door was
`mem::with_active_space`: any safe kernel module could pass an arbitrary
closure and receive `&mut AddressSpace` whose `Reach::Everywhere` deliberately
permits the kernel half. The same value that maps a stack also exposes
`reclaim(None)`, which can free the root and tracked tables the CPU is walking,
and `unmap`, which can remove an owned live stack and return its frames. No
caller used those operations against live kernel state; the signature made the
soundness boundary depend on that convention.

**Decision.** The closure and the `SPACE` owner are private to `mem`. Production
exports the two operations it actually needs: map one guarded stack and map one
validated device extent. Neither returns or accepts an `AddressSpace`.

Machine-only mapping probes remain, but their cleanup authority is linear.
`map_owned_for_test` returns an `ActiveMapping` whose base and length are
private; `unmap_for_test` consumes that value and can therefore remove only the
fresh mapping which minted it. The stale-stack proof receives the same token
beside its `MappedStack`. User-copy setup can add a user mapping but has no
removal door. The six invalid-unmap probes move behind one fixed, argument-free
operation in `mem`, so a caller cannot substitute an owned kernel address and
cause the probe itself to remove it.

**Rationale.** `AddressSpace` is the right owner while tables are under
construction and for each isolated user space; splitting its public methods
would not make the live kernel instance narrower. The authority boundary is
the holder of that instance. Operation-shaped entry points preserve D-85's
token-bearing lock acquisition while making reclaim and arbitrary removal
unnameable to callers. A consumed mapping token keeps the one legitimate
machine cleanup without turning a test API into the original hole under a new
name.

**Alternatives.** Relying on the existing callers was the defect. Adding a
runtime `is_active` refusal to `AddressSpace::reclaim` would protect only one
door and complicate reclamation of user spaces without removing arbitrary
unmap. A public guard with a reduced trait could still be forgotten or widened
and was more machinery than two production operations need. Removing live
mapping entirely would regress guarded dynamic stacks and discovered device
windows.

**Consequences.** Every former caller now goes through a narrow operation.
QEMU's existing mapping-after-switch, user-copy, rollback, owned-unmap,
invalid-unmap, stale-stack and NVMe device-window checks all remain green in
the 194-check image. The host source proof requires the only closure-shaped
borrow to remain private; its persistent mutation exports that function and
was broken once against the exact named test. No machine check or unsafe
operation was added. The mutation register now contains 94 entries.

## D-190 Page-table ownership grows before allocation, and cleanup refusal is data — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-117 and closes PW-104

**Context.** D-117 made a retired program return its mappings and page tables,
but `AddressSpace` remembered only thirty-two non-root table frames. Every later
table was deliberately forgotten: its mapping remained correct and reclamation
returned a `(tables, lost)` count which admitted the leak. The ordinary program
needs only a handful, so forty steady launch/exit cycles did not cross the
ceiling and could not prove the general ownership claim.

The refusal contract was also too weak at its only production caller.
`AddressSpace::reclaim` returned `None` for an already reclaimed, still-bound,
wrongly released or currently active space. The zombie collector converted any
of those into `(0, 0)`, so a cleanup failure looked like a successful process
which happened to own no table frames. The frames stayed safely leaked, but the
failure was no longer observable after the collector returned.

**Decision.** An `AddressSpace` keeps every non-root table address in a
fallibly grown `Vec<Paddr>`. Before `set` takes and forgets a table frame it
reserves one ownership slot. If that metadata cannot grow, mapping returns
`MapError::OutOfMemory` before a new frame exists; once a frame is taken, its
address is always retained until terminal reclamation. The root remains a
separate field because it must exist before the space can own anything else.

Reclamation now returns `Result<usize, ReclaimError>`. Its errors distinguish
an already reclaimed space, a bound space without release evidence, evidence
for another root, and the space currently in `CR3`. The process collector logs
the exact refusal, carries it in `Reclaimed`, and increments a refusal tally.
The repeated lifecycle proof requires that tally not to move.

**Rationale.** Raising the array ceiling only chooses a later leak. Dynamic
ownership makes memory pressure a refusal before ownership changes rather than
an unbounded loss after it. Walking tables recursively at reclaim time could
recover frames without metadata, but would add a second raw traversal which
must distinguish user-owned lower tables from shared kernel tables. Retaining
the addresses when they are minted is smaller and keeps that distinction out of
the unsafe path. Automatic `Drop` reclamation is not an alternative: a bound
space needs task-table release evidence, and only its construction owner knows
which mapped frames must be removed before the tables.

**Consequences.** `a large space returns every table frame` maps one described
page at thirty-four addresses separated by two megabytes. That creates
thirty-six non-root tables plus the root, beyond D-117's ceiling, and the check
requires both the reported count and the physical allocator to return exactly
to baseline. The existing bound-space refusal now also requires an unchanged
frame tally, and forty program lifecycles require no process table-reclaim
refusal. Limiting the reclaim drain to thirty-two entries reddened only the new
check; that defect is mutation 95. No unsafe operation was added. The image now
carries 195 machine checks.

## D-191 Process construction owns one rollback transaction until the thread is runnable — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-100, D-106, D-115 and D-117; closes PW-103 and PW-109

**Context.** `user::spawn` created an `AddressSpace` and then used `?` through
image, stack, time-page, ring, binding, channel, handle-table and thread
construction. `AddressSpace` deliberately has no automatic `Drop`: only the
process owner knows which owned mappings must be removed before its tables.
Consequently every refusal after the root existed abandoned at least that root;
later refusals also lost image and stack frames, shared-mapping keepalives,
ring pages and table ownership. A `Bootstrap` assembled before
`thread::spawn_in_space` had the same problem when slot fabrication or binding
failed.

The loader had a related ownership gap. Successful placements were published
through the global `PLACED` record and taken by the next `load` call, so a
second or re-entrant construction could replace another call's cleanup data.
The ELF entry was checked only after every segment had been mapped and
`PLACED` written; an invalid entry therefore returned an error whose mappings
no caller could identify. While driving the thread failure edges, the second
fabrication also faulted at address `-24`: `task::retire` replaced the slot with
`Slot::VACANT`, erasing the arena stack top which `fabricate` promises to reuse.

**Decision.** `ProcessConstruction` owns the private address space and the
exact owned ranges mapped into it. Its destructor unmaps those ranges, asks the
task table for release evidence and reclaims every table. The transaction
survives through `thread::spawn_in_space`; only its reserved-slot `arrange`
callback converts it into the `Bootstrap` and `Launch` records immediately
before the scheduler marks the thread ready. All channel, table and ring values
remain ordinary owned locals captured beside the transaction, so their normal
destructors cover every earlier refusal. The callback borrows rather than owns
the prepared transaction: if publication refuses, thread construction retires
the bound task first, and only then can the caller drop and reclaim its tables
with release evidence.

Thread construction exposes three machine-only refusal points after scheduler
reservation, task fabrication and address-space binding. Its arrangement
callback can also refuse publication before the slot becomes runnable. Each
rollback returns both scheduler and task state; the task-table retirement path
preserves the slot's immutable arena stack top while clearing its live state
and binding.

`load_image` now returns a `LoadedImage` containing its entry and exact
placements. The entry is checked during preflight and must lie within the
unrounded memory extent of an executable load segment before the first frame is
taken. There is no global last-load ownership record.

**Rationale.** One linear owner makes the commit boundary visible in the type
and makes ordinary `?` correct. Giving `AddressSpace` a general destructor
cannot remove owned leaf mappings it does not enumerate and cannot prove a
bound task released the root. Scattering cleanup across every error arm would
duplicate ownership transitions whose order must remain explicit.
Returning placements makes concurrent constructions independent by value; a
lock around global last-call state would serialize calls without giving the
right caller durable ownership.

**Alternatives.** Keeping the bounded leak was the defect. Preallocating every
resource before the address space would still leave mapping and thread binding
as fallible steps and would hold scarce objects longer. Making the thread
runnable and then asking it to self-destruct on construction failure cannot
reclaim the stack or tables it is running on. Validating the entry only at the
ring-3 crossing remains safe against execution but is too late to make loading
fail-atomic.

**Consequences.** `every refused spawn returns every resource` stops after each
of fourteen construction edges twice, warming retained allocator backing on the
first pass and requiring an exact second-pass baseline for physical frames,
live heap allocations, returned page/table tallies, handle slots and arena
commitment, channel ends, rings, scheduler slots and process records. It
includes reserved, fabricated and bound task states plus refused launch-record
publication. The loader check now requires an invalid entry to refuse without
changing the frame count and keeps two successful loads' returned placement
records independent.

Skipping transaction table reclamation or the scheduler release after refused
arrangement reddened only the resource-ledger check; skipping entry preflight
reddened only the loader check; restoring the stack-erasing retirement
reproduced the exact pre-verdict page fault. They are mutations 96 through 99.
The first full debug boot then overflowed a guarded kernel stack in a nested
3.9 KiB `finish` return frame; committing the completed values directly into
the reserved slot removed that by-value return, and the same debug image passed
all 196 checks. No unsafe operation was added. The image now carries 196
machine checks.

## D-192 A terminal completion retains its operation until publication succeeds — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-115 and D-167; closes PW-106

**Context.** Cancellation, timer expiry and process teardown removed a pending
operation before posting its terminal completion. They treated a missing
reserved slot as unreachable with `debug_assert!`, then returned. In a release
image that assertion vanished: the operation was gone, its completion
reservation remained outstanding forever, and process collection could see an
empty pending array and release every page the lost operation had been allowed
to reach. D-167 required teardown to wait, but its implementation had turned a
failed wait into unobserved success.

There were two distinct refusal points. A missing completion reservation can be
reported before queue accounting changes. A completion-page bounds failure is
discovered only after the reservation has advanced; returning `false` there
would invite a retry against already-spent accounting even though the slot is
derived entirely from the queue's internal capacities and fixed page layout.

**Decision.** A pending entry remains in its array and carries a private
settling marker while a terminal path posts. Other cancellation, expiry and
teardown paths skip that marker. A post refused before accounting changes
restores the entry to live state and increments a kernel-side refusal tally;
only a successful post removes it. Cancellation reports `STATUS_NO_ROOM` for
its own operation while leaving its target retryable. Expiry and teardown stop
their sweep and let the next caller retry.

Process collection keeps the complete `Bootstrap` in the zombie table while it
settles the ring. It removes and reclaims that exact owner only after
`Queue::is_quiet`; a refusal is warned, counted and leaves the zombie intact.
The final completion-page write is a release assertion because its bounds are
an internal construction invariant and reservation accounting has already
changed. It is diagnosable fatal corruption, not a recoverable post refusal.

**Rationale.** Pending ownership and completion reservation are one
transaction: neither may commit alone. Keeping the operation in place makes a
refusal recoverable without allocating, copying target memory or inventing a
second reservation. A separate teardown side list would duplicate ownership
and need its own capacity and reclamation rules. Treating every post failure as
fatal would prevent silent loss but would discard the available retry path
before queue state changes. Letting collection proceed after a logged refusal
would preserve diagnosis while reintroducing reuse beneath live work.

**Consequences.** `a refused settlement retains every owner` injects the
pre-accounting refusal through cancellation, deadline expiry and a real
faulting process. It requires the pending and reservation tallies to remain
live, cancellation to report pressure, the first collector to retain the
zombie, and a retry to publish exactly one terminal record before reclaim.
The release image passed all 197 checks. Removing the pending-entry restoration
reddened only that check with `passed=196 failed=1 expected=197`; it is mutation
100. The former teardown, deadline and cancellation mutations were retargeted
to the new ownership path and still apply uniquely. No unsafe operation was
added. The image now carries 197 machine checks.

## D-193 An unguarded boot thread cannot open the user boundary — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-92; closes PW-107

**Context.** D-92 deliberately kept booting on the bootloader's unguarded
stack when the guarded replacement could not be allocated. At that point no
shipped path ran untrusted code, so the decision called this a lost guard
rather than a lost boot. D-116 later made a user program part of every shipped
boot without revisiting the fallback. `boot_continue` did not remember which
stack path reached it, and `user::spawn` therefore built a process and opened
ring 3 even when the trusted kernel itself lacked the stack boundary the
security baseline promises.

**Decision.** The boot continuation records whether it was reached through
`continue_on_stack` with a `MappedStack`. The state begins false, and any
unrecognised continuation value also records false. Process construction reads
that boot-global state before allocating an address space and returns the typed
`UnguardedBootStack` refusal unless it is true.

Failure to map the stack remains a degraded boot rather than a panic. The
existing mapping error and the fallback warning diagnose it, the console,
interrupt and storage paths may continue, and the shipped launch reports that
ring 3 is closed. Only the crate root can mark the production state true; the
self-test build can temporarily inject the false state around one attempted
launch and then restores it.

**Rationale.** The guard protects the kernel while it handles untrusted work,
so losing it must revoke that work rather than every diagnostic service. A
panic would be fail-closed but would throw away the machine's ability to say
what failed. Keeping the earlier fallback unchanged would make a best-effort
allocation silently weaken a privilege boundary. Retrying allocation cannot
guarantee progress under the memory pressure which caused the first refusal.
A boot-global fact is smaller than threading a token through every later
process caller, and its sole production writer is the continuation that knows
which path actually ran.

**Consequences.** `an unguarded boot stack closes the user boundary` injects
the exact state left by `boot_continue(0)`, requires the typed refusal, no new
syscall crossing and an unchanged frame, heap, arena, channel, ring, thread and
process-record ledger. Restoring the state lets all later user checks run,
which proves the degraded state is controllable rather than sticky test damage.
Bypassing the process gate launched a real ring-3 program and reddened only
that check with `passed=197 failed=1 expected=198`; it is mutation 101. No
unsafe operation was added. The image now carries 198 machine checks.

## D-194 A forgotten spin-lock guard is an accepted, bounded liveness violation — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-66, D-69 and D-85; closes PW-105

**Context.** `SpinLockGuard::drop` releases the lock, decrements this CPU's
held-lock state and restores the interrupt flag. Safe Rust does not promise
that `Drop` runs: `core::mem::forget(guard)` consumes the guard and leaves all
three states permanently held. The forgotten reference cannot be used again,
so this does not create aliased access to the protected value, but on this
single-CPU kernel the disabled interrupt flag makes the liveness loss global.

Hiding the guard behind a closure does not strengthen that boundary. Safe code
inside the closure can diverge, and a closure API still needs a guard internally
whose destructor panic-abort never runs. An explicit critical-section token can
itself be forgotten or held across a non-returning call. Rust can make accidental
movement or nesting difficult; it cannot guarantee progress from arbitrary safe
code.

**Decision.** Guard destruction is an explicit first-party liveness contract:
code that acquires a `SpinLock` must return through the guard's destructor and
must not deliberately forget it. Violating that contract may halt progress, but
does not widen memory or privilege authority. The bound is the current CPU and
every waiter for that lock; while the kernel has one CPU, that is the whole
machine. D-66's runtime backstops remain mandatory: enabling interrupts,
switching context, abandoning a stack and entering ring 3 all refuse while the
per-CPU held count is nonzero. Production does not force-release a forgotten
guard because it has no proof that a still-live holder cannot resume; only the
terminal panic path has that proof through `PanicToken`.

The self-test build gets a controlled witness, not a recovery API for shipped
code. It consumes a real guard, transfers its interrupt state into a
non-dereferencing recovery owner, marks the lock as deliberately forgotten and
calls `core::mem::forget` on the original guard. The machine can then distinguish
ordinary contention from that deliberate leak before dropping the recovery
owner and restoring the exact lock, accounting and interrupt state. Neither the
marker nor the controlled-forget entry point exists in a shipped build.

**Alternatives.** A closure-hidden lock was rejected because divergence has the
same outcome and converting every call would buy no stronger invariant. A
critical-section token was rejected as the liveness proof because safe code may
forget it, and `Drop`/allocator paths cannot receive one; D-69's thread-context
token remains useful for excluding blocking and accidental nesting. Making
`SpinLockGuard` private was rejected because the kernel must borrow protected
values and would merely move the internal guard that can be leaked. General
force-unlock was rejected as unsound without the panic path's proof that the old
holder can never resume.

**Consequences.** `forgotten lock ownership is distinct from contention` holds
an ordinary guard and observes contention, then deliberately forgets that guard
through the controlled test seam and observes the distinct forgotten state. It
also requires the lock to stay unavailable until recovery and the original
interrupt state and acquisition ability to return afterwards. Removing the
forgotten-state transition reddened only that check with `passed=198 failed=1
expected=199`; it is mutation 102. The release image passed all 199 checks.
The witness adds no unsafe operation and no shipped-image state.

## D-195 NVMe reads cross the doorbell only as validated transfers — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-169; closes PW-203

**Context.** `Controller::read_blocks` multiplied an unchecked block count by
the namespace's block size, built `CDW12` as `blocks - 1`, and submitted it.
Zero underflowed in debug and encoded the maximum transfer in release. Counts
above 65,536 were truncated by the command's sixteen-bit zero-based NLB field.
Neither `lba + blocks` nor the reported namespace extent participated, and the
driver proved only that the DMA run had an address, not that it held every byte
the controller was told it could write.

These are arithmetic obligations, so the controller was the wrong place to
own them. They also fail before publication: treating any as a command error
would ring a doorbell with a malformed extent and make the refusal itself a DMA
memory-safety hazard.

**Decision.** `libs/nvme::ReadTransfer` is the only value the read submission
path accepts. Its constructor requires a non-empty count no greater than 65,536,
a non-zero block size, an end which adds without overflow and does not exceed
the namespace, a byte length which multiplies without overflow, and a DMA byte
capacity at least that large. It retains the LBA, exact byte length and the
already-proved zero-based NLB encoding behind read-only accessors.

`DmaSegment` exposes its owned byte length as an `Option`, alongside its
optional physical address: retained memory is neither addressable nor sizeable.
The controller converts raw caller arguments into `ReadTransfer` before taking
a command identifier, touching a queue entry, changing DMA ownership or writing
a doorbell. The private submission function accepts only that validated value.

The self-test build can intercept that private submission seam. Invalid raw
requests run through the production validator; if a defect admits one, the
interceptor counts it and returns before queue or MMIO mutation. That permits a
real-machine proof that zero, oversized-NLB, namespace-end/overflow and short
DMA requests stop before the doorbell without asking hardware to execute a
known-invalid command.

**Rationale.** A checked length alone is insufficient: a representable byte
count can still describe blocks outside the namespace or a count the command
field truncates. Checking after PRP construction is too late to make the command
shape authoritative, and PRP construction cannot know the allocation's end.
A validated value makes each downstream field a projection of one proof rather
than a second transcription of raw arguments.

**Alternatives.** Inline conditionals in `kernel::nvme` were rejected because
pure bounds would lose host tests and the submission path would still accept raw
values. Clamping was rejected because a successful short read silently changes
the requested operation. Relying on current one-block callers was the defect:
the driver API, not today's call sites, owns the DMA boundary. Submitting the
invalid commands to QEMU for a negative check was rejected because an oversized
DMA write can corrupt the test kernel before it reports a verdict.

**Consequences.** Host tests exhaust the entire encodable NLB count boundary
and cover empty, namespace-last, wrapping, zero-block-size, length-overflow and
one-byte-short DMA cases. The machine check uses the actual controller and DMA
owner while intercepting the final submission seam, requires every malformed
request to be refused, and requires command and interception counts to remain
unchanged. Empty, NLB-width, namespace-wrap, short-buffer and driver-integration
mutations each reddened their exact check; the last produced only `invalid nvme
reads stop before submission` with `passed=199 failed=1 expected=200` and could
not ring real hardware while broken. The release image passed all 200 checks;
the mutation register now contains 107 entries. No unsafe operation was added.

## D-196 Namespace Identify data is a validated 512-byte, metadata-free format before I/O queues exist — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-169 and D-195; closes PW-204

**Context.** `Controller::identify_namespace` copied `NSZE`, masked the low
four bits of `FLBAS`, selected an `LBAF` entry without checking `NLBAF`, and
evaluated `1u32 << LBADS`. A zero namespace became an apparently usable device.
An unavailable or out-of-table format was read as if supported; a hostile
`LBADS` of 32 panicked in debug and used an invalid shift in release; and the
driver silently discarded both per-LBA metadata and enabled protection
information. I/O queues were then created from those unproved fields.

The current storage caller is deliberately narrower than NVMe. D-170 accepts
only 512-byte FAT sectors and uses one fixed sector buffer. The driver supplies
no metadata pointer, does not include metadata in its transfer lengths, does
not implement protection information, and never enables the Host Behavior
