Support feature's 64-format LBA extension. Accepting a format outside that
contract would not be compatibility; it would tell the controller and the
filesystem different byte extents.

**Decision.** `libs/nvme::Namespace` parses the 192-byte mandatory prefix this
policy consumes: the fixed header and all sixteen `LBAF` entries available
without the extension. A value exists only when `NSZE` is non-zero, zero-based
`NLBAF` describes no more than sixteen entries, the low `FLBAS` index is inside
that table, the reserved `FLBAS` bit is clear, the selected `LBAF` has no
reserved bits, `MS` and `DPS` are zero, and `LBADS` is exactly 9. It returns the
namespace extent and the policy's 512-byte logical-block size behind read-only
accessors. No device-controlled shift is evaluated.

The two high `FLBAS` index bits are ignored, as the NVM Command Set requires
when the format extension is not enabled; the extended-metadata placement bit
is likewise inapplicable once `MS` is zero. Relative-performance bits are
accepted because they describe a supported format rather than changing its
layout. Metadata capabilities are not metadata settings and therefore do not
make an otherwise metadata-free selected format unusable.

The kernel reads exactly that prefix out of the completed Identify DMA owner
and passes it to a single configure-and-create function. That function can set
the controller's namespace fields and create I/O queues only after it owns a
`Namespace`. In self-test builds the queue-creation seam can be intercepted
before allocation, command construction or MMIO; malformed synthetic Identify
data must never reach it.

**Rationale.** Supporting 4 KiB blocks would require a storage caller and FAT
policy which consume them; supporting metadata or protection information would
require command fields, buffers, transfer lengths and verification which do not
exist. Those are future features with concrete prerequisites, not encodings to
accept optimistically. Parsing in `libs/nvme` makes every byte-domain and
format-table bound host-testable, while the private typed value prevents the
kernel sequence from reconstructing an unvalidated size.

**Alternatives.** Clamping `LBADS`, treating unavailable formats as 512 bytes,
or falling back to LBA format zero were rejected because each silently reads a
different address space from the one the controller reported. Deferring refusal
until FAT mount was rejected because queue memory and commands would already
have been given to an unsupported namespace. Accepting every power-of-two LBA
size was rejected because the only caller still refuses every size but 512 and
because metadata is independent of the data-size exponent.

**Consequences.** Host properties exhaust `NLBAF`, `FLBAS`, `LBADS`, selected
format control and protection byte domains, every metadata size, the zero and
maximum namespace extents, and the exact 512-byte success corpus. A machine
check feeds the production configure path malformed namespace, format,
metadata, protection and size cases while intercepting queue creation; it
requires exact errors, unchanged namespace/command state and no interception.
Nine parser defects each reddened their exact host check. Replacing a refused
device response with a synthetic valid namespace reddened only `invalid nvme
namespace stops before io queues`, with `passed=200 failed=1 expected=201`;
the interceptor observed the bypass before allocation or MMIO. The release
image then passed all 201 checks and the complete CI matrix; the mutation
register now contains 117 entries. No unsafe operation was added.

## D-197 A refused PCI command enablement closes NVMe before a window exists — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-168 and D-169; advances PW-206

**Context.** The boot path asked the claimed PCI function to enable memory
decode and bus mastering, logged when the command register refused, and then
continued through BAR selection, MMIO mapping, controller reset, DMA queue
allocation and command submission. A controller without bus master cannot
complete DMA and has no separate error to report, so the resulting bounded
timeout described the consequence rather than the cause.

`Device::enable_bus_master` also treated the configuration write as a
one-directional operation. If the write or its readback failed, or if only one
required bit stuck, the command register could retain a partially changed value
while the caller received only `false`. Stopping the driver was necessary but
not sufficient to make the device state attributable.

**Decision.** `libs/pci-config::enable_bus_master` owns a host-testable command
transaction. It reads the original command, returns immediately when memory
decode and bus master are already verified, otherwise writes the preserved
command plus both required bits and reads them back. Any refusal or access loss
after the write attempt triggers an exact original-command restore and another
read. The error distinguishes an access failure or explicit refusal whose
rollback was verified from a restore that could not be verified.

The kernel's `Device` adapts that transaction to the claimed CF8/CFC pair. The
boot sequence can obtain BAR0's validated memory `Window` only from a private
admission function which first completes the command transaction. Failure logs
its exact reason and returns no window; all MMIO mapping, controller register
access, DMA allocation and NVMe commands remain syntactically downstream of the
`Some(Window)` boundary.

Self-test builds can construct a claim-shaped device whose enablement is forced
to fail before any configuration cycle. Passing it through the production
admission function must produce no window and exactly one enable attempt. This
makes the historical log-and-continue defect observable without disabling the
real boot controller or mapping a fabricated physical address.

**Rationale.** Checking only the write's return value proves that the access
mechanism existed, not that a device accepted the bits. Stopping without
rollback avoids host DMA but leaves decode state dependent on which write
failed. Moving the whole rule into `pci-config` keeps configuration sequencing
and failure injection on the host; keeping BAR admission in the kernel keeps
the hardware claim and logging at their real boundary.

**Alternatives.** Waiting for the inevitable NVMe timeout was the defect and
was rejected because it allocates and publishes DMA memory to a controller
known unable to use it. Clearing bus master unconditionally on failure was
rejected because the pre-call command is the only state the transaction owns
and because firmware may have supplied a working enablement already. A boot
feature which disables the real QEMU controller was rejected because it would
erase every later storage check; the claim-shaped injected device exercises the
same admission function without perturbing the live controller.

**Consequences.** Host fakes cover the already-enabled, successful enable,
readback refusal, every access-loss edge, exact rollback and unverifiable
rollback cases. Omitting bus master, accepting a write without readback and
returning without rollback each reddened their exact host check. Restoring the
historical log-and-continue path reddened only `a failed bus master enable stops
before nvme mapping`, with `passed=201 failed=1 expected=202`; the injected
claim performed no configuration access and the check never mapped its fake
address. The release image then passed all 202 checks and the complete CI
matrix; the mutation register now contains 121 entries. No unsafe operation was
added.

**Current disposition (2026-08-30).** Later PCI authority work moved live DMA
admission to `prepared.admit_bus_master` after verified controller disable and
before `nvme::start`. The injected pre-mapping proof above is historical and
does not close that current ordering. PW-206 is `READY`; its remaining proof is
the causal `a failed bus master admission stops before nvme start` machine red
and restored boot.

## D-198 Hardware-free namespaces do not depend on device discovery — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-90 and D-172; closes PW-207

**Context.** `tmpfs` and `devfs` need neither a disk nor PCI, but the shipped
boot surveyed them at the end of `survey_the_bus`. Failure to claim CF8/CFC or
failure to read configuration space returned before that point. PCI discovery
was itself called from interrupt bring-up after the local APIC, so a machine
which correctly refused interrupts also skipped the language-neutral namespace
foundation. The log nevertheless claimed both backends were exercised whatever
the bus held.

**Decision.** The boot continuation owns three separate steps while interrupts
are still disabled: attempt PCI/NVMe discovery, initialize and exercise the
hardware-free filesystems regardless of that attempt's outcome, then bring up
the interrupt controller and clock. PCI discovery keeps its local early returns
and no longer calls filesystem code. A returned bus outcome is deliberately not
used to authorize `tmpfs` or `devfs`; their constructors and VFS survey are an
unconditional sibling step.

The shipped-only degraded image enables a narrow `refuse-pci` fault-injection
feature. Before discovery it permanently claims one configuration-address port
through `wost`'s safe port capability, making the production all-or-none
CF8/CFC claim refuse without issuing a configuration instruction. The same boot
still uses the CPU without x2APIC required by D-90. Its harness now requires the
PCI refusal, tmpfs enumeration, both devfs device resolutions, the no-x2APIC
diagnosis and the final steady-state marker.

**Rationale.** Moving only the filesystem call past the two PCI returns would
leave it dependent on successful interrupt setup, another unrelated hardware
precondition. Enabling interrupts before the existing polled NVMe survey would
change the lock/preemption environment of the storage path for no benefit.
Keeping discovery and the namespace survey adjacent in `boot_continue` retains
the established interrupt-disabled device order while making their lack of
dependency visible in the call graph.

**Alternatives.** A self-test helper returning counters was rejected because it
would prove a model of boot ordering rather than boot the refusal path. Removing
PCI devices from QEMU was rejected because q35 and its UEFI firmware still
provide configuration space, so it does not exercise either early return.
Adding a fifth boot was rejected because the existing degraded boot can carry
both independent refusals without weakening D-90. Treating `tmpfs` and `devfs`
as optional after PCI failure was rejected because their concrete future Wizzy
callers are precisely programs which must still start without storage hardware.

**Consequences.** The degraded feature is built only for the gate image and is
included in the kernel configuration passes so it cannot become an unlinted
crate graph. Harness marker constants are checked against the kernel source.
The unmodified degraded image logged both refusals, enumerated tmpfs, resolved
both devfs devices and settled. Restoring the historical PCI-conditioned call
removed only the filesystem lines and failed the task exactly on missing
`tmpfs:`. The complete CI matrix then passed with 202/202 release and debug
self-tests, shipped liveness and the strengthened degraded boot. The mutation
register now contains 122 entries; no self-test count or unsafe operation was
added.

## D-199 NVMe selection advances only from a completely retired candidate — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-88, D-138, D-168 and D-188; closes PW-208

**Context.** Enumeration counted every NVMe function but remembered only the
first. A malformed, unsupported or non-responsive controller therefore hid a
later usable controller in deterministic BDF order. Simply putting the
addresses in a loop was not sound: a PCI claim and its dynamic I/O windows were
permanent, the enabled command word was not owned for later restoration, and a
device mapping could not be removed. An enable-time NVMe failure could also
return queue frames before a cleanup-owning `Controller` existed.

**Decision.** Permanent claims remain the ownership model for a selected
driver. Candidate discovery gets a narrower **lease** which occupies the same
function and I/O-window registries but may be consumed in one of two ways:
commit it after the controller passes its smoke read, or retire it after exact
rollback. The pure PCI claim registry and port-space bitmap gain all-or-none
release operations; `wost` exposes release only through the unique dynamic
port-span values. Successful command enablement returns the exact original
command, which a retiring lease restores and reads back before either registry
is released. A failed restore leaves the lease quarantined and stops selection.

A device mapping may now be claimed as a releasable register capability. That
capability is the only value which can yield the non-accessing mapping token
again; consuming it ends all safe MMIO access before `AddressSpace` removes the
exact physical/virtual extent, invalidates its pages and makes the last device
window reusable. Ordinary firmware and selected-driver mappings keep the old
permanent `MmioRegion` door.

NVMe constructs its cleanup owner before enabling a controller with host queue
addresses. Every later error explicitly stops the controller and verifies
`RDY = 0`; only a quiesced controller yields its mapping for removal. An
unverified stop retains every reachable DMA run, keeps the mapping and PCI
lease quarantined, and ends fallback. The boot walks candidates in the bus
enumerator's stable bus/device/function order, commits the first controller
which completes bring-up and a one-block smoke read, and tries the next only
after all five retirement boundaries report success.

**Rationale.** A retained DMA run is safe but is not complete teardown, and a
released function claim beside a still-live mapping is a stale capability
which makes reacquisition fail for a reason the registry denies. Conversely,
making every device claim releasable would reopen D-138's stale-handle window
for drivers which are meant to own their hardware for the boot. The lease is
therefore a pre-commit state, not a general unclaim API.

**Alternatives.** Keeping failed candidates permanently claimed as
"quarantined" was rejected because a bounded eight-slot registry would make
the ninth otherwise usable controller unreachable and because the row requires
proof of no leaked claim. Retrying after an unverified reset was rejected even
with retained DMA memory: bus mastering and a live register mapping would
remain outside the selected driver's ownership. Pre-probing controllers before
claim was rejected because reading or writing their BARs is precisely the
access the claim authorizes. A fake-only selector was rejected because it
would not exercise QEMU's real configuration, MMIO, reset or DMA teardown.

**Consequences.** The ordinary QEMU machine carries an earlier namespace-less
NVMe controller and the existing corpus-backed controller. The shipped and
self-test boots must show the first retiring and the second mounting; the
self-test additionally compares claim, device-mapping and free-frame baselines
across the failed attempt. Host tests exhaust release refusal, exact command
restoration and lease reuse. Manual breaks proved that the witnesses reject a
port bit left claimed, a function slot left claimed, a skipped command restore,
a retained mapping record, a missing device-window rollback, a missing dynamic
port return, selection stopped after the first candidate and enablement before
the cleanup owner exists. The releasable token, rather than every fixed
physical-ownership record, carries its virtual extent; the debug boot caught
the redundant alternative overflowing a guarded kernel stack. The complete
gate must pass 203 release and debug boot checks plus shipped and degraded
boots. The mutation register contains 130 entries, and the `wost` unsafe
measure remains within budget at 372 of 380.

## D-200 File reads leave trap context through one bounded worker, and NVMe waits use monotonic deadlines — Status: Accepted (2026-08-27), amends D-153, D-164, D-169 and D-181; closes PW-205 and PW-209

**Context.** `Read` had the asynchronous ring entry but performed the complete
VFS and polled NVMe path inside `RingEnter`. The syscall gate has interrupts
masked, and `nvme::with_controller` held a `SpinLock`, so one delayed command
could suppress the timer and keyboard for its whole five-million-read bound.
The same driver converted `CAP.TO` and command waits to iteration counts even
after the monotonic counter had been calibrated; debug, release and different
processors therefore assigned different real durations to the same policy.
Wizzy's filesystem client is the concrete future caller of this boundary.

**Decision.** `RingEnter` copies, validates and authorizes a Read once, reserves
its terminal completion as before, records an immutable read request, and
offers it to one kernel file worker. The global work queue has eight fixed
slots and allocates nothing at admission. Full means an immediate
submission-time `STATUS_NO_ROOM`, before the device or destination is touched.
The work item holds an `Arc` to the ring, so its three shared pages and data
area remain pinned even if the program retires.

Pending operations distinguish timers, queued reads and running reads. A
queued read may be cancelled without reaching the device; a running read is
too late to cancel and still owns its promised target completion. Program
retirement cancels what has not started but retains the complete zombie while
a running read exists. Only the worker's terminal post makes that ring quiet.
`RingWait` registers on the ring's existing wait queue before rechecking its
completion generation, then switches through the live trap frame. A timer
deadline or a worker completion may wake the same wait; there is no polling
door and no second event plane.

The controller moves to a `ThreadLock`. Only the file worker performs runtime
reads, so it may be preempted while owning the controller without another
thread or interrupt handler waiting for that lock. NVMe I/O queues remain
polled with `IEN = 0`; an MSI-X path would add interrupt allocation, sharing
and controller state without removing the need for deferred VFS service.

`libs/nvme` owns a clock-or-attempt poll limit. Once the monotonic clock exists,
controller-ready waits expire at `CAP.TO` (with the existing 500 ms minimum)
and commands at the kernel's documented five-second service limit, independent
of code generation or CPU rate. Before calibration, bring-up uses the explicit
old fallback: five million command polls, and 20,000 ready polls per millisecond
capped at twenty million. A poll chooses its mode once; a missing boot clock
cannot become an accidental unbounded wait.

**Rationale.** A single worker is the smallest design which moves filesystem
and device service off the trap stack while preserving the read-only driver's
one-command discipline. The fixed queue makes pressure an admission result,
not late allocation. Keeping the existing polled hardware queue avoids
inventing interrupt routing for one controller, while the preemptible worker
removes polling from interrupt latency. Consumed completion reservations and
the queued/running distinction preserve exactly-once settlement through
cancel, completion and death.

**Alternatives.** Polling for a measured short interval inside `RingEnter` was
rejected because the syscall gate still masks interrupts and any acceptable
interval would be a latency policy disguised as an iteration count. Enabling
interrupts inside the handler was rejected because preemption cannot carry a
live trap frame away through an ordinary lock path. A worker per request or an
unbounded pool was rejected by the sixteen-slot thread budget and because
queue pressure would become a completion-time resource failure. MSI-X was
rejected for this slice because the queue was deliberately created with
interrupts disabled and no second controller exists to shape sharing.

**Consequences.** Release QEMU holds a real NVMe command after its doorbell and
observes `RingEnter` return while timer preemption and an injected keyboard IRQ
both progress. Retirement retains the ring until that running read posts one
exact completion. A second check fills all eight worker slots while the worker
is paused, sees the ninth return `STATUS_NO_ROOM`, then observes every admitted
request settle. The shipped program submits a Timer and reaches `RingWait`
through its trap frame rather than polling.

Host tests give a controlled clock arbitrarily many polls without extending
its deadline, exhaust the clockless limit at the exact attempt count, and
cover saturating deadline arithmetic. The six new witnesses were each broken
once; their persistent mutations bring the register to 136. The complete gate
passes 206 release and debug machine checks plus shipped and degraded boots.

## D-201 Ring three opens only with enforced non-execution and a progressing clock — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-12, D-32, D-57, D-96, D-164 and D-166; advances PW-301 and closes PW-302

**Context.** Page-table construction marks data, stacks and shared pages
non-executable, but `EFER.NXE` was enabled only when `CPUID` offered it and
process construction never asked whether the read-back succeeded. On such a
processor the intended W^X boundary was not a property the CPU enforced.
Separately, failed APIC-clock calibration logged that nothing would preempt
and then still launched ring 3. An infinite program could own the processor,
Timer could reserve a completion which no interrupt would ever settle, and
Uptime could report only zero. The first Wizzy runtime is the concrete caller
which must know whether execution and waiting exist before it starts.

**Decision — the minimum ring-3 contract is NX plus monotonic progress.** The
kernel may cross into ring 3 only after the enabled-protection read-back says
the no-execute bit is active and the monotonic/APIC clock is calibrated. The
existing guarded-boot-stack prerequisite remains independent and mandatory.
Process construction checks all three before allocating an address space, and
returns a typed refusal naming the missing prerequisite.

WP remains architectural and unconditionally enabled and read back. SMEP,
SMAP and UMIP remain enabled whenever `CPUID` offers them and remain part of
the preferred security baseline, but absence of those three is a supported
diagnostic fallback: the page-table user/supervisor boundary and checked copy
door still exist. NX is different because it is the mechanism which makes
every non-code mapping non-executable. A machine without it may continue far
enough to diagnose itself where its inherited mappings permit, but it is not a
supported userspace target and receives no weaker ring-3 mode.

Timer admission asks the same live calibration predicate before reserving a
pending slot. Without it the operation completes immediately with
`STATUS_UNAVAILABLE`; it is never recorded as in flight. The time page may
still exist as `MODE_NONE`, and Uptime still exists for the post-launch
revocation design PW-303 owns, but a boot which never calibrated cannot launch
a program merely so that both fallbacks can answer zero forever.

**Rationale.** Fail-closed admission is smaller and more truthful than a
second scheduler clock. A PIT interrupt path would need routing, tick policy,
conversion and independent validation; PW-303 must cost those against CPUID
frequency leaves and another clocksource rather than smuggle them in as a
fallback. Keeping the kernel prompt and hardware-free namespaces alive still
makes a refused machine diagnosable without granting unbounded execution.

**Alternatives.** Treating NX as optional and omitting `NO_EXECUTE` from page
entries was rejected because it changes W^X into W-or-X-by-convention exactly
where D-12 requires hardware enforcement. Launching only programs which are
expected to yield was rejected because the kernel cannot verify that property
of arbitrary machine code, including the future compiler artifact. Admitting
Timer and reporting failure later was rejected because admission already
consumed the terminal reservation and promised progress. Using an iteration
bound as preemption was rejected because code which never traps has no loop
the kernel can count.

**Consequences.** Two release-QEMU checks inject the missing prerequisites at
the same predicates production uses, observe typed pre-allocation refusals, no
syscall crossing and exact resource ledgers, and prove a clockless Timer posts
one immediate unavailable completion with nothing pending. Bypassing the NX,
user-clock and Timer-clock gates separately reddened only their named checks;
all three have persistent mutations. The degraded `qemu64` boot reports
mandatory `wp nx`, omits optional SMEP/SMAP/UMIP, and settles after the exact
clock-based ring-3 refusal. The complete gate now carries 208 machine checks
and 139 mutations. PW-301 is `REQUIRED`: the current phase-close VMware round
must show NX, calibration and successful user launch together. PW-303 still
owns clocksource qualification and post-boot revocation; this decision does
not claim those solved.

## D-202 The idle-start latch reserves an attempt and commits only a live thread — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-61 and D-117; closes PW-306

**Context.** `start_idle` claimed a one-shot latch before asking the bounded
thread table for a slot. If the table was transiently full, `spawn` returned
`Full` but the latch remained claimed. Every later call then returned before
retrying, leaving a kernel which could become idle without its idle thread or
the deferred cleanup and refusal-reporting work that thread owns. Wizzy
process churn is the concrete caller which will make transient slot pressure
ordinary rather than synthetic.

**Decision.** Idle admission has three states: unstarted, starting and
started. A caller atomically reserves `unstarted -> starting`; competing or
later callers do nothing while that reservation exists. Any spawn refusal
rolls the state back to unstarted, while a successful spawn commits started.
The new slot is marked `Idle` through `spawn_prepared`'s existing arrangement
window, while it is still reserved and cannot be scheduled, rather than being
published as an ordinary runnable thread and reclassified afterwards.

**Rationale.** The state describes the work rather than merely whether one
caller has passed a line. Rollback makes retry explicit, and the intermediate
reservation preserves exactly-one creation if multiple CPUs eventually call
the idempotent entry. Reusing the spawn transaction's arrangement window also
keeps scheduler policy true at the first instant the slot becomes runnable.

**Alternatives.** Claiming `Once` after `spawn` was rejected because two
callers could each publish a thread before either claimed it. Clearing or
extending the general `Once` abstraction was rejected because hardware
initialization uses its irreversible semantics correctly; this retry belongs
to idle-thread policy. Reserving a raw table slot in `start_idle` was rejected
because it would duplicate `spawn_prepared`'s thread/task rollback protocol.

**Consequences.** Release QEMU fills every spawnable slot, observes an
idle-start refusal with no idle thread, releases the fillers, retries more than
once, and finds exactly one live idle slot consuming exactly one resource. A
self-test-only recovery lets the deliberately burned state continue through
the rest of the suite; removing the rollback reddened only `a failed idle
start can be retried exactly once` with 208/209. Its persistent mutation brings
the register to 140 entries and the complete gate carries 209 machine checks.

## D-203 Retired programs wake one mandatory service worker for bounded reclamation — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-117, D-133 and D-200; closes PW-307

**Context.** A retired program gave its thread slot back immediately but left
its address space, mappings, ring, handles and objects in `ZOMBIES`. Only the
idle loop or the beginning of a later spawn called `collect`. Both bounded the
leak, but neither guaranteed progress: a continuously busy machine which
stopped creating processes could retain the last dead program forever. The
future Wizzy process manager is the concrete caller which needs exit to imply
eventual resource return without manufacturing another spawn.

**Decision.** The bounded file worker becomes the kernel service worker. It
continues to own every deferred Read and additionally consumes one reclamation
request per retired program. `orphan` moves ownership into `ZOMBIES`, increments
a counted request generation and wakes the worker through its existing wait
queue. That wake is legal from trap context and uses D-133's ordinary unblock
path, which makes the service thread runnable and arms the scheduler.

The worker performs at most one collection and one file operation per loop,
so sustained process death cannot starve reads and sustained reads cannot
starve reclamation. It collects only after the dying thread has switched away;
the retirement path still frees nothing on its own stack or address space.
Idle and pre-spawn collection remain safe opportunistic fallbacks. Because
this progress guarantee depends on the worker, process construction refuses
before allocation unless the worker is ready; a boot which could not reserve
that kernel thread does not open ring 3.

**Rationale.** One existing preemptible thread is enough. A dedicated reaper
would permanently spend another of sixteen slots and duplicate wait/wake
machinery, while collecting at trap exit would reclaim the stack and tables
currently executing. Polling from the timer would move allocation and object
destruction into handler context. A counted wake retains every event even if
several programs retire before the worker runs, unlike a boolean hint.

**Alternatives.** Leaving the next-spawn fallback as the progress contract was
rejected because workloads may stop spawning after any exit. Scheduling the
idle class periodically was rejected because it would no longer mean “only
when no normal work exists” and would reintroduce idle timer traffic. Giving
file work unconditional priority was rejected because a full producer could
starve cleanup; giving cleanup unconditional priority was rejected for the
same reason in reverse.

**Consequences.** Release QEMU first injected missing worker readiness and
observed typed `NoServiceWorker` refusal before any resource or syscall-count
change. With the real worker, a normal spinner kept the machine busy while a
program retired without a later spawn or direct collection; the service worker
reclaimed its pages and tables, restored the complete spawn-resource ledger,
and advanced its own reap count while the idle halt count remained unchanged.
Bypassing the launch prerequisite and separately removing the retirement wake
each reddened only `a busy machine reaps a program without another spawn` with
209/210. The two persistent mutations bring the register to 142 entries and
the complete gate carries 210 machine checks. D-204's final gate exposed one
publication-order race in this older protocol: the retirement generation
advanced before `orphan` recorded the program's last rites, so an acquiring
observer could see retirement without its promised evidence. Publishing the
generation after `orphan` closes that window; the existing bootstrap-ownership
check caught the real race with 210/211 before the repair.

## D-204 Handle-table ownership identities widen and refuse exhaustion — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-78 and D-132; closes PW-402

**Context.** The arena authorises a decoded handle with one ownership
comparison, `entry.owner == table.id`. That identity was a wrapping `u32`
allocated with `fetch_add`, so after four billion table constructions a new
table could receive an identity still held by an old table. Its mixer would
also repeat, turning the old table's handle into authority in the new table.
This is independent of the deliberately wrapping 12-bit slot generation: a
generation limits stale-handle detection for one reused slot, while the table
identity is the isolation boundary between principals. The future Wizzy
process manager is the concrete caller which will create tables for the life
of the system rather than only during a bounded boot check.

**Decision.** A table identity is a non-wrapping `u64`. The arena owns the
next identity beside quota commitment, under the same leaf lock, so reserving
the identity and committing the table's complete quota is one transaction.
`u64::MAX` is the exhausted-state sentinel and is never issued; construction
returns typed `IdentityExhausted` without changing commitment when no successor
exists. The checked successor is pure arithmetic in `libs/handle-space`, where
the maximum boundary is host-testable.

The 32-bit userspace handle format does not change. `Mixer::for_table` derives
from the identity's low 32 bits, so mixers may repeat after 2^32 tables; D-132
already makes the mixer an accidental-value defence rather than authority.
The full 64-bit identity remains on every arena entry and is the ownership
comparison, so equal mixers cannot cross tables.

**Rationale.** Refusing wrap makes the security invariant structural: no live
or dead identity is ever issued again. Widening before refusal makes exhaustion
unreachable under any plausible uptime without pretending infinity, and the
sentinel avoids a second flag or a wider atomic the target does not provide.
Keeping identity allocation inside `ARENA` also avoids a quota rollback path
and prevents two constructors from observing the same last value.

**Alternatives.** Saturating the old `u32` was rejected because process churn
can make four billion a system-lifetime concern and a permanent refusal should
not be that close. Reusing identities after scanning for live owners was
rejected because a dead table's leaked handle value could become valid again,
and the scan would turn construction into a global lifetime protocol. Random
identities were rejected because collision refusal still needs a registry and
entropy is not uniqueness. Widening the handle or mixer was rejected because
neither is the authority check and both would spend ABI bits without fixing
ownership.

**Consequences.** The host boundary check proves the penultimate state advances
to the sentinel and the sentinel has no successor; wrapping it failed that
exact test with `Some(0)`. Release QEMU held the last constructible table and
an event handle live, observed two typed exhaustion refusals with unchanged
arena commitment, resolved the original handle afterwards, and restored the
exact baseline on teardown. Wrapping the production successor and separately
stopping only its final advance each reddened only `table identities never
wrap or repeat` with 210/211; the second path constructed another table with
the live owner's identity and the witness reached the resulting authority
alias. The three persistent mutations bring the register to 145 entries and
the complete gate carries 211 machine checks.

## D-205 Every bounded I/O APIC is inventoried and one GSI has one owner — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-49 and D-86; closes PW-304

**Context.** The MADT walker logged every I/O APIC structure and retained only
the first. Paging consequently mapped and masked only that controller, and
keyboard routing fell back to polling whenever an interrupt-source override
named a GSI owned by a later controller. ACPI 6.5 section 5.2.12.3 says that
each structure supplies only a GSI base; software must read that controller's
Max Redirection Entry field to learn the other end of its range. Ordering the
structures or comparing their bases therefore cannot identify an owner.

**Decision.** `acpi-tables` builds one checked MADT interrupt inventory. The
kernel accepts at most sixteen I/O APIC descriptions, preserves every one up
to that bound, and refuses the complete inventory rather than silently
truncating a seventeenth. Sixteen is an explicit boot-resource policy: it
temporarily spends at most half of the address space's thirty-two device
mapping records and sixteen pages while leaving headroom for existing device
callers. A system above the bound keeps the safe polled-keyboard path.

After the kernel owns its active tables and before it accepts interrupts, it
maps every described controller with releasable ownership, reads the hardware
entry count and masks every reported line. Pure `x86-apic` range logic rejects
zero length, a range whose last `u32` GSI is unrepresentable, and any overlap
between controllers. It then selects the unique range containing the resolved
keyboard GSI. Every non-owner mapping is returned; the chosen controller alone
converts its mapping to permanent access and survives for routing and readback.
Any map, register, range, ownership or cleanup refusal leaves the keyboard
polled and never enables its interrupt source.

**Rationale.** The hardware count is the authority ACPI names, so reading all
bounded candidates is the only way to distinguish a gap, a later owner and an
ambiguous overlap. Masking precedes the CPU's interrupt-enable transition just
as it did for the former single controller. Releasable probing prevents a
larger correct firmware description from permanently consuming the device
window merely because most controllers do not own the one line used today.

**Alternatives.** Keeping the first controller was the defect. Choosing the
largest base not above the GSI was rejected because the preceding controller's
hardware range may end early or overlap it. Treating the next base as the
previous range's end was rejected for the same reason and cannot bound the
last controller. Mapping all descriptions permanently was correct but spent a
scarce registry slot per unused controller. Dynamic allocation without a count
limit was rejected because a checksummed but hostile one-megabyte MADT could
turn boot into unbounded device mapping work.

**Consequences.** The host MADT corpus retained two controllers in firmware
order and refused a third against a two-controller bound. Pure APIC tests
rejected empty and overflowing ranges, rejected an overlap anywhere in the
inventory, and selected a later controller across a real gap. Each of those
five properties was broken with its exact production mutation and reddened
only its named host test; their persistent mutations bring the register to 150
entries.

Release QEMU then exercised the complete hardware path: it mapped the reported
controller releasably, read and masked its hardware-sized range, returned the
probe mapping, remapped only the selected owner, routed GSI 1 to vector 33 and
passed the existing route, readback, refusal and delivered-IRQ checks. The
complete image passed 211/211. That boot also exposed an older signal-wakeup
witness racing the D-203 service worker: its global blocked-thread count could
advance before the event waiter blocked. Waiting for that exact spawned slot
removed the witness race; the repaired image passed 211/211 without changing
the signal protocol or adding a claim. No unsafe operation was added.

## D-206 Hostile inputs end at typed refusal, while internal corruption remains fatal — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-41, D-115 and D-170; closes PW-400

**Context.** The pre-Wizzy audit found four target-side `expect` calls and a
larger claim: malformed ring, image, firmware, filesystem and device data must
not panic either release or debug kernels. D-191 subsequently removed the two
kernel calls by making reserved-slot publication checked. The other two are in
`PortSpan::port_for`, behind read/write methods no driver calls: dynamic PCI
I/O windows are currently ownership leases, not register interfaces. Keeping
an unused safe hardware door solely to preserve its documented panic violates
D-41's no-speculative-API rule.

The wider inspection found one reachable arithmetic panic rather than an
`expect`. `fat32::Bpb::parse` accepted a table extent at or beyond the volume's
total sector count. `Bpb::clusters` then subtracted the larger extent from the
smaller total: a debug kernel panicked, while release wrapped and could treat
off-volume clusters as data. A valid-looking maximum file size and offset also
drove `skipped + cluster_bytes` through `u32` overflow while walking a corrupt
chain.

**Decision.** Target boundary crates deny production `unwrap`, `expect` and
direct `panic` shortcuts with compiler lints; tests may use them to state their
fixtures. `kernel` and `wost` deny production `unwrap` and `expect` across the
whole crate. A repository check keeps those declarations on the explicit
boundary inventory. This is deliberately not a blanket ban on assertions:
trap, scheduler and ring assertions name internal state corruption after safe
recovery has become impossible, and treating those as malformed-input
refusals would let the machine continue with two ownership ledgers disagreeing.

`PortSpan` remains an opaque, consuming ownership lease. Its unused accessors
and read/write operations are removed; the first real I/O-BAR driver must add
the smallest checked interface its registers force. FAT construction validates
that the complete reserved-plus-table extent precedes `total_sectors` and that
the root cluster lies in the resulting complete-cluster count before a `Bpb`
can exist. File-offset walking splits the offset into a bounded cluster quotient
and in-cluster remainder, so no accumulated byte counter can wrap.

**Rationale.** A parser returning `Result` while indexing or subtracting before
the refusal is not total. Establishing the geometry once gives every later
method a type invariant and avoids scattering defensive saturation that would
turn corruption into plausible addresses. Quotient/remainder expresses the
file position directly and costs no more device reads than repeated addition.
Compiler lints make the easy regression fail at its source; corpus tests remain
necessary for arithmetic and indexing whose safety comes from prior checks.

**Alternatives.** Saturating the FAT subtraction was rejected because an
impossible layout would mount as an empty or enormous volume instead of being
named malformed. Clamping the root cluster was rejected because it changes
which directory firmware supplied. Returning errors from the unused dynamic
port accessors was rejected because no caller exists to define or exercise the
right error contract. Banning every assertion was rejected because a failed
irreversible scheduler or completion transition has no safe state to return
to; the boundary proof is that hostile values cannot select those indices.

**Consequences.** The historical four target-side `expect` calls are gone:
D-191 removed the two reserved-slot calls, and this decision removes the two
unused dynamic-port calls together with their entire speculative access API.
That deletion also lowers `wost`'s measured unsafe-operation count from 372 to
370. Compiler lints now guard `kernel`, `wost` and the explicit nine-crate
boundary inventory; inserting a production `expect` made Clippy fail at that
line, while removing a lint declaration or restoring a `PortSpan` accessor
made the repository check fail.

Three FAT host witnesses cover an impossible table extent, a root cluster
outside the complete data area and a maximum file offset on a corrupt chain.
Each was broken against the old expression and failed for its named reason:
the first and third reproduced debug arithmetic overflow, and the second
accepted the malformed geometry. The existing adversarial ACPI, ELF, PCI,
NVMe, ring, path, keyboard and APIC corpora continue to exercise the other
checked constructors. Five persistent host mutations retain the new source
and arithmetic witnesses, bringing the registry to 155. Release and debug
QEMU both mount and read the valid FAT corpus and pass all 211 machine checks;
no machine protocol or unsafe operation was added.

## D-207 A foreign FAT corpus is pinned as exact sparse sectors — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-16 and D-170; closes PW-210

**Context.** D-170's oracle has two readers but one writer: `fatfs` creates the
volume which both it and `libs/fat32` read. Agreement catches a reader defect,
but a misconception shared with that one formatter can make both readers agree
about bytes no independent formatter would emit. PW-210 makes that proof gap
finite. Pulling `mkfs.fat` or `mtools` into the ordinary build would instead
reopen D-16's host-tool dependency and make CI depend on the host distribution.
A raw valid FAT32 volume is at least tens of MiB even when almost every sector
is zero, so committing it literally would also make the working tree pay for
empty space.

**Decision.** One 64 MiB FAT32 volume is produced outside the build by the
Ubuntu `dosfstools` 4.2-1.2build1 `mkfs.fat` and `mtools` 4.0.49-1 packages.
Their package versions, archive paths, package digests, upstream homes and
licenses are recorded beside the artifact. Neither package nor executable is
vendored. The resulting volume has its own SHA-256 and is committed as a
versioned sparse-sector envelope: the header states the exact expanded length,
sector size and full-image digest, each following record carries one complete
non-zero sector, and every absent sector is exactly zero. The test parser
rejects duplicate, partial, out-of-range and malformed records before
reconstructing the bytes and checking the full-image digest.

The foreign formatter uses non-default reserved geometry and the population
tool leaves valid layouts chosen to defeat the local corpus's conveniences: a
root directory spanning several clusters, a deleted slot before later live
entries, long-name fragments and a file whose cluster chain crosses separated
holes. Host tests read the same reconstructed bytes with `fatfs` and
`libs/fat32`, compare their complete root inventories and file contents, and
independently inspect enough raw layout to prove those cases are present. The
existing locally generated corpus stays: it is the byte-identical image the
kernel boots, while the foreign corpus is an independent host-side format
witness.

**Rationale.** The output bytes, not availability of the generating tools, are
the evidence the reader needs. Pinning both the envelope and expanded image
distinguishes corruption in the compact representation from a change to the
filesystem itself. Whole non-zero sectors keep reconstruction auditable and
need no compression dependency or decoder with its own format surface. A
multi-cluster directory and fragmented file force both kinds of FAT chain walk;
deleted and long-name entries force the two skip cases between live entries.

**Alternatives.** Installing the tools in WSL or requiring them in CI was
rejected because the repository gate must remain self-contained. Generating a
second image with another Rust crate at test time was rejected because that is
still a live dependency rather than pinned independent evidence. Committing
the raw image was rejected because zero-filled sectors convey no additional
proof. Replacing the local corpus was rejected because only it proves that the
host oracle and booted NVMe bytes are identical.

**Consequences.** The 133-line envelope carries 129 non-zero sectors and
reconstructs to exactly 67,108,864 bytes with SHA-256
`06a6ad589c3652731fc60bc669e4e20bc4576da7761c18be0dc9c800fa4d1576`;
the adjacent vendor listing separately pins the envelope itself. Raw host
inspection proves the 64 reserved sectors, two tables, multi-cluster root,
deleted entry before later live entries, volume label, long-name fragments and
40-cluster non-contiguous file are in those bytes rather than merely intended
by the generator.

`fatfs` and `libs/fat32` agree on all 44 root entries, the long file through its
respective long and short names, a nested file and every position-dependent
byte of the fragmented file. Permitting a duplicate envelope sector made the
exact envelope test fail; ending a directory at its first cluster made the
reader lose `FRAG.BIN` and the exact disagreement test fail. Two persistent
host mutations retain those witnesses, bringing the registry to 157. The
ordinary corpus and shipped image are unchanged; release and debug QEMU still
mount and read those exact NVMe bytes and pass all 211 machine checks.

## D-208 Mutation sweeps run from a journalled tracked-file copy — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-119, D-134 and D-175; closes PW-502

**Context.** D-119 restores a mutated file before any ordinary error may leave
the runner, but a process killed between the write and restoration has no Rust
error path to execute. The live checkout and its index are therefore exposed
for the entire build and boot behind every mutation. A 157-entry phase-close
sweep turns that small interval into hours of repeated risk, and an interrupted
run starts again at mutation one because it records no durable progress.

**Decision.** A mutation sweep requires a clean `HEAD`, inventories Git's
tracked files with optional index refresh disabled, and records the commit plus
exact source and index digests. It copies only those tracked files beneath
`target/mutate/<commit>-<registry>/workspace`, gives that copy a private Cargo
target directory, and directs every host build, image build and QEMU boot there.
The source checkout is read-only input to the runner. It is verified against
the recorded digests when a sweep starts, resumes and finishes.

One OS advisory lock covers the mutation state root. The lock file may remain,
but the kernel releases its lock when the process dies; a live second runner is
refused while a killed runner can be resumed without deleting a sentinel or
guessing whether its PID was reused. The lock is not inherited as a protocol
by build or QEMU children.

Progress uses two alternating, checksummed journal slots. Each complete slot
names the source commit, mutation-registry digest, source and index digests,
generation, active mutation and every completed exact outcome. The newer valid
generation wins; if a kill tears its write, the prior valid slot remains. The
active mutation is journalled and synced before its sandbox file changes. On
resume that one file is first restored from the still-verified source and
checked byte-for-byte, then the same mutation runs again. An outcome is synced
only after restoration is verified. Completed mutations are not repeated.

At a completed sweep, a durable result summary replaces the resumable slots;
the copied workspace and private build cache may remain under ignored `target/`
for the next invocation. No recursive cleanup is required for correctness.

**Rationale.** A signal-safe restoration handler cannot cover termination,
power loss or a killed process, and promising that every exit runs a destructor
would restate the defect. Moving the only writes out of the checkout makes
interruption harmless by construction. A tracked-file copy is smaller and
less stateful than `git worktree`: it neither changes `.git/worktrees` nor
requires cleanup of Git metadata after a crash. Alternating whole-state slots
avoid depending on rename-over-existing semantics, which differ on Windows,
while retaining the last known complete state.

**Alternatives.** A `Drop` restoration guard was rejected because process death
does not run it. A signal handler was rejected because filesystem and allocator
work is not signal-safe and Windows termination is not the Unix signal model.
An isolated Git worktree was rejected because it protects source bytes but adds
repository metadata which an interrupted cleanup can strand. A fresh copy per
mutation was rejected because it discards Cargo's cache and durable progress
without buying more isolation than one commit-pinned copy already provides.
An unchecksummed single journal was rejected because the interruption being
handled can occur while that journal itself is being written.

**Consequences.** `mutation_workspace::Session` owns the advisory lock, exact
Git baseline, immutable tracked-file snapshot, writable workspace, private
build directory and alternating journal. The runner restores an interrupted
active file before rerunning it, records an outcome only after exact restore,
and verifies the source plus index before retiring the journal. Host witnesses
also receive the private Cargo target explicitly.

Real helper processes were killed after announcing both build and boot work.
A live second lock was refused; after each kill the OS-released lock was
reacquired, the active journal reloaded and the sandbox restored while fixture
source and index bytes remained exact. A real temporary Git repository proved
that only tracked files reach a distinct workspace and that ignored files and
`.git` do not. A two-slot test selected the newest complete generation and fell
back after its newest slot was torn. Redirecting the workspace to the checkout,
bypassing the private Cargo target, bypassing the lock, omitting restore and
selecting the oldest journal each made only its named test red. Five persistent
host mutations retain those witnesses, bringing the registry to 162.

## D-209 A mutation is causal only across a green baseline and an exact new verdict — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-119, D-134 and D-175; closes PW-504

**Context.** D-134 requires a mutation's named check to fail, but observes only
the mutated run. A check already red in the pristine source therefore satisfies
the same comparison, and an unrelated failure which prevents the named check
from running is currently called a survivor rather than distinguished from a
green mutation. The three mutations whose expected outcome is a kernel panic
are weaker still: any panic, regardless of its message, is credited to them.
D-208 makes a pristine, commit-pinned source snapshot available before every
fresh or resumed invocation, so the missing causal comparison is now finite.

**Decision.** Before writing any remaining mutation, each invocation runs one
green baseline for every witness class those mutations need: the complete host
suite, the release self-test image and the degraded release image. A resumed
invocation first restores its active sandbox file and then reruns the relevant
baselines. Baseline success is intentionally not journalled; after a killed
process, repeating the evidence is what proves the restored build cache and
source still produce green artifacts. If any baseline is red, panics, times
out, fails to build or misses a required marker, the sweep stops before
journalling or writing a mutation.

The self-test harness returns a typed observation to the mutation runner:
`Passed`, `Failed` with the exact ordered check names, or `Panicked` with the
exact serial panic transcript. Ordinary `test-boot` still accepts only `Passed`.
Against the green baseline, a `Check` mutation is caught only by a final failed
verdict containing its complete check name, and a `Panic` mutation only by a
panic transcript containing its registry-pinned marker. A passed mutated run is a
survivor. A different failed check, different panic, malformed verdict, build
failure, timeout or harness failure is inconclusive and never credited. The
degraded-image witnesses retain their exact missing-marker comparison, now
after one baseline which proved every required marker was present.

The baseline is per witness class, not per mutation. Every mutation in an
invocation starts from the same byte-exact snapshot and is restored before its
outcome is durable, so repeating an identical clean boot hundreds of times
adds no causal information. One baseline per invocation adds at most the host
suite and two boots, while a resume deliberately pays that bounded cost again.

**Rationale.** Causality needs both sides of the transition. “This check is red
after the edit” does not establish that the edit made it red; “the pristine
artifact passed, then this exact check or panic marker appeared” does. Treating
a wrong failure as inconclusive also keeps two different repairs distinct: a
survivor needs a stronger check, while a wrong verdict needs a narrower or
corrected mutation. Typed observations keep that distinction out of formatted
`anyhow` text.

**Alternatives.** Trusting the last `ci` run was rejected because it may name a
different commit, target directory or process lifetime and is not resumable
evidence. A baseline before every mutation was rejected because the immutable
snapshot makes those runs identical and the extra machine hours prove nothing
new. Recording only a generic panic was rejected because a mutation can panic
earlier for an unrelated reason. Requiring the named check to be the only red
check was rejected because several deliberate defects legitimately violate
multiple downstream invariants; the causal claim is about the named transition,
not the mutation's entire blast radius.

**Consequences.** `cargo xtask mutate` now restores any active mutation and
then proves the full host suite, release self-test image and/or degraded release
image green exactly once for the witness classes still ahead. The self-test
harness preserves a typed pass, all named failures, or the complete serial
panic transcript; it rejects a failed count whose names are incomplete. The
runner credits only the registered check name or panic marker and reports every
other failure as inconclusive rather than caught or survived.

Release QEMU measured the three terminal causes as
`faulting address 0x0000600000000000`,
`a trap handler may not take a thread lock`, and
`address 0xffffffffffffffe8`; each is pinned in the registry. Admitting a red
baseline, accepting a wrong check, accepting a wrong panic, erasing a panic
continuation, accepting unnamed failures and omitting an exact panic marker
each made only its named host check red before restoration. Six persistent host
mutations retain those witnesses, bringing the registry to 168.

## D-210 Every pure crate keeps one load-bearing break alive — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-28 and D-189; closes PW-503

**Context.** Host and `libs/` checks have always been broken once when written,
but D-119 originally admitted only machine mutations. D-189 later admitted
exact host tests for the device-transaction work that needed them, leaving the
older break evidence historical. The present registry has host mutations in
seven of the twenty-three pure crates. The other sixteen include the scheduler,
ELF loader, frame and slab allocators, MMIO bound, rooted path splitter, ring
admission, time arithmetic, page permissions and CPU table encodings. A future
change can make any of their checks stop reaching production code without the
one-off break ever running again. D-209 now supplies the missing pristine host
baseline and exact-test attribution.

**Decision.** Every current `libs/` package carries at least one persistent
mutation of production source, caught by one exact test in that same package.
The selected mutation is the highest-consequence stable transformation found
in each previously unrepresented crate:

| Crate | Deliberate defect retained | Exact witness |
|---|---|---|
| `eevdf` | an overrun slice wraps into an enormous remainder | `a_thread_past_its_deadline_has_no_slice_left` |
| `elf64` | a segment extent wraps into the image | `a_loader_can_ask_whether_the_contents_fit` |
| `frame-space` | a multi-frame free mutates before the whole run is valid | `freeing_a_run_is_all_or_nothing` |
| `mmio-range` | one byte past a region is admitted | `a_span_one_byte_past_the_region_is_refused` |
| `path-walk` | `..` at the root is clamped rather than refused | `ascending_past_the_start_is_refused_not_clamped` |
| `pixel` | a padded framebuffer is mapped by visible-row bytes | `a_padded_framebuffer_spans_its_pitch` |
| `ps2-keys` | set 1 swallows the left-shift release as a reply | `set_1_reads_aa_as_a_shift_release_not_a_self_test_result` |
| `ring-proto` | admission ignores occupied completion slots | `the_reservation_invariant_holds_under_interleaving` |
| `slab-layout` | an over-aligned zero-size allocation asks for zero frames | `a_zero_sized_request_too_aligned_for_a_class_still_gets_a_frame` |
| `stack-layout` | a stack begins where its guard begins | `every_stack_has_its_guard_immediately_below` |
| `timebase` | updates discard their fractional nanosecond carry | `a_thousand_updates_do_not_drift_from_one_conversion` |
| `trap-cause` | the write-fault reader tests the user bit | `every_page_fault_bit_is_read_on_its_own` |
| `x86-cpuid` | a compacted-state offset truncates through `u32` | `a_layout_that_overflows_a_u32_offset_is_not_consistent` |
| `x86-paging` | permission intersection becomes union | `intersection_keeps_only_what_both_hold` |
| `x86-pit` | calibration floors instead of rounding to nearest | `rounding_is_to_nearest_not_floor` |
| `x86-tables` | a user-callable IDT gate receives the wrong privilege bits | `a_user_callable_gate_differs_only_in_privilege` |

A host repository check derives the package domain from `HOST_PACKAGES` and
requires every non-`xtask` package to appear in a `HostTest` mutation. Its own
mutation removes one package from that coverage. This is a floor, not a quota:
existing crates with several independent high-risk transactions keep several
mutations, and a new property still gets its own mutation under D-119.

Only transformations that apply exactly once, compile, execute the intended
test and make that test's own verdict red are admitted. Mutating a test,
depending on timing, breaking compilation, or relying on another test's
failure proves nothing and remains inconclusive under D-209.

**Rationale.** One live defect per pure crate proves the complete path from
production source through that crate's tests and the mutation runner. It does
not claim every assertion is independently mutation-tested; that would turn
PW-503 into an unbounded score. Choosing authority, bounds, ownership and
hardware-encoding defects keeps the floor about consequences rather than line
coverage.

**Alternatives.** Keeping the historical red records was rejected because
they cannot detect a check that stops reaching its subject. Registering every
old hand break was rejected because many are duplicate routes to one property,
unstable textual edits, or test-fixture mutations. Selecting only the newest
storage crates was rejected because those seven are already represented while
the scheduler, memory and ABI foundations are the uncovered part.

**Consequences.** Sixteen production mutations now give every pure crate at
least one live break, a seventeenth removes `eevdf` from the derived coverage
floor, and an eighteenth admits a successful command that selected no test.
Each transformation compiled and made its exact named test red before its
source was restored. The ring defect demonstrated why the
name is measured: `admission_stops_before_a_completion_could_be_dropped` stayed
green, while `the_reservation_invariant_holds_under_interleaving` caught the
missing occupied-completion term. The timebase entry likewise initially named
`tests::…`, selected zero tests, and was corrected to `published_tests::…`
before admission. Host attribution now requires the exact test's own `ok` or
`FAILED` line, so a successful zero-test run is inconclusive and earns no
mutation credit.

The restored registry passes its exact-application, named-function,
non-duplication and all-host-library coverage checks. Eighteen persistent host
mutations retain the evidence, bringing the registry to 186.

## D-211 A boot image names and verifies the kernel it actually carries — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-135; closes PW-500

**Context.** D-135 repaired the VMware phase-close image after finding that it
was built with an empty feature slice and therefore ran none of the checks. Its
guard reads one dispatch arm as source text and looks for `SELFTEST_FEATURE`.
That protects yesterday's spelling at one caller, not the boundary: every
image caller can still pass any `&[&str]`, including no feature for a check
image or both test-only features together. The builder also trusts the path it
copied. Nothing reopens the FAT image to establish which kernel bytes will
reach Limine.

**Decision.** `image::Kernel::{Shipped, SelfTest}` is the complete selector for
normal boot images. Its exhaustive private mapping is the only place where a
kernel identity becomes Cargo features; no raw feature slice crosses the image
module boundary. The fault-injected PCI witness has a separately named
`build_degraded` constructor which fixes the identity to `Shipped` and adds
only `refuse-pci`, so a self-test/degraded combination is not expressible.

After Cargo and the ELF verifier produce the source artifact, the image builder
reads it once, writes those bytes into the ESP, reopens `/boot/wizard-kernel.elf`
through `fatfs`, and requires byte equality. It then identifies the bytes by
the `selftest: verdict ` signature already consumed by the QEMU harness. That
literal is compiled only with the kernel's `selftest` module; presence means
`SelfTest`, while absence means `Shipped` only after the bytes have matched the
verified ELF. The requested and observed identities must agree before an image
path is returned.

**Rationale.** An enum removes the ambiguous empty slice and the invalid
feature combinations from every caller. Reading the filesystem payload checks
the artifact the firmware will consume rather than the host path the builder
intended to copy. The verdict signature is behavior the self-test kernel must
retain for the existing harness, so it is stronger evidence than a sidecar
label written from the same selector.

**Alternatives.** Keeping the source-text VMware check was rejected because a
rename can satisfy it without constraining the API, and it says nothing about
the other callers. Separate `build_shipped` and `build_selftest` functions were
rejected because the enum makes selection explicit while keeping one assembly
path. A kind file in the ESP was rejected because the builder and its label
could agree while the compiled kernel disagreed. Distinct phantom-typed image
handles were rejected for now because QEMU and VMware only consume a path; the
defect is at construction, where an exhaustive selector and artifact read-back
close it directly.

**Consequences.** The former VMware source-text test is replaced by direct
selector and raw-image round-trip checks. Both kinds were written into test
images, read back through their partition and FAT path, compared byte for byte,
and identified. Mapping `SelfTest` to no features made
`selectors_build_only_their_named_kernel` red; opening `hello.elf` in place of
the kernel made `both_kernel_kinds_are_read_back_and_identified` red. Both
transformations compiled, made their exact host witness red and were restored.
Persistent mutations retain them, bringing the registry to 188.

The real release shipped image then reported `shipped kernel read back`; the
release self-test image reported `self-test kernel read back` before QEMU ran
all 211 checks to a passing verdict. The same post-write verification is on
every normal, VMware, gate and degraded image construction path.

## D-212 The local gate is one registry rendered three ways — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-22, D-124 and D-147; closes PW-501

**Context.** `PASSES` already drives the Cargo configurations used by check,
clippy and rustdoc, but `ci` is a handwritten sequence. Two repository tests
recover that sequence by splitting `tasks.rs` as text: one counts calls whose
spelling looks like a boot, while the other searches for eight exact call
fragments and then special-cases the ninth. The README separately spells the
boot count and still says Cargo checks three configurations although
`refuse-pci` made four. Help says `ci` runs “every check above” even though the
standalone `check` task is deliberately not a second CI pass. Each copy can be
locally plausible and globally wrong.

**Decision.** One typed `gate::Registry` owns both dimensions of the local
gate: every Cargo crate graph and every ordered CI stage. Cargo-driven tasks
iterate its graph slice. `ci` can obtain the stage slice only through an
accessor which first verifies README's marked Markdown rendering, then it
exhaustively dispatches each enum variant. The help renderer lists both slices
directly. A host check exercises the same preflight.

The registry remains a local, self-contained sequence. It adds no hosted
service, network lookup, generator prerequisite or tool the repository cannot
vendor. The standalone `check`, VMware, TLC and mutation tasks retain their
existing policy; only the authority for what `ci` executes moves.

**Rationale.** Data can be iterated, rendered and compared without parsing the
Rust that consumes it. One entry now determines execution order, help output
and the reviewable documentation snapshot. The snapshot is intentionally
checked in rather than silently rewritten: changing the gate must produce a
diff that says which coverage was added or removed.

**Alternatives.** Strengthening the source scanner was rejected because a new
wrapper, reordered expression or renamed function would require another
parser convention without making the body authoritative. Generating README at
build time was rejected because documentation changes would disappear into
untracked output. Listing only boot stages was rejected because the already
stale Cargo-graph count demonstrates that the non-machine half is the same
contract. Running standalone `check` in addition to clippy was rejected as an
unrelated duplicate build, not evidence missing from the present gate.

**Consequences.** The handwritten CI body, source scanners and prose number
words are removed. The registry retains the same four Cargo graphs and nine
ordered stages the green gate ran before this change. Help now shows those
graphs and stages directly; README's marked table is their exact Markdown
rendering.

Removing the `refuse-pci` graph made
`the_ci_registry_drives_help_and_documentation` red with the missing table row.
The real `cargo xtask ci` also refused that mismatch before its first stage,
so removing the host-test stage cannot remove the only observer. Adding a
second `ShippedBoot` made the same exact host check red with a tenth stage. Both
transformations compiled, were restored and persist as host mutations, bringing
the registry to 190.

## D-213 Stable rustc resolves the public foundation surface — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-41 and D-158; closes PW-505

**Context.** D-41 forbids speculative public API, but the last sweep searched
source text for names. Text cannot distinguish two same-name methods, a real
call from documentation, or a re-export from executable use. Stable rustc does
not apply `dead_code` across a library's public boundary, and rustdoc JSON is
still a nightly interface. The result was an unenforced rule and a public
surface that lint-driven `is_empty` additions could grow without a caller.

D-158 removed the duplicate ELF loader and deliberately left the section walk
in `xtask`, but that walk still read `e_shoff`, `e_shentsize`, `e_shnum` and
`e_shstrndx` from four private numeric offsets. The section-entry and string
interpretation has one host caller and does not belong in the target loader;
the file-header field locations are nevertheless ELF knowledge the loader
already owns.

**Decision.** `cargo xtask api-audit` copies the Cargo inputs, `libs/`, `wost`,
`kernel`, `tools` and `xtask` into a locked workspace under `target/api-audit`
and compiles all four D-212 graphs offline with a private target directory. It
uses `syn` and `proc-macro2` source spans to give every public item declaration
and enum variant in `libs/` and `wost` a unique `#[deprecated]` marker. An
equal-weight antichain schedules those markers so every ordered pair is
separated in at least one compiler round. Stable rustc's resolved diagnostics
then establish calls between audited items and calls from code outside the
inventory; transitive reachability from those external roots is the live
surface.

A public re-export is exposure, not a caller, and is excluded by its resolved
source span. Host graphs compile all targets, so tests and examples are real
roots. Exact source identity keeps same-name items separate, while comments
and rustdoc prose emit no compiler use and therefore cannot keep an API alive.
The audit is an ordered CI stage between clippy and rustdoc.

The inventory deliberately excludes fields. A measured prototype reported
nine apparently dead fields, including fields demonstrably read by pattern
destructuring: stable rustc does not emit a deprecation diagnostic for every
such use. Claiming compiler proof there would be false. Fields remain in the
manual semantic surface review until a stable compiler interface can resolve
them completely; this decision proves item declarations and enum variants
only.

`libs/elf64::SectionTable` now parses and owns the section table's four
file-header values. `xtask` consumes that typed value and retains only the
host-specific section-entry walk and symbol/string checks. No private offset
transcription is described as canonical.

**Rationale.** Compiler name resolution is the authority the text sweep was
trying to approximate. Deprecation diagnostics are stable, carry resolved use
spans, work across the actual feature/target graphs, and need no network tool
or nightly artifact. The antichain reduces 1,466 one-item builds to thirteen
rounds without losing direction: for any caller and callee, one round marks the
callee while leaving the caller unmarked, so suppression inside deprecated
code cannot hide that edge.

Keeping the isolated copy is part of the evidence. Instrumentation never
rewrites the checkout, and an interrupted compiler leaves only replaceable
state below `target`. The same exclusive-lock and private-target properties
that make mutation runs resumable prevent two audits from corrupting one
another or a normal build.

**Alternatives.** A stronger text search was rejected because parsing syntax
still does not resolve names. Adding an external public-API tool was rejected
because it would add a network/toolchain exception and still answer API
compatibility rather than caller reachability. Nightly rustdoc JSON or compiler
internals were rejected because the repository's stable toolchain is a gate,
not a suggestion. Treating re-exports as roots was rejected because it would
preserve an API merely for being public. Moving the complete section reader to
`elf64` was rejected because the target loader has no section-entry consumer.

**Consequences.** The first compiler run inventoried 1,489 non-field items and
found 29 with no resolved caller. The unused surface was deleted: one ACPI
revision accessor, one ELF byte-slice accessor, one FAT source conversion, one
MMIO emptiness query, four NVMe register/configuration constants, one PCI bus
count, one x86-APIC bit constructor, and nineteen `wost` address/count/accessor,
frame/segment, port, xstate and lock operations. Four narrow
`len_without_is_empty` expectations state why their types are constructibly
non-empty instead of manufacturing dead `is_empty` methods to satisfy a style
lint. Removing the unused raw frame writer reduced the pinned `wost` unsafe
surface from 370 to 368 lines without raising its 380-line budget.

After the typed ELF metadata additions, all 1,466 audited declarations and
variants have a compiler-resolved path to a real caller in thirteen rounds.
Re-export-as-use, doc-as-use and wrong-same-name defects each made only
`reexports_docs_and_same_names_are_resolved_by_the_compiler` red. Reading the
section offset from `e_phoff` made only
`the_section_table_fields_are_where_the_file_header_puts_them` red.
Reintroducing the dead MMIO `is_empty` made the complete audit report exactly
`method impl::is_empty`; it also proves the mutation runner's new typed
API-audit baseline and attribution route. All five transformations were
restored and persist, bringing the registry to 195 and the local gate to ten
ordered stages.

## D-214 Hardware-retained pointers need irrevocable mappings, and unsafe review needs an exact revision — Status: Accepted (2026-08-28), amends D-41, D-125 and D-139; closes PW-506

**Context.** The final `wost` review covered 169 unsafe block expressions and
38 unsafe declarations across eighteen files. The 368-line measurement stayed
below the unchanged 380-line budget, but a total alone did not say which
revision of the surrounding safe wrappers and `// SAFETY:` grounds had been
read. Adding one unsafe block while deleting another could preserve both the
budget and the measured total.

The adversarial caller pass found two safe doors whose sole current callers
were careful but whose types were not. `set_double_fault_stack` accepted a
`MappedStack`, checked the mapping once and stored its top in `TSS.IST1`.
Afterward `AddressSpace::unmap` could remove that exact owned range while the
processor retained its address. D-125 fixed evidence that was stale *before*
installation; it did not keep the installed mapping alive afterward. A later
double fault would fault while constructing its own frame and reset the
machine.

`open_fast_syscall_doors_for_test` returned with `EFER.SCE` set and relied on
the kernel self-test to call the matching closer immediately. D-139 checked
every normal ring-3 entry, but a safe public operation should not rely on an
arbitrary future caller preserving a hazardous interval, especially if it is
ever reached from a trap path that resumes an existing program.

**Decision.** `AddressSpace::map_pinned_stack` maps the guarded stack and the
paging module publishes its checked root, base and length before returning
`PinnedStack`. It is available only for the address space this CPU is currently
walking, which prevents an old token becoming valid again after a reclaimed
physical root is reused. Keeping the one hardware pin beside the one global
active-root record also leaves `AddressSpace`'s size unchanged; debug builds
had no stack headroom for another inline extent. `unmap` refuses every range
that overlaps the recorded half-open stack extent, including a strict subrange
or a request extending across either edge.
`segment::set_double_fault_stack` now accepts only `PinnedStack`. The active
space itself cannot be reclaimed, so safe code has no operation that can
invalidate the address retained by the TSS.

The overlap arithmetic lives in `libs/stack-layout::Slot::stack_overlaps`, is
host tested at both adjacent edges, inside the extent and on overflow, and
fails closed. This does not implement PW-703: ordinary `MappedStack` evidence
still re-walks only its top page, and complete dynamic-stack validation remains
stopped until stacks can actually grow or shrink.

The fast-syscall probe is one operation now. It excludes interrupts, records
the initially shut state, opens `SCE`, observes it, runs the private closing
path, reads back both doors and restores the prior interrupt state. No safe
caller can return, forget a guard or resume ring 3 during the open interval.

`xtask::unsafety` now parses Rust syntax for the line budget instead of looking
for the word `unsafe`; comments, strings and unsafe declarations cannot be
mistaken for block expressions. Beside the budget it records the normalized
SHA-256, syntactic unsafe-block count and unsafe-declaration count of every
unsafe-bearing `wost` source. The complete file is fingerprinted deliberately:
changing a safe wrapper or the prose that grounds its operation requires the
