the ordinary production timeout arm. Its self-test therefore observes the
same `fail_submitted` cleanup a real expired command uses. The stale queue
mutation names `PendingTable::slots` explicitly again, preserving its original
compiled ownership-loss defect.

**Alternatives.** Crediting any red verdict was rejected because it recreates
the pre-D-134 causal hole. Retrying survivors was rejected because a green
mutant is already a valid negative result and repeated sampling could hide a
nondeterministic proof gap. Unlimited retry was rejected because qualification
must terminate. Keeping the NVMe shortcut and retargeting the mutation to test
code was rejected because it would prove a seam instead of the production
cleanup arm.

**Consequences.** The repaired NVMe path passed all 215 checks; removing its
terminal cleanup then failed only `an nvme timeout quiesces before dma memory
returns` at 214/215 and the check repaired the deliberately live DMA state
before continuing. The corrected queue mutation compiled and failed its named
teardown check. Unchanged reruns of the trap-context, refused-arrangement,
refused-settlement and unguarded-stack mutations reached their exact expected
outcomes. Reducing the observation bound from two to one failed only
`an_inconclusive_machine_observation_gets_one_bounded_retry`; mutation 277
retains that defect. The complete successor sweep remains PW-001 work and none
of the failed 276-entry attempt is promoted into closing evidence. No unsafe
operation, wire ABI or machine-check count changed.

## D-233 Restoring mutation source invalidates its compiled package — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), amends D-208 and D-232; advances PW-001

**Context.** The first successor run after D-232 reproduced the supposedly
incidental user-boundary failures in a causal sequence. Mutation 12 removed
`wost`'s address-space installation and Cargo built that changed dependency.
The runner then copied pristine `task.rs` bytes from its snapshot and applied
mutation 13 in the kernel. Cargo rebuilt only the kernel and linked the stale
mutated `wost`; mutations 13 and 14 consequently ran with the wrong page tables
and could not answer their own questions. The source and journal digests were
correct throughout. On Windows, `fs::copy` restored the snapshot's old
timestamp, so Cargo had no reason to discard the newer object. D-232's retry
could only repeat the contaminated build. Its bounded retry policy remains
valid, but its attribution of these four observations to incidental machine
failure is superseded by this reproduced build-cache cause.

**Decision.** Restoring or recovering a mutated compiled source invalidates
that package in the session's private Cargo target before another witness may
run. The mapping is exact: `kernel` names `wizard-kernel`, `wost` and `xtask`
name themselves, and `libs/<package>` names that library. Documentation,
models, fixtures and supply-chain inputs have no compiled package and require
no clean. The invalidation uses `cargo clean --package` inside the isolated
workspace and target; it never touches the user's ordinary build artifacts.

**Alternatives.** Touching the restored file was rejected because timestamp
granularity and future-time handling differ by filesystem. Deleting the whole
private target after every mutation was rejected because it would discard all
unrelated dependencies and turn a bounded sweep into repeated cold builds.
Assuming the next mutation changes the same crate was rejected because the
observed transition was exactly from `wost` to the kernel.

**Consequences.** A host reproduction builds a mutated mini-`wost`, restores
its pristine source and requires every package artifact to be absent before
the next build. Removing only the package invalidation left those artifacts
live and failed that exact test; mutation 278 retains the defect. The aborted
277-entry run has no closing-evidence value, although its first twelve exact
outcomes remain diagnostic. PW-001 now belongs to a clean 278-entry successor
run. No target code, unsafe operation, wire ABI or machine-check count changed.

**Superseded in part by D-237 (2026-08-29).** The cause recorded here is
right, and D-237 acts on it directly: the remedy chosen instead — invalidating
the package by hand — treated a clock as a cache. What survives is the
diagnosis and the sequence that produced it.

## D-234 A terminal observation keeps exact failures that preceded it — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), amends D-209 and D-232; advances PW-001

**Context.** The complete 278-entry diagnostic successor to D-233 ran every
mutation on clean commit `8de1d4de9c3740617999cfef9ac564b35f706f48` in
56 minutes 30 seconds. It found no survivor and caught 274 entries exactly.
Mutation 14 twice failed unrelated ring-3 checks before its late trap-logging
trigger. Mutations 123 through 125 each made their own ownership check red,
then the deliberately corrupted state caused a later page fault at
`0xffffffffffffffe8`. The serial observer had already recorded those named
failures, but `SelftestOutcome::Panicked` discarded them and exposed only the
later panic. Retrying reproduced the information loss rather than resolving
it.

**Decision.** A terminal self-test outcome carries both its exact panic
transcript and every named check that failed before the panic. A check mutation
is caught if its own named failure is present, even when later consequences
stop the kernel before its verdict. A different earlier failure remains
inconclusive. A panic mutation still requires its exact panic marker; an
earlier check cannot stand in for it.

The unknown-syscall adversary runs before the long stateful ring-3 group. It
has no dependency on an earlier user program and waits for its own retirement,
so placing it first gives the trap-context logging mutation its exact terminal
assertion before unrelated later state can obscure it.

**Alternatives.** Crediting any panic was rejected because three ownership
mutations and one unrelated fault would become indistinguishable. Discarding
the named check because a later panic occurred was rejected because it throws
away the exact causal observation D-209 requires. Adding more retries was
rejected because both observations already contained the same evidence.
Masking the later page fault in each check was rejected because corrupted
ownership is allowed to have further terminal consequences after its exact
check has reported it.

**Consequences.** The unmutated reordered image passed all 215 release checks.
Restoring trap-context logging then stopped at the first adversarial user
program with exactly `a trap handler may not take a thread lock`. Discarding
the pre-panic failures failed only the serial-outcome test, and refusing to
credit the exact retained name failed only the mutation-assessment test.
Mutations 279 and 280 retain those two observer defects. No unsafe operation,
wire ABI or machine-check count changed.

## D-235 VMware evidence starts from two identified, separate machines — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), advances PW-003 and PW-004

**Context.** `cargo xtask vmware` could generate only the self-test image, while
PW-004 separately requires the shipped image users boot. Regenerating `vm/`
also reused one machine directory and whatever `serial.log` an earlier round
left there. The task printed the `vmrun` identity but not the exact image
digest, so the two required human observations had no direct command-level
boundary between their state or bytes.

**Decision.** `cargo xtask vmware` remains the self-test default and
`cargo xtask vmware --shipped` is the explicit PW-004 selector. The self-test
machine remains in `vm/`; the shipped machine lives in `vm/shipped/`, so its
NVRAM, logs, disks and Workstation state cannot overwrite the check-bearing
round. Generation truncates that machine's serial transcript before launch and
prints the image kind, byte length, SHA-256 digest, resolved `vmrun` identity
and quoted VMX command. Instructions are image-specific. The keyboard rounds
remain human evidence as D-18 requires; generation does not pretend that
creating a VM booted it.

**Alternatives.** Manually copying a shipped image over the self-test flat disk
was rejected because the command and resulting identity would be implicit.
One shared VM directory was rejected because a stale verdict or NVRAM state can
cross the two evidence rounds. Automating GUI keystrokes through host window
focus was rejected because Workstation exposes no bounded, owned input channel
equivalent to QEMU's QMP route.

**Consequences.** Host checks distinguish both CLI selectors, require separate
machine directories and replace a stale serial fixture with an empty file.
Disabling the selector, merging the directories and appending the transcript
each fail only their named check; mutations 281 through 283 retain the three
defects. The generated image digest and pinned tool identity are now ready to
copy directly into the dated PW-003/PW-004 record. No kernel, unsafe operation,
wire ABI or machine-check count changed.

## D-236 Restoring a target dependency invalidates everything linked against it — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), amends D-233; advances PW-001

**Context.** The 283-entry successor on clean commit
`095b624bd1601cb3e669b5ade7c614bc5e224405` made 21 outcomes durable before
being stopped during mutation 22. Nineteen of the first twenty outcomes were
exact and none survived, but mutation 14 remained inconclusive twice. Its
serial transcript said user threads were running on tables that were not their
own: mutation 12's `wost` thread-switch defect was still present in the linked
kernel even though the isolated source had been restored and mutation 13 had
completed. Mutation 13's earlier terminal user-copy fault had hidden that
contamination from its own exact outcome.

D-233 invalidated only the package whose source was restored. That removes a
restored host artifact, but the package-only command names no target and
reported that it removed zero files after a cross-target kernel build. Cargo
therefore retained both the `x86_64-unknown-none` dependency artifact and the
already-linked `wizard-kernel` artifact and incremental state which consumed
it. A later kernel mutation can be evaluated alongside an older dependency
mutation. Cleaning the dependency alone would not have been enough either:
restored bytes rebuild to their old fingerprint, so the consumer stays fresh
with the defect already inlined into it.

**Decision.** Every target-side invalidation names the fixed
`x86_64-unknown-none` target and every target artifact that already linked the
restored one. Restoring `wost` invalidates both it and `wizard-kernel`.
Restoring a `libs/` input invalidates that library, `wost` and `wizard-kernel`
for the target, and every host member of the workspace for the host. A library
is inlined into whatever links it, so naming only the far end of a chain
leaves the near one holding the defect: `wost` carries libraries into the
kernel, and `xtask` links three of them itself. The host list is read from the
manifest's `default-members` rather than repeated here, and a restored library
missing from it is an error rather than a silent partial clean. Kernel inputs
invalidate the target kernel; `xtask` inputs invalidate the host package,
which nothing else links. The invalidation remains package-scoped rather than
deleting the private target: third-party dependencies keep their cheap
incremental path, while every later witness must rebuild from restored
first-party sources.

**Alternatives.** Trusting Cargo's timestamp and incremental dependency graph
was rejected because the clean successor reproduced linked behavior absent
from the restored bytes. Cleaning the entire private target after every
mutation was rejected because it would repeatedly rebuild unrelated host
dependencies and turn a bounded one-hour qualification into a much longer
one. Crediting mutation 14's many red checks was rejected because none was its
registered terminal cause.

**Consequences.** Two regression fixtures build against a mutated dependency
and require every artifact that consumed it to be absent after the restore.
The first cross-builds `wizard-kernel` against no-std `wost`. The second adds
an inlined `libs/` crate beneath both `wost` and a host consumer standing in
for `xtask`, and requires all five artifacts to go. Disabling reverse-consumer
invalidation leaves the kernel artifact present, cleaning the host target
leaves both cross-target artifacts present, stopping the target chain at
`wizard-kernel` leaves the `wost` artifact that inlined the library present,
and naming only the restored library on the host leaves the host artifact that
inlined it present. Mutations 284 through 287 retain those four defects. The
interrupted 283-entry run is diagnostic only. PW-001 belongs to a clean
287-entry successor. No target code, unsafe operation, wire ABI or
machine-check count changed.

**Superseded by D-237 (2026-08-29).** The reverse consumers named here are
real, and so is the evidence that found them; naming them one by one is what
D-237 removes. Restoring a source forward in time makes Cargo invalidate every
one of them, including the ones this decision would still have missed.

## D-237 A restored mutation is written, not copied — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), supersedes the mechanism of D-233 and D-236; advances PW-001

**Context.** D-233 already named the cause: on Windows `fs::copy` restores the
snapshot's old timestamp, so Cargo sees a source older than the object built
from the mutation and has no reason to rebuild it. It then rejected the direct
remedy — "touching the restored file" — as filesystem-dependent, and
invalidated the package with `cargo clean --package` instead. D-236 found the
half that reached: a package-only clean names no target, so the cross-target
dependency and the kernel linked against it both survived, and the fix grew
into a target-aware, graph-aware clean naming the library, `wost`,
`wizard-kernel` and every host member. Two rounds of naming consumers, each
closing the case it had measured, is the signature of a symptom.

The rejected remedy was rejected as the wrong thing. Writing bytes is not
touching a file: it chooses no timestamp, so there is no granularity to
reconcile and no future time to handle — the filesystem stamps it exactly as
it stamps every other write. The harness already depends on this. `Session`
applies a mutation with `fs::write` and the mutation becomes visible; only the
undo reached for `fs::copy`, and only the undo was invisible. The asymmetry
was the whole defect. `copy_tracked` carries it too, reachable because a
completed sweep retires its journal but keeps its workspace and objects for
the next sweep to re-copy over.

**Decision.** The harness writes source files and never copies them. Restoring
a mutation and re-copying a tracked workspace both read the snapshot's bytes
and write them to the destination, so every source the harness lays down is
newer than anything already built from it. Cargo's own dependency tracking
does the invalidation from there — transitively, for the host and the kernel
target alike, through however many crates inlined the value. No package
mapping, no target flag, no reverse-consumer graph, and no `cargo clean`.

**Alternatives.** Keeping D-236's clean was rejected because it restates the
dependency graph inside the harness, over-cleans to stay safe, and still
invalidates only what someone remembered to name. Hash-based freshness
(`-Z checksum-freshness`) would retire the timestamp question outright but is
nightly, and D-24 pins a stable toolchain. A private target directory per
mutation is correct and unaffordable. Stamping a timestamp explicitly after a
copy was rejected as the same write by a longer route, and it is the only
reading under which D-233's portability objection holds.

**Consequences.** The fixture is a three-crate chain whose value is inlined
twice, so nothing short of rebuilding the chain can change what its binary
prints, and both checks assert the printed value rather than the bytes on
disk. That distinction is the point: byte equality passes under this defect,
which is why it survived two decisions. One check restores a mutation, the
other re-copies a tracked workspace over a live build directory. Mutations 278
and 279 put the copy back in each path, and the resume mutation drops the
write where it used to drop the copy. The registry falls from 287 to 284 as
five clean-based mutations retire with the code they broke, and
`invalidate_package`, `clean_packages` and `source_package` are gone with it.
PW-001 belongs to a clean 284-entry successor. No target code, unsafe
operation, wire ABI or machine-check count changed.

## D-238 A chain walk is bounded by the volume that could hold it — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), amends D-170 and D-206; advances PW-006

**Context.** PW-006's hostile-input re-attack reached the chain walking in
`libs/fat32`. Its bound was the fixed `MAX_CHAIN = 1 << 24`, and the comment
directly above the constant stated a different rule: "the bound is the cluster
count, because a chain longer than the volume has visited one twice." The
pigeonhole argument is right; the constant does not implement it, and nothing
noticed because a bound only has to be finite to look correct.

The gap runs both ways. On a volume smaller than sixteen million clusters — the
shipped 64 MiB image holds about 130,000 — a cyclic table drives the walk to the
fixed ceiling instead of to the volume's own end, and every step is a sector read
a caller waits for. One `OpenAt` on a corrupt volume therefore occupies D-200's
file worker for as long as the device takes to serve tens of millions of reads.
Above sixteen million clusters the same constant refuses a legitimate chain as
`Unbounded`.

`read_file`'s skip loop had no bound at all. It advances `offset / cluster_bytes`
clusters, which the caller's own offset caps near 2^23 for the smallest cluster:
finite, but bounded by the number ring 3 supplied rather than by the volume, and
with no loop detection of its own.

**Decision.** The chain bound is the volume's cluster count, computed from the
mounted `Bpb` rather than written down. `chain_limit` is where the pigeonhole
argument lives, and the directory walk, the file read and the skip that precedes
it all use it. A chain that visits more clusters than the volume holds has
visited one twice and is refused as `Unbounded`; a chain that uses every cluster
in the volume still completes.

**Alternatives.** Lowering the constant was rejected because any constant is the
same defect at a different scale — it is either above the volume, and useless, or
below it, and wrong. Detecting the cycle exactly, with a visited set or Floyd's
algorithm, was rejected because a set needs allocation this reader does not have
and a second cursor doubles the device reads to learn what the count already
proves. Leaving the skip loop bounded by the caller's offset was rejected because
that is ring 3 choosing how much work the kernel does.

**Consequences.** A sixty-two-cluster volume with a two-cluster cycle now refuses
the directory walk and the maximum-offset read within four reads per cluster it
holds; before the change both ran to the counting source's ceiling and returned
`Unreadable`, which is the walk leaving its leash rather than finding the loop.
Restoring the fixed ceiling fails only `a_cyclic_chain_is_refused_within_the_volume`
and mutation 285 retains it. The existing maximum-offset check is unaffected: its
volume holds thirty-three million clusters and its skip is 65,535. No unsafe
operation, wire ABI or machine-check count changed.

## D-239 The arriving bytes say which numbering they are in — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), supersedes the arbiter of D-178 and D-179; advances PW-003 and PW-006

**Context.** PW-003's human VMware round decoded every key wrongly. `a` typed a
newline, `b` typed two `m`s, `c` typed two `f`s. Those are set 2's codes for
`a`, `b` and `c` read against set 1's table — `1C` is Enter there, `32` is `M`,
`21` is `F` — and the doubling is set 2's `F0` release prefix, which a set 1
decoder does not know, so it reads the code after it as a second press. The
stream was set 2 and the driver had decided set 1.

D-178 had already met the opposite machine. That VMware reported its
translation bit clear and translated anyway, so the configuration byte lied and
the identity reply — `(0xAB, 0x41)` for a translated MF2 against `(0xAB, 0x83)`
for an honest one — was the thing it could not fake. D-179 made the identity the
arbiter on that evidence. This VMware answers `(0xAB, 0x41)` to the identity
*and* `0x41` to the scancode-set query while delivering set 2, and its
configuration byte is the honest one. Two real machines, each with a different
probe lying, and no static probe correct on both.

The check that should have caught it could not. `decoder_reads_what_arrives`
asked `identity()` and compared the answer with a decoder that `identity()` had
configured — one value re-derived from the source the other came from. It agreed
on every machine, including this one, while certifying a decoder reading set 2
as set 1. Its own doc claimed it tested "the numbering arriving"; it never read
an arriving byte. The registry's neighbouring comment had even recorded why the
blind spot was there: on QEMU the bit and the identity agree, so no gate boot can
tell an arbiter apart from a guess.

**Decision.** The stream decides. `libs/ps2-keys::SetProbe` reads the numbering
off the bytes, and the two rules are read from the tables rather than chosen:
set 2 prefixes every release with `F0` and has no `70` key to make `F0` a set 1
release, so `F0` means set 2 wherever it appears; set 1's makes stop at `5D` so
its releases run to `DD`, while set 2's makes stop at `83`, so a byte above `83`
that is not a protocol reply means set 1. `AA` is excluded because both sets can
send it.

The identity supplies the opening guess and nothing more. Until a decisive byte
arrives the driver *holds* what it has read, because decoding a held byte under
the wrong numbering names a different key; the decision is one keystroke away
and the held bytes are then replayed through the right decoder. Changing
translation re-opens the question rather than re-answering it from the bit that
was written. A keystroke's worth of bytes that distinguishes nothing keeps the
opening guess, so no input is held for ever.

**Alternatives.** Trusting the configuration byte was rejected because D-178
measured it lying. Keeping the identity was rejected for the same reason in the
other direction. Trusting whichever two of the three agree was rejected because
on each machine the two that agree are the two that are wrong together. Deciding
without holding was rejected because it mis-decodes the first keystroke, which
is the one the self-test's human rounds press. Widening `Decoder::feed` to
return several events was rejected as an API change to pure logic that is
already correct for both sets: the ambiguity is the driver's, and so is the
buffer.

**Consequences.** The correction is invisible on any machine whose probes are
honest, so the self-test now seeds the numbering *against* the stream before its
translated round and the round can only succeed by reading the bytes. Release
QEMU passed all 215 checks through that path; deciding the numbering and then
not adopting it failed `a translated keystroke decodes to the same key` and
`the keyboard's numbering and the decoder's are the same` together at 213/215,
and the second of those is a check that could not previously fail at all. Its
assertion moved to after the translated keystroke, where a byte has provably
arrived, and the scancode-set query it used to carry is now a diagnostic warn
rather than a claim. Host tests bind both probe bounds to the two tables and
fail if either grows past them; the `F0` rule, the bound and the adoption each
reddened only their own witness and persist as mutations 154 through 156. The
registry is 288. No unsafe operation or wire ABI changed, and the machine-check
count is unchanged at 215.

## D-240 A round a human answers is bounded by their clock, and prompted on their screen — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), amends D-18, D-135 and D-145; advances PW-003

**Context.** D-239 fixed the decoder and PW-003's human round still failed. Four
more VMware boots found four defects, none of them in the kernel's behaviour and
all of them in what the round asks of the person D-18 requires.

The keystroke wait was `for _ in 0..WAIT_SPINS`, two million iterations of a
lock and a status read. On a 3.4 GHz machine that is a fraction of a second, so
the ten-second deadline beside it was never once consulted and the prompt
scrolled past in the same burst as everything around it. Its own doc already
described the rule it did not implement — "a deadline on the clock for the
honest case, and an iteration cap so a dead clock converts the wait into a red
check rather than a hang" — which is the third comment stating a bound the code
did not hold this month, after `MAX_CHAIN` (D-238) and the identity arbiter
(D-239). Raising the deadline to forty-five seconds changed nothing, because the
spin count was the real bound.

Beside it, the storage-delay round sampled interrupt progress over one second
after printing its prompt. Ten seconds and one second were both sized for QMP,
which injects in microseconds; a person reading an instruction meets neither. A
prompt that waits one length and a measurement that samples another is how a
round comes to be unanswerable in two independent ways.

And `log.rs` sends records to the serial port alone, so that a diagnostic never
scrolls the banner away. The three `awaiting …` prompts are log records. The
human was being asked to answer prompts that were never rendered on any
screen they had. The round was not merely unlit: it was **unobservable**,
and a check whose subject cannot see what it is being asked is a defect in
the evidence path, not a cosmetic one. PW-003 requires a human transcript,
and the human could not read the question.
Five boots were spent on instructions to watch for text that did not exist, and
the operator was right each time they said they had never seen it.

**Decision.** A wait whose answer comes from a person is bounded by the clock,
not by iterations. `PollLimit` — written for NVMe's polls in D-200, whose own
doc says a monotonic limit does not spend attempts — moves to `libs/timebase`
and both callers share it; the spin count stays as what it always claimed to be,
the fallback for a clock that is not running. One constant, `HUMAN_WAIT_MS`,
gives every human round the same forty-five seconds, so the prompt and the
measurement beside it cannot disagree.

A prompt for a person is written where the person is looking. `awaiting` logs
the marker verbatim — the harness matches it and the transcript records it — and
also writes the instruction to the framebuffer, in the register `panic` already
uses for the other thing someone has to be told.

**Alternatives.** Keeping the iteration cap as the primary bound was rejected
because it makes the wait a function of processor speed, which is what hid this.
Duplicating `PollLimit` rather than moving it was rejected: two copies of one
rule is how the wait came to disagree with the measurement beside it. Routing
every log record to the framebuffer was rejected — D-135's reason holds, a
diagnostic must not scroll the banner away — so only the three prompts cross.
Automating the round was rejected again for D-235's reason: Workstation exposes
no bounded, owned input channel.

**Consequences.** The round is answerable. On VMware, `passed=214 failed=1`
against `passed=208 failed=7` before D-239: every keyboard check green, and
`delayed read evidence … interrupts=true` where five previous transcripts read
`false`. `the_human_wait_fits_the_harness_patience` reads `HUMAN_WAIT_MS` from
the kernel and fails if three unanswered rounds could outlast the harness, so an
unanswered round stays the kernel's red check rather than a killed emulator;
doubling the constant fails it, and mutation 290 retains that. The three moved
`PollLimit` mutations now name `libs/timebase`. The remaining VMware failure,
`a later nvme controller survives an earlier failure`, was not a keyboard
defect and not answerable by any keypress: the VMware machine had one NVMe
controller where the check asks for a useless candidate and a usable
sibling, which QEMU has offered since D-199. The template now offers both,
and restoring a namespace to the first fails only the machine-shape test;
mutation 291 retains it. That change is unbooted at this writing and is
not claimed as evidence.
No unsafe operation or wire ABI changed, and the machine-check count is
unchanged at 215.

## D-241 A described region is described by every region that holds it — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), amends D-177 and D-224; advances PW-006

**Context.** `libs/memory-map`'s `covers` says, in its own words, "Input order is
not assumed, so each bounded step searches the complete map." It searched the
complete map and took the *first* region holding the cursor, then advanced to
that region's end — so with two regions sharing a base, which one was listed
first decided both the verdict and the stride. Swapping them swapped the answer.

Three consequences followed from the one cause. `covers` and `covers_memory`
were order-dependent. `first_memory_run` could name a base that `covers_memory`
denied was memory, because the filter chose from a direct-mapped region while
the walk landed in a reserved one overlapping it — two stated contracts about
one address, disagreeing, with D-177 saying callers act on the first.
`allocatable_bytes` summed lengths bare, which panics under the debug gate and
wraps under release, handing a frame allocator a total smaller than the memory
it describes.

Nothing anywhere required regions to be disjoint. `grep -niE
"overlap|disjoint|sorted"` over the crate, `001-boot.md` and `007-memory.md`
returns nothing, and `limine_glue::take_memory_map` passes the bootloader's
entries through unsorted and unchecked. What keeps this latent is the Limine
protocol, which specifies that usable and bootloader-reclaimable entries do not
overlap any other entry — a guarantee this repository never records. So the
crate was correct by an external promise that is neither stated in its doc,
checked at its boundary, nor written in the boot document, which is a worse
position than being wrong in a visible way.

**Decision.** A step of the walk consults every region holding the cursor. It
advances by the furthest of their ends, so the stride cannot depend on order,
and a region whose kind is not admitted refuses the range wherever it overlaps
— the safe direction under a contradiction, since the distinction exists to
keep a cacheable alias off device registers. `first_memory_run` returns only a
base its sibling contract agrees is memory, making the two answers consistent by
construction rather than by the caller checking both. `allocatable_bytes`
saturates. On a conforming map exactly one region holds any cursor, so none of
this changes what a real boot observes.

**Alternatives.** Rejecting overlap in `try_from_regions` was rejected for now:
it is the strictest closure and would refuse a firmware map this project has
never seen, which is a boot failure traded for a latent inconsistency. Stating
the precondition and documenting the queries as undefined under overlap was
rejected because it leaves a trap in a public API and the crate cannot check
that its one caller honours it. Admitting the range wherever *some* region
allows it was rejected as the unsafe reading of the same contradiction.

**Consequences.** Found by a second session running a property tier against a
detached copy of the crate, transcribing the claims from the doc comments rather
than from the bodies — which is the only way this class is reachable, since the
code is total on every input and stays total while implementing the wrong rule.
Three checks now carry the three claims; restoring first-region-wins, dropping
the cross-contract agreement and restoring the bare sum each redden only their
own, and the last reproduces the overflow panic itself. Mutations 292 through
294 retain them. No unsafe operation, wire ABI or machine-check count changed,
and the Limine guarantee this rested on is now stated where the walk relies on
it rather than nowhere.

## D-242 A check is admissible when it cites a claim it did not read off the code — Status: Accepted (2026-08-29), extends D-84 and D-112; advances PW-516 and PW-517

**Context.** D-84 adopted `proptest` and `shuttle` for `libs/ring-proto`, and
said so in as many words: "for `libs/ring-proto` only". D-112 made it three
tiers and added the rule that governs them — each tier is asked only the
question it can answer — which it earned by experiment rather than assumed: a
model whose only fault was `Relaxed` where `Release` belonged passed ten
thousand shuttle schedules, because shuttle explores schedules under sequential
consistency and does not model store buffering.

That apparatus reached one crate of twenty-five. The other twenty-four carried
example tests only, which means every input in them was chosen by a person.
D-241 is what that costs: `libs/memory-map` had two tests over five public
functions, and three of its stated contracts disagreed with each other on
overlapping regions. The code was total on every input and stayed total while
implementing a rule its own doc contradicted, so no amount of generating bytes
at a parser would have reached it. What reached it was transcribing the doc
sentence and checking the code against it.

That is the shape of the gap. Six of the eight defects repaired on 2026-08-29
were bounds or arbiters whose doc comment stated the correct rule while the
code did something else: `MAX_CHAIN`'s comment argued the pigeonhole case
against a fixed constant, `await_key`'s doc described a deadline over a spin
count, `decoder_reads_what_arrives` claimed to read the arriving numbering and
never read a byte. In each the prose was right and the code was wrong.

**Decision.** The tiers reach every pure crate, and one rule decides what may
join them:

> A check is admissible when its claim cites a stated invariant — a doc
> comment, an ADR, or a format specification — that it did not derive from the
> code. A check whose text could be recovered by reading the function body is a
> restatement of the implementation, not a check on it.

The technique follows from the shape of the domain, not from the tier, and
three are admitted equally. **Generated inputs** where the domain is too large
to walk. **Bounded exhaustion** where it is finite, which needs no dependency at
all and makes a strictly stronger claim than sampling. **Derived quantities**,
which compare a constant against a number read from another place and involve no
inputs — the shape of `the_two_tables_still_bound_this_probe`, and the only one
of the three that could have reached `MAX_CHAIN`.

Two obligations travel with the rule. A generated-input check **states the
measured rate at which it reaches the accepting path**, because a property
guarded by an early return on a refused constructor passes vacuously when the
guard almost always fires, and a suite of those is indistinguishable from a
suite that works. And a shrunk counterexample is **committed**, not ignored: it
is the only "break it once" artifact this tier produces on its own, and
discarding it leaves the tier unable to re-run its own findings.

**Alternatives.** Restricting the tier to `proptest` was rejected: it cannot
reach the derived-quantity class, which is where six of eight of the evening's
defects lived, and adopting a tier aimed at the wrong class while claiming it
was working is worse than not adopting one. Pinning the RNG seed for a
reproducible gate was rejected because it degrades the tier to 256 fixed inputs
in perpetuity; D-216 binds source bytes and tool identities, not test-run
entropy, and a shrunk counterexample committed as a regression is the durable
half. Measuring line coverage as the meter was rejected on evidence: `-C
instrument-coverage` cannot link on this toolchain — `rustc` answers `E0463 can't
find crate for profiler_builtins`, and no `rust-std` this project can install on
`x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` carries the runtime — so the check would be permanently
red on the only host that exists. Differential oracles against `object` or a
host FAT implementation were rejected for now as a D-220 inventory change
bought before the cheaper tier had been spent.

**Consequences.** Six crates carry the tier. `libs/memory-map` failed three of
four properties and is D-241. The other five hold, and the negative results are
the point rather than a disappointment: `libs/path-walk` carries the crate's own
blockquote property, `libs/stack-layout` the "no two slots touch" the module doc
promises as host tests, `libs/port-space` the "false — and nothing recorded"
atomicity claim, `libs/frame-space` the ledger that returns to its baseline, and
`libs/slab-layout` walks its whole finite domain rather than sampling it.

Two traps are recorded here so the next author does not pay for them. Inline
format capture does not work inside `prop_assert!` — the format string is
expanded through `concat!`, so `"{base:#x}"` fails to compile with "there is no
argument named base", and positional arguments are required. And a red property
writes `tests/*.proptest-regressions` into the tree, which makes the next
`cargo xtask mutate` refuse on an unclean checkout; the file is committed, which
is both proptest's intent and D-28's.

The limit is worth stating as plainly as the rule. This tier verifies code
against claims. It is blind to a defect in the reading of a verdict, which is
what put two agents' gate results in doubt on the same evening — both read a
pipeline's exit status, which is the filter's and not the gate's. No property
over code can catch that. The mechanism that can is one that refuses to proceed
on a bad premise rather than reporting accurately into a void, which is what
`prove_green_baselines` did when it declined to credit mutations against a red
tree.

## D-243 Release authority is linear, and hostile layouts must be complete — Status: Accepted (2026-08-30), amends D-87, D-106, D-117, D-123, D-177 and D-241; closes PW-110, PW-111, PW-112, PW-211 and PW-308

**Context.** The post-handoff audit treated every earlier `DONE` claim as an
unproved hypothesis. It found five safe-boundary failures.

`AddressSpace::map_boot` stripped ownership but accepted `Flags::USER`. A
`BootRegion` proves only that firmware described physical bytes; it does not
prove that kernel or firmware contents may be published to ring 3.

Address-space release had a deeper authority split. `AddressSpace::bind`
minted a one-shot `Binding`, but `task::release_address_space` accepted the
root as a plain integer. A caller could mint `Released` before installing the
binding, reclaim the tables, and then install the stale binding through safe
APIs.

Three hostile descriptions also passed their preflights. A long usable memory
region let `covered_by` jump over a nested reserved claim. FAT32 accepted more
data clusters than its FAT could index and always read FAT 0. XSAVE accepted an
enabled component with no CPUID sub-leaf and AVX without SSE.

**Decision — privilege and lifetime.** Boot-evidence mappings reject `USER`,
as allocator-owned mappings already did. Refusal is chosen over silently
stripping the bit: attempting to publish kernel bytes is an authority error,
not a request for a nearby weaker mapping.

Release no longer accepts an address. Installing `Binding` returns a linear
`Bound` token which the process owner stores beside the `AddressSpace`.
Releasing a live task returns that same token unchanged; after retirement it
becomes `Released`. Construction that stops before installation consumes its
still-uninstalled `Binding` directly. Thus no safe caller can hold both release
evidence and something that can later install the same root.

The process transaction binds only after its other fallible objects exist and
returns the appropriate token through every thread-construction refusal. Its
region ledger is now a tuple array plus an explicit used count, rather than an
array of tagged optional tuples. Besides being the data's actual shape, this
makes the debug construction record smaller; the first token-carrying draft
exceeded the guarded kernel stack and double-faulted, so stack size is part of
this boundary's correctness.

**Decision — complete descriptions.** Memory coverage first arbitrates every
nonempty region intersecting the requested interval, then walks the union of
admitted regions. A forbidden nested claim therefore cannot be skipped by a
larger span's end.

FAT32 preflight requires room for the two reserved entries and every advertised
data cluster. `BPB_ExtFlags` selects FAT 0 when mirroring is enabled and the
named in-range copy otherwise; table addressing includes that copy's offset.

Compacted XSAVE preflight requires every enabled extended component to have a
present sub-leaf and enforces AVX's SSE dependency before any hardware write.
Contradictory virtual hardware is refused rather than delegated to `XSETBV` or
an undersized state area.

**Alternatives.** A global registry of pending roots would duplicate ownership
already represented by Rust values and introduce synchronization into task
construction. Checking only the task table was the defect because a pending
binding is deliberately not there. Sorting the boot memory map would not
resolve contradictory overlapping claims; safe arbitration is independent of
input order. Deferring FAT and CPUID contradictions to later reads or hardware
faults would move hostile input past the boundary that has enough information
to reject it.

**Evidence and consequences.** Two debug QEMU mutations independently failed
only `a boot mapping cannot publish kernel memory` and `a bound space is not
reclaimed`. The memory-map byte oracle exhausts every query over two regions in
the bounded address space 0 through 6 and caught both the original nested hole
and its retained mutation. FAT32's fifteen host tests trace the exact selected
table sectors and kill four capacity/selector/offset mutations. XSAVE's exact
presence and dependency checks each failed under their retained mutation. The
unsafe block and declaration counts did not change; the paging and task source
fingerprints were re-reviewed because the safe wrappers around those blocks
did.

## D-244 Exceptional evidence records executions, not installed tools — Status: Accepted (2026-08-30), amends D-216, D-218 and D-235; closes PW-007 and PW-008; advances PW-009

**Context.** The rejected phase handoff treated exceptional tools as though
recording their identity recorded their work. Mutation's `last-run` journal
had no overall verdict, did not retain failed completed evidence and let an
older pass authorize closure after a newer sweep failed. The model observer
accepted any nonzero exit which contained the expected invariant text, even
beside unrelated failure, and could wait forever. An initial qualification
layer bound mutation and model inputs, but its VMware path retained the same
execution defect: `begin_vmware` probed `vmrun`, then discarded the resolved
tool, and `qualify` accepted a transcript already present on disk without
executing VMware's observer. A synthetic marker fixture passed the check.

The surrounding provenance was weaker than its prose too. D-235 truncated one
shared serial name but left every other file in each machine directory, and
the live tree contained older NVRAM, suspend metadata and scoreboards beside
new descriptors. A copied mutation snapshot was verified only when opened; if
it changed later, completion restored from the changed copy and still wrote a
report for the original digest. Evidence parsing accepted reordered fields and
one missing terminal LF, and a broken staging symlink could survive
invalidation. These are stale-success, substitution and path-authority defects,
not missing explanatory comments.

**Decision — exceptional records.** Mutation, TLC and each VMware selector own
one sorted, checksummed qualification record under ignored target output. An
attempt removes the older success before its first fallible preflight and can
commit `result=pass` only after its terminal operation. Every record binds the
clean Git commit and tree. Mutation additionally binds the registry, source
and index digests and the durable complete report. TLC binds the resolved Java
bytes and version, the TLC jar and the complete tracked model tree. VMware
binds the resolved `vmrun`, generation receipt, both disks, both descriptors,
VMX, serial transcript and execution observer. The release evidence format is
v3 and carries every one of those support files and digests; offline
verification reconstructs their inner schemas instead of trusting only the
outer manifest.

Every record rechecks clean source immediately before rename. The mutation
runner also re-digests its supposedly immutable copied source at completion,
before publishing `last-run` or a passing report. A changed copy can therefore
invalidate work, but cannot authorize pristine source.

Mutation completion writes a canonical, checksummed, immutable sequenced
report whose caught, survived and inconclusive totals determine its explicit
verdict. Older reports remain available, but only the greatest sequence for
the current clean commit, registry, source and index can authorize a pass. The
returned current-pass value owns the mutation sweep lock until its consumer
finishes; mutation qualification and the release-evidence snapshot retain that
value through publication, so a newer failed sweep cannot race an older pass
into the bundle.

TLC gets a hard 30-second process deadline. Its observer requires empty
diagnostics, exactly one terminal verdict before exactly one final completion
record and an exit status consistent with that verdict. A clean verdict has no
counterexample trace; an invariant violation has exactly one later behavior
header and at least one state before completion. Wrong invariants, mixed
verdicts, truncated traces, unrelated `Error:` records, Java throwables, stack
records and fatal worker text are refusals rather than mutation catches.

**Decision — one generated VMware machine.** D-235's selectors now own
`vm/self-test/` and `vm/shipped/`. Generation removes only that exact selector
directory after real-directory and canonical-parent checks, then constructs an
exact initial inventory: five authoritative machine artifacts, one empty
`serial-<generation>.log`, and the generation receipt (the incomplete receipt
occupies that seventh name until the atomic rename). NVRAM, locks, logs,
scoreboards and suspend state are absent at generation. VMware may create them
after boot, but they are explicitly runtime extras and carry no authority.
The five artifact names, receipt and transcript must remain regular files;
substituting a link, directory or another canonical parent is a refusal.

The generation ID is a new per-invocation local identifier derived from the
host clock, process and an in-process sequence. Its purpose is to give VMware a
new serial destination and stop accidental reuse of `serial.log`; it is not a
secret, nonce supplied to the guest, or cryptographic attestation. The receipt
binds the empty reset, exact source, selector and initial artifact digests.
Qualification requires the transcript at the receipt's generated name to have
become nonempty and rechecks every authoritative digest before and after it is
copied.

**Decision — observe execution.** `VmwareAttempt` retains the exact resolved
tool. Qualification probes those bytes, executes that path with exactly
`-T ws list`, requires successful exit and the canonical VMware count header,
and accepts exactly one absolute VMX path. Canonicalizing that path must produce
the generated selector's regular VMX. The tool is probed again around the
observation and before commit. The normalized command output is stored as
`vmrun-list.txt`; its length and digest are in the checksummed inner record and
the outer evidence manifest. Availability text can no longer stand in for
execution, another running VM cannot share the observation, and a foreign VMX
cannot donate it.

All destructive evidence and qualification paths are revalidated at the point
of use. A real root and every real parent are required before recursive reset,
copy or record commit, canonical children must remain under the exact configured
root, and new staging/support files use exclusive creation. Qualification and
generation records require their one canonical sorted LF encoding and
checksum; the outer manifest requires canonical encoding and verifies every
recorded digest. These checks prevent a linked parent with identical bytes
from substituting provenance, not merely a different digest from being
noticed.

**Trust boundary.** This is strong local qualification, not remote
attestation. It proves that the recorded `vmrun` returned one running canonical
VMX at the observation, that the selected generated files retained their
recorded bytes, and that the accepted transcript occupied that generation's
serial path. It does not prove that `vmrun` started the VM, that those serial
bytes were emitted by that process, or that a privileged operator, host
filesystem, hypervisor or `vmrun` did not fabricate them. In particular, an
operator can copy an older valid transcript into the fresh path. There is no
guest-consumed per-generation challenge with which to reject that act, and the
checksums are integrity checks rather than signatures. PW-531 stops stronger
process-to-transcript binding until a concrete guest-readable challenge channel
or platform attestation mechanism exists.

**Alternatives.** Keeping a fixed serial filename plus truncation was rejected
because it gives accidental replay one stable destination. Treating every
post-boot VMware file as evidence was rejected because their formats and
lifecycle belong to Workstation; authority rests in the generated inputs and
explicit observer. Parsing any positive `vmrun` count was rejected because it
allows an unrelated running machine to donate execution. Inventing a
cryptographic claim from host-generated metadata was rejected because the
guest never consumes or returns that metadata. Deleting the whole `vm/` root
was rejected because one selector must never destroy its sibling.

**Evidence and consequences.** Host fixtures complete and consume a clean
isolated mutation sweep, retain an older pass beside a newer failure, reject
failed and stale reports and block a concurrent replacement until the current
pass is consumed. TLC fixtures distinguish clean success and the exact named
invariant from wrong status, wrong invariant, mixed verdict, truncation,
unrelated error, diagnostic output, Java throwable, fatal output and a
missing or contradictory behavior trace; a parked child proves the deadline.
PW-007 and PW-008 are therefore closed as observer implementations, while the
real current-registry mutation and TLC executions remain PW-001 and PW-002.

Other host fixtures reject zero, noncanonical and multiple `vmrun` counts,
missing and extra paths, relative and foreign VMXs, linked selector and
qualification parents, stale NVRAM, authoritative-name substitution, shared
serial names, linked evidence roots, broken staging links, reordered manifests
and a changed mutation snapshot. The command seam executes exact pre-probe,
`-T ws list` and post-probe order, and production requires the real observer
before result and commit. Each guard was removed or weakened once and its exact
fixture went red; the restored defects persist in the mutation registry. No
real exceptional close is claimed here: PW-009 is `REQUIRED` until one clean
final commit completes mutation, TLC, both human VMware rounds, both execution
qualifications, evidence creation and independent offline replay.

## D-245 Cleanup authority survives every refusal, and partial construction is fail-atomic — Status: Accepted (2026-08-30), amends D-106, D-117, D-190, D-191, D-206 and D-243; closes PW-527

**Context.** Re-auditing cleanup as hostile code found the same defect at four
ownership layers. The process region ledger silently discarded its final entry
when a maximum-size image also owned a stack. Loader rollback, construction
drop and zombie collection discarded `unmap` or release refusals; in the last
case `.ok()` consumed the only `Bound` token that could authorize a retry.
`AddressSpace::Drop` deliberately cannot walk or free live mappings, so those
discarded results were safe from use-after-free only by leaking every remaining
owner.

Boot paging had the production form of the same problem. A failed kernel-space
build dropped an unreclaimed root, stack-arena construction kept the prefix it
had already mapped, and boot continued with that partial arena. Guard
verification also ignored rollback refusal. Separately, task construction
ignored a retirement refusal before returning its scheduler slot, and a free
scheduler slot could still have an older process zombie attached to the same
index. A later orphan could then replace the retained owner. Finally, user
launch remained open when XSAVE isolation was unavailable, and `Frame` and
`Segment` drop ignored allocator-ledger refusal even though D-206 classifies
such internal ownership contradiction as fatal.

**Decision.** Cleanup state is complete, typed and retryable. The fixed process
ledger has one entry for every admitted image segment plus the stack, and
overflow is an error rather than a dropped record. Loader and process rollback
return the refusal and exact page progress. A zombie retains either its `Bound`
or `Released` authority, its remaining mappings and its returned-page tally
until the next attempt. Page-table reclaim refuses while any owned leaf remains
reachable and returns the release token on refusal.

`AddressSpace::Drop` remains non-reclaiming: drop has neither the fallible API
nor, for an installed space, the linear release evidence needed to reclaim
tables safely. Every owning production path therefore calls `unmap` and
`reclaim` explicitly. Stack teardown returns a linear progress token, so a
partial refusal resumes below already-unmapped slots rather than failing on
them. Range mapping snapshots its table ownership, clears every written leaf
and detaches newly linked empty tables in reverse order; a contradictory
rollback walk fails stopped before a still-addressable run can be freed.
Kernel-space construction applies the same transaction. `Frame` and `Segment`
drop release the allocator lock and then fail stopped if their live handle is
absent from the ledger.

A zombie table records both stored and currently-collecting owners. Scheduler
selection excludes either state, and process commit checks the slot again
before publishing launch records. Commit refusal returns the still-bound
`PreparedProcess` with its `Bound` token; retirement first yields `Released`
authority, which rejoins construction before drop. Task retirement is completed
before the scheduler slot is released: one injected first refusal is retried,
and a second refusal is an internal contradiction.

Ring 3 also requires isolated extended state before its first allocation.
Absent or contradictory XSAVE state now produces `NoExtendedState`; boot may
continue, but user launch stays closed. Kernel stacks remain guarded and are
32 KiB: the linear construction path exceeded the former 16 KiB debug stack,
while a measured publication point on the restored build retained 11,216 bytes
above the guard and the complete debug and release machine suites crossed it.
No guard was weakened.

**Alternatives.** Treating cleanup refusal as a harmless leak was rejected:
it loses retry authority and turns bounded pressure into permanent exhaustion.
Reclaiming implicitly from `Drop` was rejected because drop cannot return a
typed refusal or manufacture installation authority. Reusing a scheduler slot
and relying only on the final process-commit check was rejected because it
makes ordinary admission perform and then unwind avoidable construction.
Growing stacks again after one unreproduced fault was rejected after the clean
build's measured headroom and interrupt-frame disassembly did not support it.

**Evidence and consequences.** Machine checks prove the maximum image-and-stack
ledger, refusal after one successful unmap, resumable full-prefix and guard
rollback, failed boot-space and range-map table reclamation, commit-authority
reunion, retirement retry, zombie non-aliasing/retry and the no-XSAVE gate.
Host ELF tests prove power-of-two `p_align` and file/address congruence; the
machine loader additionally refuses non-page placement before taking a frame.
The integrated release QEMU suite passed 218/218. Exact retained breaks cover
progress-token loss, forgotten table rollback, rollback-walk refusal,
commit-owner loss, loader alignment and activation privilege/cache drift. The
new table transaction remains inside `wost`'s reviewed unsafe boundary.

## D-246 An independent grader judges frozen host logic — Status: Accepted (2026-08-30), extends D-28 and D-119; qualification tracked by PW-025

**Context.** The project-authored mutation registry and the checks named by it
can share an assumption. Its last `cargo-mutants` experiment was an old blocked
research run, not a grade of the accumulated foundation.

**Decision.** Run unmodified `cargo-mutants` 27.1.0 against every host-testable
workspace package from one clean source-frozen commit. Each package gets an
isolated work tree, target directory and machine-readable output. Project code
does not choose or rewrite the grader's mutants. Every survivor, timeout,
unviable mutant and build failure is adjudicated; an actionable result gets a
test or fix, followed by a complete current-source rerun. Equivalence requires
a source-level argument, not merely a familiar-looking mutant.

The grade records the commit, exact commands, package coverage, per-package
and aggregate totals, and every adjudication. It passes only with no
unadjudicated miss, timeout, unviable mutant or build failure.

**Evidence.** This entry fixes the method without inventing the result. PW-025
remains open until the frozen run is complete; its factual totals and artifact
locations will be appended here before phase close.


**Evidence (2026-09-06).** `cargo-mutants 27.1.0` ran unmodified over every
host-testable library, each package in its own work tree, target directory
and output directory, unshuffled, with `--jobs 4 --timeout-multiplier 3`.
The first grade, on `95c88f2`, tested 3,447 mutants across the 26 libraries:
3,039 caught, 147 missed, 249 unviable, 12 timeouts. Every non-caught outcome
was adjudicated; the gaps were closed on `c17dabd` and `46ff365`, and the
complete grade was rerun after each. The final grade, on `46ff365`, tested
3,422 mutants: 3,072 caught, 90 missed, 248
unviable, 12 timeouts, with every miss an adjudicated equivalent
and no unadjudicated timeout, unviable mutant or build failure. `xtask`
itself, about 3,460 mutants that each rebuild and run its 622-test suite, is
graded separately; its result is appended here when it exists. The
machine-readable outcomes of every package, with the exact commands, are
archived beside the other qualification records under
`target/qualification/cargo-mutants/<commit>/`, which the evidence bundle does
not yet carry.

Real gaps, each closed by a test: the NVMe admin command layouts
(`number_of_queues`, both queue creations and the PRP high halves) had only
been exercised with counts of one, queue one and addresses below 4 GiB, where
every shifted field is zero; the 8.3 decoder's one fixture used an `ARCHIVE`
attribute byte equal to a space, so an eight-byte base, a three-byte
extension under another attribute and an invalid byte in the extension's
second position were never decoded; `first_fit_by` never saw a zero length or
a non-power-of-two alignment; `free_contiguous` never saw a run leaving the
space while an earlier frame was already free, where D-105's ceiling must win;
`reap_up_to` never claimed exactly the posted head; the add-only
`Cr4Additions` doors were never applied to a register already holding their
bits; `BarAuthority::index`, `PhysicalAddressWidth::bits`,
`DeviceRange::physical` and `SharedLayout::bytes` were read only by `wost` or
the kernel; a lease the BAR authority was not bound to, an unmapped BAR
index, a retired command phase, a second memory-space admission and a command
readback that differs after probe restoration were never presented to
`pci-config`; and nine `Display` bodies had no oracle. Three simplifications
fell out: `copy_rows_up` lost a span guard that the constructor's
`span = pitch × height` and `width × 4 <= pitch` already prove unreachable
once rows are clipped to the height; `decode_slot` lost a dot-entry check no
decoded name can reach, because `.` is an invalid short-name byte; and the
NVMe buffer setter lost the PRP2 parameter every caller passed as zero.

Equivalent mutants, by argument: `|` replaced by `^` between operands that
occupy disjoint bit positions, including the cases where `^` binds tighter
than `|` and so joins two disjoint constants (descriptor, control-word,
rights, flag, slot, command and address fields whose disjointness the
constructors enforce); `>` replaced by `>=` where both branches yield the
clamp value at equality; `1 << 0` replaced by `1 >> 0`; comparisons whose
extra case feeds a `max` that already holds the value or is refused by the
following guard (`covered_by`, `first_fit_by`, `first_memory_run`);
`first_boundary` replaced by zero, which the page-run iterator skips as an
uncovered prefix; the `visited` counters in `read_file`, whose bound the
cycle hare reaches with the same `Unbounded`; `Bpb::parse`'s active-FAT arms,
which line 166 already forces to agree; `valid_short_name_byte`'s space
bound, which the scans never present; `Entry::one_shot`'s zero timer-mode
constant; the set-2 fake-shift guards, whose fallback arm yields no event
either; and the wide-BAR-at-last-register check, since `probe_bars` refuses
that window and no authority for it can exist.

Timeouts are all non-termination: loop indices whose `+=` became `*=` and
boundary walks that stopped being strictly increasing, for which the harness
bound is the only possible oracle. Unviable mutants are not programs: the
grader asked for `Default` on typed proofs and classes that deliberately lack
it, called `Default::default` inside `const fn`, invented `Range`, `Vec`,
`Box` and `std::iter` constructors in `no_std` crates, produced
cast-then-compare text that parses as generics, or changed const arithmetic
that the crates' own compile-time ceilings refuse. One ring-proto entry in
the first grade was a mingw linker collision, not a mutant property; the
reruns graded it caught.

## D-247 Type errors and typed ownership make two review claims durable — Status: Accepted (2026-08-30), amends D-85, D-150 and D-223; closes PW-529 and PW-530

**Context.** D-85 recorded three compiler experiments: a live token-bearing
spin guard made a second lock and reuse of its `ThreadContext` fail with
`E0499`, dropping the guard made reuse compile, and removing the guard's
`Drop` implementation made both refusals disappear under non-lexical
lifetimes. They were the right breaks and remained a one-time transcript.
D-223 later built the missing durable mechanism — a host test that
cross-compiles a throwaway crate against the real `wost` — but used it only
for the guards' `!Send` contract.

D-150 had the inverse problem. Its semantic rule is intentionally not a
whole-program source analysis: whether an operation can wait is a design fact,
not a function-name fact. Its direct-call surface nevertheless had no
mechanical inventory, so adding a variant or a wildcard arm could bypass even
the point where that fact must be decided.

**Decision.** The actual-`wost` probe now carries D-85 as well as D-223. Two
negative programs use `SpinLock::lock` and the real `ThreadContext`: one takes
a second token-bearing lock and one passes the still-borrowed token to a
blocking-shaped operation. Each compilation must fail with exactly one coded
diagnostic, `E0499`, at the probe source. A positive control explicitly drops
the guard and must compile. The assertion classifies rustc's diagnostic code;
it does not depend on English diagnostic wording.

The direct user-call surface has a typed registry beside that compiler
harness. A structural `syn` walk requires the registry, the `Call` enum and the
`Call::decode` dispatch to name exactly the same variants, with no wildcard or
duplicate arm. Every variant is classified `CannotWait` or
`CompletionPlane`. The sole completion-plane owner must invoke `wait_ring`
directly, and a cannot-wait arm may not. A new direct door therefore cannot
compile its host proof until its ownership is classified.

This does not pretend to infer transitive waiting from arbitrary Rust. The
reviewer still owns the semantic classification D-150 requires; the machine
now makes omitting that classification impossible and pins the one deliberate
trap-side wait to the completion plane that owns it.

**Alternatives.** Copying `ThreadContext` and a guard into a host-only crate was
rejected because it would test a model that can drift from `wost`. Matching
rustc's prose was rejected because wording is not the language contract;
`E0499` is. A name search for `wait`, `yield` or `block` was rejected because
both false positives and renamed helpers would turn prose convention into a
claimed call-graph proof. Whole-program analysis remains rejected for D-150's
original reason.

**Evidence and consequences.** The three compiler probes and both existing
guard `!Send` probes pass against the current target. Compiling out `Drop for
SpinLockGuard` made the two negative programs compile and failed only
`contracts::a_live_spin_guard_keeps_the_thread_context_borrowed`; restoring it
returned the test to green. Deleting `RingEnter`'s typed row failed
`contracts::every_direct_door_has_an_explicit_wait_owner` with the enum/registry
set difference, and restoration returned it to green. Both exact breaks are
retained as host mutations. No kernel behavior, unsafe operation, ABI or
machine-check count changed.

## D-248 The shipped object surface stops at one opaque bootstrap identity — Status: Accepted (2026-08-30), amends D-95, D-110, D-111, D-127, D-130, D-181 and D-217; advances PW-532

**Context.** The pre-Wizzy caller audit asked D-184's question of every kernel
surface: what concrete current caller forces this mechanism? `Event`, channel
messages, send/receive, backpressure, blocking, peer-close and HandleTable
send/accept/close/duplicate operations were reached only by self-tests or by
prose about a future userland. They made their own tests look like demand.
Queue `Duplicate` was the only shipped handle operation, and it already owned
reservation, attenuation and completion without those HandleTable wrappers.

The remaining channel pair was also test-shaped runtime state. Production
`spawn` created two `Arc<Channel>` values joined by weak references, inserted
one in the child and immediately dropped the other. The peer existed solely so
`Spawned` and `Birth` could prove pairing. Every shipped process therefore
began with an already-orphaned fictional endpoint and a lock no production
operation could use. Several scheduler weights, failure seams, object ledgers
and last-rites snapshots were likewise compiled into the shipped kernel only
for machine checks. Raw self-test `AddressSpace` setup refusals could abandon
page-table frames while purporting to prove cleanup.

**Decision.** The current `Channel` is one opaque, counted identity. `spawn`
creates exactly one, installs it as the child's sole handle and creates no peer
or transport state. The `Channel` tag remains because the current bootstrap
ABI and the future Wizzy handoff need a concrete typed identity; removing the
tag would either break that birth contract or substitute an untyped placeholder.
Bytes, transferred handles, waiting, close and pairing return only when the
post-gate bootstrap caller fixes their protocol. `Event` is removed. The
direct `WaitQueue::wait_unless` lost-wakeup proof remains because production
ring waiting uses that primitive independently of either speculative object.

Channel has no type-specific rights. The child's initial entry still carries
the universal rights, and ring-3 `Duplicate` requests `INSPECT`, not a fictional
channel `READ`. Queue owns the one implemented reservation/commit delegation
path; duplicate HandleTable convenience operations are removed. Test weights,
fault injection, resource counters, birth/death snapshots and inspection APIs
compile only under `selftest`. `Spawned` and `Birth` correlate through the
authority table's existing non-repeating identity rather than an invented
object peer. Every retained raw self-test address space reclaims its tables on
every setup refusal and verifies the exact frame-ledger baseline. All
`expect(dead_code)` attributes are gone: a surface is shipped because a caller
uses it or is explicitly self-test-only.

**Alternatives.** Keeping mechanisms because tests exercised them was rejected:
it reverses the caller/dependency direction and freezes a pre-Wizzy protocol.
Keeping the weak peer only under `selftest` was rejected because the pairing
claim itself described no production invariant. Deleting `Channel` entirely
was rejected because the one typed bootstrap entry is a current machine and
handoff contract. Replacing queue delegation with the removed wrappers was
rejected because it would move ownership away from the only concrete caller.

**Evidence and consequences.** The machine suite now has 213 checks rather
than preserving eleven tests for deleted behavior. Retained mutations corrupt
the exact birth-table identity, widen Channel's meaningful rights, bypass the
WaitQueue condition recheck, erase the test weight and skip raw-space reclaim.
The complete mutation source matcher passed after the rewrite. Target checks,
API audit, Clippy and restored debug/release boot evidence remain PW-532
acceptance work; historical Phase 5 channel and Event sections remain design
history but no longer claim to inventory the current kernel. No unsafe
operation was added.

## D-249 Device refusal is transactional, and internal contradictions fail in every build — Status: Accepted (2026-08-30), amends D-37, D-41, D-48, D-115, D-133 and D-206; verification tracked by PW-533

**Context.** Several safe hardware boundaries returned refusal and their
callers discarded it. Framebuffer reads substituted zero and writes updated
the RAM shadow even when checked MMIO changed no device byte. The i8042 path
continued after a failed flush or controller command, so a later read could
consume stale output; configuration writes were neither admitted nor verified.
Queue and time-page helpers likewise ignored impossible shared-page bounds.

The same policy split by build mode. Queue reservations, handle commitments,
page-table indices and TSS alignment supported permanent ownership or unsafe
pointer preconditions, yet `debug_assert!` removed them from release kernels.
Some syscall answers, test cleanup, the NVMe timeout repair, the shipped tmpfs
survey and the synthetic degraded PCI claim also discarded their results.
Those are not graceful fallbacks: they leave a stale register, false evidence,
or divergent ownership while execution continues.

**Decision.** A framebuffer lease is checked at construction; any later MMIO
refusal contradicts that geometry and fails stopped before the shadow changes.
Framebuffer scroll arithmetic is a checked `libs/pixel` row plan. Each visible
source row is published through one bounds-checked MMIO slice before the same
span commits to the RAM shadow; the device boundary performs only volatile
word writes. This removes the raw copy shortcut and avoids copying padding
while retaining the pitch as the stride.
The i8042 controller admits every required command, verifies each required
configuration byte and types refusal as `TransportRefused` or
`ConfigurationRefused`. All six operations that begin by draining output stop
immediately when draining fails. The redundant best-effort set-2 command is
removed: reset already establishes the protocol default, while arriving bytes
remain the decoder's arbiter under D-239.

Internal queue, handle, heap, page-table, TSS, framebuffer-shadow, time-page and
shared-memory bounds use release assertions. Operation-style boolean APIs and
the time-page publication outcome are `#[must_use]`; predicates remain ordinary
booleans. A source contract keeps that distinction explicit and another rejects
known discarded or saturating cleanup results. Every returning syscall uses one
answer helper which records refusal and then fails stopped. NVMe invokes its
cleanup primitive directly, tmpfs reports enumeration failure, the keyboard's
one-shot interrupt handoff is asserted, and the degraded image must prove it
reserved PCI configuration.

**Alternatives.** Treating MMIO refusal as a blank pixel was rejected because
it made the shadow lie. Continuing an i8042 query after command refusal was
rejected because there is no way to attribute the next buffered byte. Silent
release-only recovery was rejected under D-206: a missing promised slot or an
unsafe bound contradiction has no coherent state to return to. Making every
boolean `#[must_use]` was rejected because predicates are routinely and safely
queried for control flow; only operations with a refusal outcome carry it.

**Evidence and consequences.** Three machine checks inject configuration,
flush and transport refusal while requiring exact live-state restoration.
Framebuffer qualification shortens both the validated lease and nonempty
shadow by one word and names each terminal marker. Host row-plan checks cover
12,400 small geometry/request combinations plus
distinct padded-stride and short-shadow cases. Copying padding, advancing by
visible width, accepting downward copies and omitting the source bound each
reddened its named host check before restoration. Heap corruption mutations
name slot, frame and direct-map provenance failures. Every target graph checks,
the integrated release suite passed 218/218 before the final result-audit
edits, and all 505 retained mutation patterns match exactly. PW-533 closes on
the restored debug, release and degraded boots. No ABI changed.

## D-250 Shared kernel mappings require positive runtime evidence — Status: Accepted (2026-08-30), amends D-81 and D-91; verification tracked by PW-534

**Context.** D-81 declined KPTI because this kernel's target hardware reports
`RDCL_NO`, but process admission never checked the processor actually running
the image. D-91 correctly kept an absent `IA32_ARCH_CAPABILITIES` distinct from
an all-clear word, yet that distinction only affected reporting and eIBRS.
Ring 3 still received page tables containing the kernel on a silent processor,
which is exactly the boundary KPTI exists to protect.

TCG makes a blanket fail-closed policy insufficient for the development gate:
the pinned QEMU does not expose `IA32_ARCH_CAPABILITIES`, so it cannot report
`RDCL_NO`. A generic hypervisor or vendor signature is not a substitute. QEMU
can use another accelerator, user configuration and later command-line options
can replace its CPU or machine, and a hostile virtual-machine monitor can spoof
CPUID. The gate needs a narrow statement about the controlled emulator it
started, not a claim that CPUID attests the host.

**Decision.** A process may be constructed with shared kernel mappings only
for one of two opaque reasons: an affirmative `RDCL_NO` in a described
architectural-capability word, or the exact QEMU TCG base tuple. The latter
requires the CPUID.1 hypervisor bit, maximum hypervisor leaf `0x40000001` and
the twelve-byte `TCGTCGTCG` signature. Missing capability evidence, VMware,
other hypervisors and every near match refuse. Positive `RDCL_NO` remains
sufficient regardless of environment.

The TCG reason is trusted local development configuration, not attestation and
not a hardware security claim. Every repository QEMU launch disables ambient
user configuration, selects `-accel tcg`, and exposes the hypervisor and
`tcg-cpuid` features in both normal and degraded CPU profiles. Interactive
arguments may still select displays, debuggers, devices and diagnostics, but
the runner rejects every CPU, machine, accelerator, global-property or config
file avenue that can replace the fixed profile, including long aliases and
machine-embedded accelerator selection. Legacy `-set` remains permitted
because it addresses an existing named QemuOpts group and cannot replace these
scalar machine, CPU or accelerator selections.

Boot evaluates the policy once and records a distinct admission state before
process construction. An accepted reason is logged; refusal leaves diagnostic
kernel service running but returns `NoSharedKernelIsolation` immediately after
the guarded-stack check and before page tables or any other process resource
exist. Automated QEMU success additionally requires exactly one exact
`qemu_tcg` log record, proving that the guest consumed the policy chosen by the
runner. It does not prove that an untrusted hypervisor told the truth.

**Alternatives.** Treating silence as `RDCL_NO` was rejected by D-91 and would
fail open on the processors that most need isolation. Refusing every silent
machine was rejected for the controlled TCG loop because it would remove all
ring-3 machine evidence without improving native-hardware safety. Accepting a
generic QEMU, VMware or hypervisor signature was rejected because those names
do not constrain the execution engine or CPU model. Inferring TCG solely from
the host command was rejected because later arguments and ambient config can
override it and because the guest must demonstrate that it reached the same
decision. KPTI is not silently waived: PW-706 triggers it before supported
native hardware without `RDCL_NO` may launch user programs.

**Evidence and consequences.** Pure host tests refuse an undescribed word, a
described zero word, the historical VMware tuple and every one-bit mutation of
all four QEMU tuple registers; they also prove that the hypervisor leaf is not
read without the hypervisor bit. Host runner tests pin every launch site,
reject all profile-changing aliases and config avenues, allow unrelated debug
arguments, and require the exact guest marker only for a passing verdict.
Each guard was broken once and its named host witness went red before
restoration. The machine check injects the production refusal, requires the
typed error, no syscall crossing and an unchanged resource ledger, then proves
the accepted state was restored. Its retained mutation and the current QEMU
and VMware observations remain PW-534; no boot result is invented here.

## D-251 Hardware observations mint exact, non-derivable authority — Status: Accepted (2026-08-30), amends D-188, D-205 and D-249; advances PW-130 and PW-213

**Context.** Pure `nvme::DmaState` claimed whether hardware was quiesced, and
the boot module converted a forgeable enum into permission to enable and route
external interrupts. Neither representation tied the permission to the device
whose register state supplied it.

**Decision.** Pure NVMe state records only reservation, publication,
